Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to Śrī Sarasvatī.
Om, salutations to that Brahman.
That single form which pervades the three worlds, seen clearly by yogis, and which the venerable ones call the state beyond the three qualities (guṇas)—
that, indeed, I am, whose nature is knowledge and liberation.
In every direction, I contemplate Brahman as possessing manifold power. ||1||

The son of Kṛṣṇadeva, the crest-jewel of the Haribhava family, has repeatedly revealed the essence of the Yogaśāstra for the benefit of those who bow before him, as elucidated by the lords of sages who know Brahman.
Bhavadeva writes for the prosperity of Satyavatī. ||2||

Truth is declared to be Brahman throughout the three worlds; the contemplation of that [truth] is likewise possessed by it, and that very [contemplation] is celebrated as "Brahman" by those of matured intellect who have attained prosperity.
Its essential nature is the light of the flame of the lamp of the Self, manifesting as pure consciousness alone.
The sages teach that very state as the supreme liberation.
Since the Lord Viṣṇu is described here as being endowed with *bhava*, the title of the work is revealed as *Yuktabhavadeva*. (4)
In the treatise named *Prajñāsatyavatī*, that meditation on Brahman which is taught is said to be achievable through yoga; therefore, "yoga" is what is being proclaimed here. (5)
In this context, yoga primarily consists of the cessation of the fluctuations of the internal organ.
Thus it is stated in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra]:
"Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
"Then the seer abides in its own nature"—this is the meaning. ||6||
The Self is of the nature of the direct realization of bliss existing at all times and in all places.

Its abiding in its own essential nature is the state of liberation, according to such scriptural passages as: "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss; that is the form of Brahman, and it is established in liberation. (7)

The mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) is a function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that has been shaped into the form of objects such as pots produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). In this state, due to the internal organ’s movement toward other objects, the condition of the Self’s direct realization of its own essential bliss (*svarūpānanda*) is lost; this alone is called bondage, because of the disappearance of the direct realization of the bliss of the state of liberation. ||8||
This was stated by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:

"Liberation is abiding in one's own true nature; its deviation is called bondage. And that mental modification (vṛtti) is threefold, being rooted in the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, and is distinguished by its respective effects. ||1||
And its effects have been described by Vyāsa and others:
"When sattva arises, there is happiness, tranquility, affection, modesty, lightness of limb, forgiveness, fortitude, lack of miserliness, self-control, knowledge, and clarity. (10)
Upon the arising of the quality of rajas, there is gain, distress, anger,
conflict, pride, falsehood, worldly activity, and even hypocrisy.
Upon the arising of the quality of darkness (tamas), there occurs lethargy, delusion, sleep, heaviness of the limbs, indolence, lack of discernment, negligence, and so forth. (12)
In the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti."
They bind the imperishable embodied self within the body, O mighty-armed one.
Among them, *sattva*, because of its purity, is illuminating and free from affliction; it binds, O sinless one, through attachment to happiness and attachment to knowledge. (14.5–14.6)
Know that *rajas* consists of passion, arising from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action.
(14.7) Know, however, that *tamas* arises from ignorance, deluding all embodied beings.
O Bhārata, it binds them through negligence, laziness, and sleep.
(14.8) Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, O Bhārata; but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence. (14.9), and so forth.

In this context, happiness is of two kinds: innate and that which arises from connection with sense objects. Of these, the former is the very nature of Brahman, produced by devotion to the Lord, and to be directly realized through His grace; it is worshipped day and night by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sanaka, Sanandana, Nārada, and others. ||18||

The second [type of happiness], however, which is produced by unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) born of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, is to be disregarded by those who have realized the bliss of Brahman; because it is permeated by suffering and demerit, it is like eating food mixed with honey and poison, and is thus ignored by the discerning, while being pursued according to their capacity by the undiscerning. The superiority of the bliss of Brahman over sensual pleasure is indeed well known. (19)
Likewise, in the *Bhāgavata*, the Blessed One replied to Uddhava:
"O bull among men, those persons whose intellects are deluded by my māyā... [BhP 11.14.8–14]... [and so forth].
They declare that the highest good is non-absolutistic, according to one's karma and according to one's inclination. ||20||
Some speak of Dharma, others of fame; some of desire, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility; others indeed speak of their own interest, sovereignty, renunciation, and enjoyment. (21)
Some [practitioners] perform sacrifices, austerity, charity, vows, observances, and restraints;
yet for them, the worlds fashioned by karma have both a beginning and an end. (22)

Those whose end is suffering, who are rooted in darkness, whose joy is trivial, and who are consumed by grief— how could that bliss which belongs to one who has offered their self to Me, who is established in truth and indifferent to everything else, ever belong to those whose minds are fixed on sense objects? (23)
For one who possesses nothing, who is self-controlled, tranquil, and even-minded, whose mind is contented with me—every direction is filled with happiness. 24.
"Neither the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the netherworlds;
neither the perfection of yoga nor even liberation from rebirth—one whose self is dedicated to Me desires nothing other than Me. (25) And so forth.
The Upaniṣad also says:
"He who among men is successful and prosperous, a lord over others, and most fully endowed with all human desires. (26)

Having stated that this is the supreme bliss of human beings, he declares the bliss of the ancestors to be a hundredfold that; the bliss of the gods by action (karmadeva) to be a hundredfold that; the bliss of the gods by birth (ājātadeva) to be a hundredfold that; the bliss in the world of the gods (devaloka) to be a hundredfold that; the bliss in the world of the Gandharvas to be a hundredfold that; and the bliss in the world of Prajāpati to be a hundredfold that. ||27||

Now, these hundred joys that exist in the world of Prajāpati constitute one joy in the world of Brahman—[the joy] of one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from blemish (*vṛjinah*), and untouched by desire (*kāmahata*), and so forth. ||28||
If a person were to know the Self, thinking "I am this," what would he desire, for the sake of what longing, that he should wander about following after the body? [BāU 4.4.12; PD 14.5]

Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through celibacy, sacrifice, austerity, faith, and fasting. Having known this very Self, one becomes a sage (*muni*). Desiring this world alone, wandering mendicants go forth into the life of renunciation. This, indeed, they have always said. 30.

"In former times, learned and wise Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas did not desire offspring, saying: 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is the world? They, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wives, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, wandered about as mendicants," and so forth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)

Therefore, it is with this intention that the nature of the Self is described as happiness free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). [The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad states: "Sons are not dear for the sake of the son; rather, sons are dear for the sake of the Self. Such descriptions of other things as being conditioned by the Self (*ātmaupādhika*) are merely illustrative. //32//

Therefore, one should restrain the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), as it is opposed to the direct realization of the supreme bliss that is the very nature of Brahman. In this regard, this self-realization—which is preceded by the restraint of all activities of the internal organ—is itself non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), because of the constant absence of conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*). And that alone is *rājayoga*. 33.

Because it is a yoga that is supremely desirable and accomplished without effort, and because of the primacy of the eightfold yoga beginning with *yama*, there is the conceptual (*savikalpa*) samādhi, which is its most intimate internal state and consists of the direct realization of the self as free from conceptual construction. ||34||

When the causal complex for qualified cognition—such as the cognition of qualifiers and so forth—is eclipsed by bliss arising through the power of that practice, the direct realization of the self as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) manifests of its own accord; this has been explained at length in the *Prajñā-satyavatī*. Furthermore, this [realization] arises from the practice of knowledge concerning the self and from the practice of dispassion (*vairāgya*). Likewise, it occurs precisely when there is one-pointedness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). (35)
And so it is said in the Gītā:
"By practice and by dispassion, O son of Kuntī, it is grasped" (6.35cd). || 36 ||
In the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra] as well—[1.12–16]:

"Their cessation is achieved through practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). Practice is the effort toward stability therein. Therein, when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion, it becomes firmly grounded. Dispassion is the mastery of one who is free from craving for objects seen or heard of in tradition. That which follows is the absence of craving for the *guṇas* due to the discernment of the *puruṣa*. (37) And so forth.

Thus, for the yogin seated in a comfortable posture in a place free from disturbances and fixing the mind upon the Self, four obstacles arise in Rājayoga. These are: lethargy (laya), distraction (vikṣepa), impurity (kaṣāya), and relishing the taste [of meditative states] (rasāsvāda). [38] (= Vedāntasāra 212)

Laya (dissolution) is the state of the mental fluctuations [resulting] from the non-support of the undivided reality, namely sleep. Vikṣepa (distraction), however, is the mental fluctuation’s support of something else while not supporting the undivided reality. Kaṣāya (impurity), moreover, is the failure to support the undivided reality due to the mind’s becoming stagnant through the latent impressions of passion and so forth, even in the absence of dissolution and distraction. (39)

The tasting of flavor (*rasāsvāda*), however, is the savouring of a conceptualized flavor by the mental modification even when there is no support for the undivided reality. When the mind, free from these four obstacles, remains unmoving like a lamp in a windless place and abides as nothing but the bliss of undivided consciousness, then *rājayoga* is accomplished.
As it has been said:
"One should awaken the mind during dissolution and again pacify it when it is distracted."
One should recognize that which is accompanied by passion; when equanimity is attained, one should not disturb it.
One should not relish the flavor therein, but become detached through wisdom.
Like a lamp standing in a windless place that does not flicker—this is the simile taught. Thus it is said. (Also quoted in the *Vedāntasāra*).
In the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra] as well—[1.30–32, 23, 25, 27, 28, 29]:

"Illness, languor, doubt, carelessness, indolence, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these distractions are the obstacles. Pain, mental distress, trembling of the limbs, and irregular breathing are concomitants of distraction. To prevent these, one should practice concentration on a single principle, or through devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*). In that regard, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed. His designator is the sacred syllable *praṇava*; the designated is the Lord. [The practice consists of] the repetition of the *praṇava* and meditation upon its meaning."
Thence follows the realization of the inward-turned consciousness, as well as the absence of obstacles.
The Gītā also says (6.24–32):
"Having abandoned all desires born of volition without exception, and having fully restrained the collection of the senses by the mind alone... (44)
One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all. ||45||
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone. 46.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from blemish. 47.
Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogi, freed from all taint, easily attains the infinite bliss that is the touch of Brahman. ||48||
One whose self is disciplined by yoga sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he perceives the same everywhere.
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me, for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me. ||50||
The yogi who, established in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all beings— whatever his mode of conduct— he abides in me. [51]
"O Arjuna, he who, by comparison with himself, sees everywhere the same—whether it be happiness or suffering—that yogi is considered supreme. (52) And so forth.
The Śruti also says (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23):
"This has been declared by a Ṛk verse:
'This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. Having known that path of his very Self, he is not tainted by evil action. (53)

Therefore, one who knows this, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and possessed of faith, should see the Self alone within the self; he should see everything thus. He becomes the Self of all and crosses over all evil. Evil does not cross over him; he leads across all evil, and evil does not lead him away. Free from evil, free from stain, free from old age, free from thirst, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa—he who knows this. Thus [ends section 54].
Concerning the King of Yogas, in the Kulārṇava, the venerable Śiva said:
"Now I shall explain Yoga, which directly bestows pure consciousness, [attained] through a mind joined with the non-duality of the individual soul and the Supreme Self. (55)
Yoga, however, should be understood as that which arises from meditating upon the deity.

Meditation (dhyāna), however, is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross (sthūla) and subtle (sūkṣma). That which possesses form (sākāra) is called gross, while that which is formless (nirākāra) is subtle.
Some declare that gross meditation is for the sake of stabilizing the mind.
If the mind becomes motionless with respect to the gross, it will be well-established in the subtle—the Supreme Lord who is devoid of hands, feet, belly, eyes, and so forth. //58//
One should meditate upon that which consists of all splendor, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
it neither rises nor sets, it neither increases nor undergoes decay. (59)
It shines by itself and then illuminates other things without any external means;
it is never-setting, consisting of light, pure existence, and beyond the reach of words; that knowledge, which is to be realized by the self alone, is designated as Brahman. (60)

With the movement of the vital breaths completely ceased, as motionless as a stone, the yogi who knows the vital point of the identity of the supreme Self and the individual soul is called a knower of yoga. [Or: who knows the single abode of the supreme Self and the individual soul?
He remains like a calm ocean, manifesting only that which is the ultimate reality.
That meditation which is devoid of its own objective form is prescribed as *samādhi*. ||62||
Simply by not thinking of anything at all, reality itself is revealed;
when reality is revealed by itself, one becomes identical with it in that very instant. //63//
He who remains like one asleep even during the states of dreaming and waking, and is devoid of inhalation and exhalation—he is certainly liberated. (64)

With the collection of his sense organs rendered motionless, and with the mind—along with its vital breath—dissolved into his own Self, he who remains as if dead is called one truly liberated while living. 65.
He does not hear, nor does he smell; he is not terrified, nor does he see; he does not touch, nor does he know pleasure or pain, nor does the mind form conceptual constructions. [66]
He does not conceive of anything, nor does he perceive anything, like a piece of wood;
one whose self is thus dissolved in Śiva is said here to be established in samādhi.

Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, so too is the relationship between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). ||68||
Just as an insect becomes a bee through the power of meditation, so too may a human being become one with the form of Brahmā through the power of samādhi. 69.

Just as butter produced from milk, when thrown back into it, is no longer as it was before, so too here the self becomes distinct through the practice of the qualities (guṇas). [The self] would be [distinct] from the qualities;
just as one standing in dense darkness sees nothing at all.
Likewise, the yogi who is without mind does not perceive conceptual proliferation at all. ||71||

Just as one does not perceive conceptual proliferation at the time of closing the eyes, so too it should be at the time of opening them; this is the defining characteristic of meditative absorption. //72//
Just as a person perceives the itching of his own body,
so too does he who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman perceive the entire activity of the universe.
But when the supreme reality—transcending all phonemes and indeed changeless—is known, the mantras, together with the lords of mantras, truly become its servants. (74)
For one who is established in the singular state of the Self, whatever movement there is, that is worship;
whatever speech there is, that is mantra; and whatever looking there is, that is meditation. When the identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is realized— ||75|| [sanmantras?]
Wherever the mind goes, there are concentrations. ||76||
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (77)
When the Lord of Yogins attained that stainless, supreme state, it surpassed even the status of the gods and asuras which had been attained [by others]. (78)
He who perceives the all-pervading, peaceful, blissful, and imperishable Self—for him, nothing remains to be attained or known. (79)
Once the Supreme Brahman is realized, all restrictive observances are superfluous;
what need is there for a palm-leaf fan when the breeze from the Malaya mountains has been obtained? (80)
For those who perceive the Self within themselves, there is no binding of the hair-tuft, nor indeed any binding of the nose; there is neither restraint (yama) nor observance (niyama). ||81||
If one should perform self-reflection for even a moment, thinking "I am Brahman," that would destroy all sin, just as the rising sun destroys darkness. (82)
The knower of reality obtains that fruit which is multiplied ten millionfold in [the performance of] vows, sacrifices, asceticism, pilgrimages, giving, worship of the gods, and so forth. || 83 ||
The supreme state is the coemergent (sahaja); the middling is meditative concentration and dhāraṇī;
recitation and praise are the inferior; and fire-offering and worship are the most inferior. (84)
Reflection on reality is supreme; reflection on recitation is middling; reflection on the scriptures is to be known as inferior; and reflection on worldly affairs is the lowest of the low. (85)
A hymn of praise yields the fruit of ten million offerings; recitation yields the fruit of ten million hymns;
meditation yields the fruit of ten million recitations; and absorption yields the fruit of ten million meditations.
There is nothing higher than absorption; that is the ultimate goal, that is the supreme state. (86)
Indeed, there is no mantra higher than the Nāda; no deity is other than one's own Self.
There is no worship higher than contemplative integration (anusandhi), and no fruit greater than satisfaction. 87.
Without the twilight prayers and mantra-water, without recitations, fire-oblations, and austerity, and without ritual services, the yogi should constantly perform worship. 88.
The body is declared to be the temple, and the living soul is the deity, Sadāśiva.
One should discard the flower-offering of ignorance and contemplate [the deity] through the sense of "I am He. (89)
The individual soul (jīva) is Śiva; Śiva is the individual soul. That soul is Śiva alone when liberated from bonds; bound by bonds, it is known as the jīva, and freed from bonds, it is Sadāśiva.
The God resides in the sacrificial fire for the Brahmins, in the heart for the wise,
in an image for those of small intellect, and everywhere for those who have realized the Self.
He who remains equanimous toward objects such as blame and praise, cold and heat, pleasure and pain, is indeed a lord of yogis, free from both joy and dejection. (92)
Free from desire, eternally contented, viewing all with equanimity, and having conquered the senses,
that yogi who knows the supreme state dwells in the body like a traveler in a lodging.
Just as those who are lame, blind, deaf, impotent, mute, or dull-witted dwell here in this world, so too does the yogin who knows reality. || 94 ||
For yogis who perceive reality, there is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither merit nor sin, neither heaven nor hell. (95)
Just as one endowed with the power of mantras is not seen while playing with snakes,
so too the yogin is not seen while playing with the serpents of the senses. 96.
Just as the sun moves everywhere and just as fire consumes everything, so the yogi, having enjoyed all pleasures, is not defiled by sins. //97//
Just as this world laughs, loathes, and reviles,
and turns away upon seeing one from afar, so does the yogi conduct himself.
Like the wind that touches all things, and like the sky that pervades every limb.

Just as all those who have bathed in a river are pure, so too is the yogin always pure. (99) [KA 9.77] Just as water that has reached a village becomes pure when joined with a river, so too food from the house of a *mleccha* is pure when placed in the hand of a yogin. (100) [KA 9.78]
Whether one is wise or ignorant, as long as the body is sustained,
the conduct of the castes and stages of life must be performed for the sake of liberation from karma.
Once ignorance has been uprooted by knowledge through action, one attains the state of Śiva.

Liberation consists in the state of oneness with Śiva; therefore, one should perform ritual action (karman). One who desires happiness in this world and the next should perform blameless actions and avoid blameworthy ones, for otherwise he will certainly become like a pillar in his own throat. ||102–103||
It is not possible for one who possesses a body to abandon all actions;
rather, the yogi should renounce the fruit of action—he is called a renouncer. (104)
He who acts by setting aside the sense of "I," reflecting that it is the instruments that engage in their respective functions, is not defiled. (105)
Actions performed immediately after the attainment of knowledge do not touch the knower of reality in this world, just as water does not touch a lotus leaf.
In the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Śāntiparvan* of the *Mahābhārata* (12.289.11–12, 19–21, 56–61):

"Having severed through yoga these five defects—namely, passion (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), attachment (*sneha*), desire (*kāma*), and anger (*krodha*) as the fifth—they then attain that [state]. (107)
Just as large fish, having broken through the net, reach the water once more, so too do those whose impurities have been removed reach that state through yoga.
Just as a small fire, O King, is extinguished when it is weak, even if supplied with large logs of fuel, so too is yoga ineffective when it lacks strength, O Lord. (109)
And when that very fire, O King, has regained its strength once more and is joined by its friend the wind, it may swiftly consume even the entire earth.
In the same way, a yogi who has attained power, blazing with splendor and possessed of great strength, may dry up the entire world like the sun at the time of the end. ||111||
But he who, O son of Kuntī, abides in the concentrations according to the rule,
abandons death, birth, suffering, and pleasure.
This which has been established in various scriptures and proclaimed among yogas as the supreme task of yoga is certain among the twice-born. (113)

For that supreme [state], O Great-souled One, consists of Brahman; it includes Brahmā the Lord, Viṣṇu the giver of boons, Bhava, Dharma, and Ṣaḍānana, as well as those illustrious sons of Brahmā. (114)

And darkness (tamas) which is painful and very great, and passion (rajas), and pure goodness (sattva), and the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), and the goddess Siddhi, the wife of Varuṇa, and all splendor (tejas) and very great fortitude (dhairya). ||115||
He indeed beheld the stainless lord of stars together with the constellations; all the gods, serpents, and ancestors;
all the mountains and the formidable oceans; all the rivers, forests, and nagas. ||116||

Having reached one another—the Rākṣasas, the flocks of birds, the quarters of space, the hosts of Gandharvas, men, and women—the great-souled yogin, being liberated, enters that Great One before long. 117.
Likewise—(Mahābhārata 12.289.25–41):
"Neither Yama, nor Antaka when enraged, nor Death of terrible prowess, O King, have power over one who possesses yoga and immeasurable splendor. (118)
O bull of the Bharatas, having attained power through yoga, one may create many thousands of selves and traverse the earth with all of them.
He may enjoy sense objects through some means, yet again he should perform fierce austerity;
and once more, like the brilliance of the sun, he should withdraw those [objects] as well as the qualities.
O King, there is no doubt that for a yoga established in strength and mastery over its own bonds, there is sovereign power both in binding and in liberation. ||121||
O lord of the people, these powers attained through yoga have been described by me; furthermore, I shall speak again to you of the subtle ones for the sake of illustration.
O Lord, one should be vigilant regarding the stabilization of the self or the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), just as a focused archer strikes his target with precision. ||123||
Likewise, the yogi who is properly disciplined attains liberation without a doubt, having fixed his mind immovably upon the vessel filled with oil. (124)
Just as a man with a concentrated mind ascends a staircase at night,
so too this yoga, when applied, O King, makes the self steady and causes the self to appear like the sun.
And just as a focused helmsman, O son of Kuntī, would swiftly lead a ship upon the great ocean, O best of kings; 126.
In that same way, O King, the knower of reality, having joined himself in self-concentration through yoga, attains the difficult-to-reach state after casting off this body.
And just as a charioteer, having yoked excellent horses, being well-composed, quickly leads the archer to the desired place, O bull among men. ||128||
In the same way, O King, the yogi who is concentrated in the dhāraṇās quickly attains the supreme state, just as a released arrow reaches its target. ||129||
The yogin who, having absorbed the self into the Self, remains immovable,
destroys the sins of his predecessors and attains the ageless state.
In the navel, the throat, and the head; in the heart, the chest, and the two sides;
and likewise in the eyes, the sense of touch, and the nose—[the Lord of] immeasurable prowess [is present].
The yogi who, devoted to the great vow, being composed, correctly perceives the subtle self by means of the self within these locations—
he, having quickly burned away auspicious and inauspicious karma that is like a mountain, [attains liberation].
By resorting to the supreme yoga, if one so desires, one is liberated.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, by consuming what kinds of food and by conquering what things does a yogin attain power? You ought to explain that. (134)
Bhīṣma said:
O Bhārata, a yogi who is intent on eating grain-husks and oil-cakes, and who is devoted to abstaining from all oily substances, shall attain strength. ||135||
O subduer of enemies, by eating dry barley-gruel for a long time, the yogi who delights in solitude and whose self is purified shall attain strength. ||136||
Having drunk water mixed with milk for fortnights, months, seasons, days, years, and likewise for [longer periods], the yogi shall attain strength. ||137||
Or, O lord of men, by fasting continuously for an entire month, the yogi, having thoroughly purified his soul, shall attain strength. ||138||
Having conquered desire as well as anger, cold and heat, rain, touch, and likewise sleep which is so difficult to overcome, O best of kings. (139)
These great-souled ones, free from passion and possessed of great wisdom, illuminate the subtle self by means of the self through the perfection of meditation and study.
But this path of wise Brahmins is considered difficult;
indeed, O bull among the Bharatas, no one travels upon it with ease. (1.141)
Just as someone might enter a terrible forest, abounding in snakes and reptiles, full of chasms, devoid of water, difficult to traverse, and thick with thorns; ||142||
Likewise, whatever twice-born man may travel upon the path of yoga, he might fall away from that path with safety; for it is remembered as being full of many dangers.
O Lord of the Earth, it is easier to stand upon the sharpened edges of razors than for those of undisciplined mind to remain steady in the concentrations of yoga. 144.
O dear one, O King, failed retentions do not lead to an auspicious rebirth, just as boats lacking a pilot do not carry men across the ocean.
Likewise (MBh 12.290.54–55):
"Desire, anger, fear, sleep, and the fifth is said to be breath—these defects are seen in the bodies of all embodied beings. (146)
They cut off anger through patience, desire by abandoning conceptualization, sleep by attending to living beings, and likewise fear through heedfulness;
they cut off the fifth, breath, by means of moderate eating, O King. Thus it is said, and so forth.
Likewise, regarding the yogin who is common to both Sāṅkhya knowledge and yoga, it is stated in that very same context for the sake of investigation:
"For that which is accepted by the learned should be grasped by those of their kind who are esteemed by the learned."
The Yoga practitioners hold that the cow is directly perceptible, while the Sāṃkhya followers have their conclusions determined by scripture.
O King, both these views are considered true and are approved by the learned.
When practiced according to the scriptures, these two lead one to the supreme goal.
O sinless one, purity is equally enjoined for both, as is compassion toward all beings;
their observance of vows is equal, and their philosophical vision is the same. (150)
Listen to this subtle teaching of mine from the Sāṅkhyas who have realized the Self—a doctrine ordained by all the lords among ascetics, beginning with Kapila. (151)
O bull among men, in whom no delusions whatsoever are seen, and in whom there are many virtues along with the total elimination of faults. (152)
O King, having thoroughly examined with wisdom all human objects of sense which are full of defects and difficult to conquer, as well as the objects of the Piśācas, [one should renounce them]. (153)

Having understood the domains of the Rākṣasas and likewise the domains of the Yakṣas; having understood the domains of kings and likewise the domains of the Brahman-sages; and having understood the domains of the Nāgas and likewise the domains of the Gandharvas. ||154||
Having understood the domains of the ancestors who wander among the animals, O King, and likewise having understood the domains of the Suparṇas and the Maruts; ||155||
Having understood the domains of the Asuras as well as those of the Vaiśvadevas, and having understood the domains of the divine sages (devarṣis) as well as the lords of the yogas; ||156||
The domains of the Prajāpatis, as well as the domains of Brahmā.
And having understood the supreme duration of life in this world according to reality, O best of beings.

O best among speakers, having understood the supreme reality of happiness, as well as the constant suffering that arises for those who seek sense objects when the time [for its attainment] has arrived; 158.
O Bhārata, [he understands] the suffering of those falling into the animal realm and that which occurs upon falling into hell, as well as all the virtues and all the defects of heaven.

O King, whatever faults there are in the Vedic doctrines, and whatever virtues belong to the Vedas; whatever faults there are in the yoga of knowledge, and whatever virtues there are in [the practice of] yoga.
Having known sattva to have ten qualities, and likewise rajas to have nine qualities, and having known tamas to have eight qualities, as well as buddhi to have seven qualities; ||161||
Having known space as having six qualities, and likewise space as having five qualities;
having known the intellect as having four qualities, and likewise darkness as having three qualities; ||162||
Having understood that rajas is twofold and sattva is once more singlefold,
and having truly discerned the path as well as the state of dissolution, [he attains liberation].
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, and cultivated by auspicious causes,
those who are subtle attain auspicious liberation, which here is like the supreme ether.
The eye is joined with form, the nose with the quality of fragrance, the ear is likewise attached to sound, and the tongue to the qualities of taste. ||165||
[He saw] the skin attached to touch, the wind resting in space, delusion clinging to darkness, and greed residing in objects of sense. ||166||
They are dependent upon Viṣṇu in his stride, Śakra in his strength, Agni attached to the stomach, the Goddess in the waters, and likewise the Moon residing in the luster. [167]
Fire is attached to air, and air is supported by space; space is joined with the mind, and the mind is dependent upon the intellect. ||168||
Rajas is likewise attached to sattva, sattva is attached to the self (ātman), and the self is attached to the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa. ||169||
The Lord is attached to liberation, yet He is not attached to liberation anywhere;
likewise, all the senses and the objects of the senses are dependent upon the Self.
And having understood, according to the scriptures, the difficulty of attaining liberation, one should understand in its true nature the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna breaths.
Then, O scorcher of foes, having understood the wind below and the Pravaha wind that was set in motion, as well as the seven winds and the royal sages, he [proceeded].
O King, having seen the great celestial rishis and other great rishis, who were as radiant as the sun, fallen from their sovereign power after a long period of time; 173.
O King, having heard of the destruction of great multitudes of beings and having understood the inauspicious destiny of those who perform evil deeds, O ruler of men.
And likewise the suffering of those fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river in the abode of Yama, as well as the impure transmigrations within various wombs.
And one dwells in the foul belly, that vessel of blood and fluids, filled with phlegm, urine, and excrement, and endowed with a pungent stench. ||176||
Likewise, in this impure city with its nine gates, which is a mass of semen and blood, held together by marrow and sinews, and strewn with hundreds of veins. (177)

O King, having recognized yourself as one who has failed to achieve the goal, as well as the various types of yoga belonging to those beings of a tamasic nature whose souls are ruined despite their pursuit of pleasure.
Likewise, having seen terrible portents, as well as the loss of the moon's luster, the falling of stars, and the displacement of the constellations; ||179||
O King, having understood the separation of couples and having seen the miserable mutual devouring of living beings, as well as their inauspiciousness; (180)
Having recognized delusion in childhood and the impurity of the body's decay, when passion and delusion arise, he remains established in some degree of goodness. ||181||
Among thousands of men, perhaps one individual takes refuge in the intellect of liberation,
having understood through the sacred scriptures the extreme rarity of liberation.
Furthermore, O King, having understood the wicked nature of sense objects, and having seen, O son of Kuntī, the inauspicious bodies of those whose life-breaths have departed; ||183||

O Bhārata, having understood that dwelling among families is a source of suffering for living beings, and having known the most dreadful fate of those who have fallen, such as the slayers of Brahmins; ||184||
Having understood the inauspicious destiny of those evil-minded Brahmins who were addicted to drinking liquor and devoted to the wives of their gurus, [he spoke]. (185)
By means of that knowledge, men existing in the worlds together with the gods, having understood the destiny of those who perform unwholesome deeds, [attain liberation].
Having seen the rising of the oceans and likewise their subsequent ebbing, and having seen the decline of wealth and its subsequent increase once again; ||187||
Having observed the destruction of unions, and especially that of the ages (yugas), and having likewise seen old age, death, birth, and indeed all sufferings; ||188||
Having thus understood the defects of the body and their suffering in accordance with reality,
and likewise having understood all the defects of the self residing within the self, and knowing them to have arisen from one's own body, one should take refuge in Sāṅkhya and Yoga. ||189||
Likewise, [he sees] this world, which arises from the foam of the waters, enveloped by hundreds of Viṣṇu’s illusions; it resembles a wall of the mind, devoid of essence, and purposeless. (190)
Having seen that darkness resembles a chasm, like bubbles in the rain, consisting mostly of destruction, devoid of happiness, followed by further ruin, and ending in non-existence; ||191||
O King, the highly wise followers of Sāṃkhya, having abandoned affection for their offspring, [abandoned you] who were submerged in passion and darkness like a helpless elephant in the mud. (192)

O King, by means of the pervasive and great Sāṃkhya consisting of knowledge and the knowable, [one abandons] inauspicious royal fragrances as well as those of a similar nature belonging to darkness (tamas). ||193||
O Bhārata, having swiftly severed with the weapon of knowledge and the staff of austerity those meritorious and pure fragrances born of touch that arise from the body, [one attains liberation].
Then [he saw] the terrible ocean of suffering, a vast lake of anxiety and grief, with disease and death as its great crocodiles and great fear as its mighty serpent. (195)

O subduer of enemies, cross once more with wisdom the darkness that is like a tortoise and the passion that is like a fish, as well as the mire of affection and the difficult passage of old age, by means of the lamp of knowledge.

The ocean of karma has actions as its unfathomable depths, truth as its shore, the steadfastness of vows as its moon, violence as its swift and great current, and it is a mine of various flavors. ||197||
It is a great jewel of manifold delights, a wind for the fever of suffering, a great whirlpool of grief and craving, and a massive elephant of intense disease. ||198||
O subduer of enemies, it was a terrifying sight: a mass of piled-up bones, with phlegm for its foam, a mine of pearls for its gifts, and pools of blood for its coral. (199)

Resounding with the noise of laughter and cries, exceedingly difficult to cross due to various forms of ignorance, salted with the brine of tears from weeping, and dedicated to the renunciation of attachments. ||200||
It has non-violence and truth as its shores, the sacrifice of life as its great waves, the Vedānta as its island, and compassion for all beings as its ocean. ||201||
O Bhārata, perfected ascetics cross the ocean of the submarine fire— the realm where liberation is difficult to attain— by means of the source that is knowledge.
Having crossed over birth, which is difficult to traverse, they enter the stainless sky;
then the sun carries those honored followers of Sāṃkhya by means of its rays.
O King, O Bhārata, the flowing wind there, moving like the fibers of a lotus stalk, receives those objects of sense, having entered them. 204.
O Bhārata, [a wind] that is subtle, cool, fragrant, and pleasant to the touch blew upon the ascetics who were free from passion, perfected, endowed with vigor, and rich in austerity.
O son of Kuntī, he who goes to the auspicious worlds as the foremost of the seven Maruts carries them to the highest goal beyond the sky.
O Indra among kings, space carries darkness as its supreme goal; O Lord of the world, darkness carries passion as its supreme goal. (207)
O Indra among kings, *rajas* carries the *sattva* to its supreme state;
O pure-souled one, *sattva* carries [the self] to the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
The pure-souled Lord carries [the self] to the highest state of the Supreme Self.
Indeed, for those who delight in truth and uprightness, and who possess compassion for all living beings. ||209||

Therefore, this is the meaning established by all the Śrutis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Yoga-śāstras: having sat upon a comfortable seat when possible, or remaining in whatever posture is suitable, one who is free from the defects of passion, hatred, anger, greed, delusion, sleep, shame, fear, and so forth, should fix the mind upon Brahman—the nature of which is consciousness and bliss, existing throughout all directions and times—by means of the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana). || 210 ||

And if that mind, under the influence of past latent impressions (vāsanā) such as desire and anger, goes toward objects corresponding to them, then one should diligently withdraw it from those [objects] by means of reflecting upon their defects and reflecting upon the qualities of the mind fixed on Brahman, and establish it in Brahman. ||211||

When practice is conducted in this manner and evil deeds, negative tendencies, and the like are being exhausted, the Blessed Lord Śrī Puruṣottama becomes gracious; likewise, a specific supreme bliss whose nature is Brahman manifests, such that the mind itself becomes steady, like a pauper who has discovered a great treasure, and the great yogic perfections (mahāyoga-siddhis) appear. ||212||

And they have been described in the *Siddhisaubhāgyavatī* as being produced by specific types of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) corresponding to them. Although these are difficult for other yogins to attain, they become extremely easy to obtain through the grace of the Great Lord of Yoga. ||213||

When enjoyed with excessive attachment, they become obstacles to the great fruit of all yoga, which consists of the non-conceptual direct realization of Brahman; therefore, they should be contemplated by great yogis—whose minds are attached to Brahman—only out of curiosity, as if they were a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). Enough of this prolixity. ||214||
And so Gorakṣanātha says: [Vivekamārtaṇḍa 1] "This is the staircase to liberation; this is the deception of Time:
that the mind has turned away from enjoyment and is attached to the Supreme Self. (215)
In the *Bhāgavatam*, the Blessed One said to Uddhava:
"Whatever perfections are attained here through birth, herbs, austerity, or mantras—all those one attains through yoga; one cannot reach the goal of yoga by other means. (Bhāg. Pu. 11.15.34)

Yogis declare these to be obstacles to the perfection of yoga; for one who is attaining union with Me, they are causes for the wasting away of time. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.15.33) Also in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra 3.37]:

"Upon being invited by those who occupy [celestial] stations, one should not feel astonishment," and so forth. When there is an invitation from those who occupy specific stations—such as gods and others who hold office in their respective realms—in the form: "Come here! Begin here! Here is the collection of objects of enjoyment for you, such as garlands, sandalwood, and women, acquired through your merit," one should not manifest astonishment or pride. (218)

"But may it be well with you; we shall accomplish our own task"—by saying this, the intended meaning is that one's own task consists precisely in the concentration of the mind upon Brahman (*brahmamanodhāraṇā*). And this yoga arises from the abandonment of volitional thought and doubt (*saṅkalpa-vikalpa*); and that abandonment results from the abandonment of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). ||219||
Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is defined as follows:

egoism is the determinative cognition "I am this" and so forth. And it is fourfold: having the mere body as its object; having the subtle consciousness residing within the body as its object; having everything as its object; and having the void (*śūnya*) as its object. ||220||

In this regard, that which brings about *saṃsāra* through passion (*rāga*) and other afflictions by way of attachment to mother, father, and so forth—though it is threefold, being divided into the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types according to such attachments to mother, father, and others—it must be abandoned by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because it generates volitional constructions (*saṅkalpa*) and the like. (221)

Furthermore, the other three [qualities] are purely *sāttvika* because they produce happiness and clarity; because they do not generate attachment, aversion, and so forth, as their objects involve a distinct relationship; and because they serve as the cause for liberation preceded by the attainment of sovereignty. Likewise, they are to be cultivated through practice by those seeking liberation. 222.
Thus it is said in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha* (5.17.14–15):
"O Rāma, the singular conviction that 'I am this body from head to foot, fashioned by my father and mother,' leads to bondage through the perception of what is unreal."
"I am more subtle than the tip of a hair, transcending all existing things. (223)
A second resolve for liberation arises in the virtuous.
Of the Naiyāyikas and others.
I am the very self of all things in the web of the world; I alone am imperishable.
O best of the Raghus, this third certainty is likewise for liberation alone:
"This world is unreal, void, and always like an empty illusion"— as it was said by our gurus.
In this very way, even the fourth certainty leads to the accomplishment of yoga.
Likewise, for those practitioners of emptiness, it is said that the first of these is characterized by a craving that is fit for bondage.
The three pure cravings are clear, like the playful sport of one liberated while living.
(226) O Great-minded One, that certainty which holds "I alone am all this"—taking hold of that, my mind no longer enters into dispute; it no longer gives rise to despair. (227)
It is said that "Māyā is the nature of emptiness" and also "the realization of Brahman";
Śiva, Puruṣa, Īśāna, and Nitya are called the Self (Ātman). ||228||
Through the playful manifestation of the world via the emergence of duality and non-duality, the power consisting of the Supreme Self unfolds as nothing but non-duality itself. (229)

Taking as his object the state that transcends all, with a mind like the full moon, consisting entirely of the one perfect consciousness, neither agitated nor overly delighted, he does not sink in saṃsāra. ||230||

The first abandonment of egoism is also twofold: that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*) and that which is to be known (*jñeya*). Among these, when one has contemplated that there is no specific relationship whatsoever between the self and objects such as the body, the abandonment of egoism in the form of a particular latent impression (*vāsanā*) belonging to one who performs actions with ease through an intellect free from attachment and aversion—that is called "that which is to be meditated upon" (*dhyeya*). ||231||

This is called *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living). Just as in the case of Śrī Rāma, Janaka, Vasiṣṭha, Śuka, and others, when a yogi—by means of an intellect free from duality—having abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and having forgotten the threefold body according to its divisions into gross, subtle, and causal, relinquishes [the body], that is called the supreme liberation known as *jñeyamukti*. ||232||
It is said in that very same work (Yogavāsiṣṭha 5.16):
"I belong to these objects, and these are my life."
I am nothing without these, nor indeed are they without me. (233)
Having thus abandoned that conviction and reflected with the mind, when one has cultivated the realization: "I am not the object, nor does the object belong to me. (234)

For one who performs actions with ease through an internally cooled intellect, that which is truly the abandonment of latent tendencies (vāsanā) is celebrated by the name "the object of meditation" (dhyeya). //235//

When, by means of an all-encompassing intellect, one effects the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) and, being free from the mind, abandons the body—this is to be known as the destruction of latent impressions. ||236||
He who, having effortlessly abandoned the latent impression consisting of the ego, remains as one who has renounced all objects of meditation, is called liberated while living. ||237||

O descendant of Raghu, know that he who has attained tranquility by abandoning the latent impressions along with their very roots—that which consists of the relinquishing of all objects of knowledge—is truly liberated. 238.
O Rāghava, these two types of renunciation are equal and established in the state of liberation;
both have attained the nature of Brahman, and both are free from the fever of worldly distress.
He who neither rejoices nor withers when pleasure and pain fall upon him incessantly and according to their time is said to be liberated. (240)

Thus, having performed the renunciation of the name of the object of meditation for the first ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), one should practice the triad of the subsequent ego-senses. One should contemplate the pure mind—or rather, that which is worshipped as pure—everywhere, at all times, and in every form; for consciousness itself, when delimited by the ego-sense, takes the form of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). (241)

Unconditioned, she is the nature of the Supreme Self; what need is there for further elaboration? She herself, when conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and other factors assuming the forms of jars and so forth, consists of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in the form of jars and the like. When uninterrupted by such modifications (vṛtti) as ignorance (avidyā) or illusion (māyā), she is designated by terms such as "knowledge" (vidyā), "the principle of consciousness" (tattva), "direct realization" (sākṣātkāra), "royal yoga" (rājayoga), and "liberation" (mukti). ||242||
Thus it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
when questioned by Bali as to who he was, who he was, or what the nature of the world was, Śukra replied to him:
"Know, indeed, that there is only this one pure consciousness; and this is composed of consciousness alone—for here, only consciousness exists."
"Consciousness is you, consciousness is I, and these worlds are consciousness"—this is the summary.
(243) If you are capable, then by this certainty you shall attain everything; if not, then even though much has been spoken, it is as if an oblation were poured into ashes for you. (244)
The cognition of the object of consciousness is bondage; its cessation is called liberation.
Consciousness is indeed the unobjectifiable Self—this is the summary of the established doctrine. ||245||
Having thus adopted this certainty, contemplate with an illumined intellect;
you will yourself, by means of the self, attain the infinite state. (246)

That which is such as a jar and so forth; and thus, just as gold is [the underlying reality] in golden earrings and the like, clay in clay jars and the like, and the Ganges current in the waves of the Ganges and so forth, so too should consciousness (cit) be contemplated everywhere as the material cause and so on. ||247||

Although the perception of everything is indeed the perception of consciousness (*cid-vilokana*), because nothing other than consciousness is real; nevertheless, there is a purpose in the practice of the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I perceive consciousness," since reflective awareness alone is the witness of the specific determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*). ||248||

For indeed, even for one who perceives [an object] as silver or a [shimmering] wave and so forth, a direct perception of silver that is unfit for the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I am seeing silver" is not capable of producing results such as the activity generated by the desire for silver. Therefore, one should practice in such a way that, upon the sight of anything whatsoever, there arises the subsequent reflective awareness: "I am beholding Consciousness. This is the general direction. (249)

Now, if it is argued that the phenomenal world of earth and so forth—which is perceived as possessing contradictory properties such as hardness—is in fact of the nature of pure consciousness, devoid of form, touch, conjunction, and the like, it is replied: the entire phenomenal world is of the nature of consciousness, just like the phenomenal world of a dream; for it is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, whose very essence is consciousness. (250)
Thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha:
"This [world], though non-existent, remains as if it were existent."
The three worlds are mere appearance; nothing else exists, O Lord of Sages.
Know that whatever is the referent of words such as "Brahmā" and the like, that is solely consciousness.
Perceiving the object of knowledge, she attains the state of being composed of consciousness. ||252||

In an instant, by means of cultivation, a person casts off the sense of "I" because that which is to be known has been cultivated, just as one [casts off] the state of being a new elephant in a dream through meditative visualization. (253)
Having attained the state of space and time within this form that is non-dual, those very friends will themselves become empty in nature. (254)

"Endowed with all those [attributes], that very existence (sattā), whose nature is designated as the individual soul (jīva), having come into being, attains the state of intellect (buddhitva) while eternally abiding in the state of ignorance. (255)

Thus, consciousness (cit) itself is the mind (manas) when qualified by the objectivity of volition and so forth; it is the ego (ahaṃkāra) when qualified by the objectivity of "I-ness" and so forth; it is the intellect (buddhi) when qualified by the objectivity consisting of the nature of ascertainment; and it is the heart (citta) when qualified by the objectivity of internal, non-conceptual memory and so forth. ||256||

The eye is that which is characterized by a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) taking on the form of color and so forth, which has gone outside through the gateway of the eyeball and other organs. Through the latent impression (vāsanā) of color and so forth, it attains the state of being color and so forth. 257.

Rudra is characterized by the quality of *tamas* brought under control; Brahmā is characterized by *rajas* brought under control; Viṣṇu is characterized by *sattva* brought under control; Īśvara is characterized by all the qualities (*guṇas*) brought under control; and Brahman is that which transcends the qualities. That very [Brahman] is denoted by such terms as Vāsudeva and Sadāśiva. The individual soul (*jīva*), however, is afflicted by the qualities beginning with *tamas* that have not been brought under control. (258)

Although everything possesses the three *guṇas*, it is designated by each individual quality—such as *tamas* and so forth—by virtue of its predominance, according to the principle that "designations occur based on what is predominant.

(259) One such as Indra is characterized by an *ahaṃkāra* consisting of the determination "I am Indra" and so forth. For this very reason, through the practice of determining an *ahaṃkāra* contrary to the currently prevailing *ahaṃkāra*, yogis attain divinity and other states corresponding to those respective *ahaṃkāras*. (260)
And so it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
"In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman. He knew that very Self as 'I am Brahman.
Therefore, he became all this."
Therefore, whoever among the gods awakened to this became that very thing;
likewise among the seers, and likewise among human beings. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized it.
"I was Manu and I was the Sun. Even now, whoever knows thus—"I am Brahman"—he becomes this all.
Even the gods are not masters over his prosperity, for he becomes their very Self.
But he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know; he is like a beast to the gods.

"Just as a beast," and so forth. Thus, that is not at all [the case]. This very Self is Brahman. It consists of consciousness, it consists of mind, speech, breath, sight, hearing, ether, air, fire, water, earth; it consists of anger and non-anger, of righteousness and unrighteousness, of joy and lack of joy, of virtue and vice; it consists of everything, and thus it consists of this [world], according to how one acts.
"One who performs good deeds becomes good; one who performs evil deeds becomes evil. One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and wicked through wicked action," and so forth.
[Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5] In the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*, in the "Questions of Śuka": [MBh 12.240.3–8ab]
The intellect is the self of a human being; the intellect alone [acts] as the self within the self.
When it undergoes transformation into a state of being, then it becomes the mind (manas). ||262||
Due to the distinctness of the sense organs, the intellect undergoes transformation by itself:
when hearing, it becomes the ear; when touching, it is called the sense of touch. ||263||
Seeing, it becomes the eye; tasting, it is known as the tongue.
When smelling, she becomes the sense of smell; the intellect is thus modified separately. ||264||
They call these the "senses," for the Unseen dwells within them.
The intellect, residing within the person, operates in three states. ||265||
Sometimes it attains peace, and sometimes it even grieves;
it is never joined here with either pleasure or pain.
This state, consisting of these qualities, transcends these three conditions. ||266||

Therefore, one should contemplate that everything is indeed Brahman, whose essential nature is consciousness and bliss. This very realization of the state [of Brahman] is the worship of the gods for the masters of yoga. 267.
And likewise, in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, Śrī Śiva, having been questioned by Vasiṣṭha, said:
"That which exists at all times, in every form, and everywhere..."

Having resolved that "All is Brahman," one should perform the perpetual vow of the Self; for by my intellect, I have understood that the eternal Self is the worship of the deity, which is pure consciousness and consists of consciousness alone.
Even that which has been obtained as it was acquired, one should honor with every means;
not even the slightest effort should be made here regarding former objects.
Neither desiring nor rejecting, having attained knowledge in accordance with reality, one should enjoy the planes of experience just as the ocean receives the rivers.
Equanimity is sweet and delectable; it is the power of aesthetic essence that transcends the senses.
By that [practice], the mind is cultivated and indeed attains identity with it.

And this knowledge consists of seven stages, namely: 1. *śubhecchā* (desire for the auspicious), 2. *vicāraṇā* (investigation), 3. *tanumānasā* (thinning of the mind), 4. *sattvāpatti* (attainment of being), 5. *asaṃsakti* (non-attachment), 6. *padārthābhāvanā* (non-contemplation of objects), and 7. *turyagā* (the fourth state). ||271–272||

In this regard, the first [desire] is the desire for knowledge of Brahman, as set forth by the Brahman [in the Upanishads]: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting," and so forth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) ||273||
The investigation of inner knowledge is the cause for engaging in right conduct; this is the second [verse]. ||274||

That state in which detachment from the objects of the senses arises through pure desire (*śubhecchā*) and discernment (*vicāraṇā*) is the third stage, *tanumānasā*, because of the absence of passion and the like, and due to having few conceptualizations and mental constructions. ||275||

These three stages are merely the means for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), but they are not included within the realization of Brahman itself, because even the notion of the reality of duality has been destroyed. ||276||

Therefore, these three [stages] are called "waking" within the fourfold division of yogic states, because they serve as the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and because the mind’s perception of the reality of the world's diversity is present, just as in ordinary waking. Through the practice of these three, one abides in the state of one's own true nature alone; this is the fourth stage, known by the name "attainment of pure being" (*sattvāpatti*). ||277||
Thus it has been said:
"Having reached the fourth stage, one remains as nothing but pure existence. And this [stage] is included within the knowledge of Brahman. 278.
Thus it has been said: "When perfect knowledge arises in the mind, resembling the rising of the full moon..."
It is free from conceptual construction, without beginning or end, for the yogi whose mind is disciplined in yoga.
"Those who have reached the fourth stage perceive everything as equal. (279)

This is the state of dream (svapnāvasthā), because the manifold diversity of the phenomenal world appears as if it were dream-like. That fifth state, named "non-attachment" (asaṃsakti), arises from the practice of these four, wherein a wonder of the mind emerges in the form of skill in grasping the supreme, most subtle bliss of Brahman. ||280||

Because the very non-attachment to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) awakens one to Brahman, that is its skillfulness at that time. Furthermore, there is the reflection that even regarding objects that are merely illusory, the habitual practice of passion results in cessation (*nivṛtti*). This state is called the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the phenomenal world due to ignorance. (281)
Thus it has been said: [Yogavāsiṣṭha 6.154.1–2] Having reached the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep...
"With all particular aspects stilled, he remains as pure non-duality alone. (282)

Through the practice of this pentad, by virtue of delighting in the Self, there occurs the non-manifestation of external and internal objects without the effort of another; this is the sixth stage, named the "non-contemplation of objects. Because of the absolute non-contemplation of objects, this is the sixth stage called "hidden deep sleep. (283)
Thus it has been said: "One gradually descends to the sixth stage, which is called deep sleep."
Wherein there is neither non-existence nor the nature of existence, neither "I" nor even the absence of ego-construction. ||284||

That state in which, through the practice of the six stages (*bhūmi*), there is no departure from meditative absorption—whether by oneself or by another—due to being established solely in the intrinsic nature, is the seventh stage, the "Fourth-Going" (*turyagā*) stage. ||285||

Because it is the fourth state (*turya*) in relation to the previously mentioned states such as waking and so forth, this is the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); liberation after death (*videhamukti*) is that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*). Thus ends the seven stages of knowledge. (286)

Now, because they are to be abandoned as being contrary to this [liberation], the seven stages of ignorance (ajñānabhūmikā) are described. Liberation is the abiding of the Self—which consists of the nature of consciousness and bliss and exists throughout all space and time—in its own essential form; the knowledge that serves as the cause for that is called "knowledge" (jñāna). ||287||

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is said to be the cause of bondage, characterized by the destruction of one's true nature through its opposite; it consists of the worldly cognition (*prapañca-jñāna*) such as the notion that the body is the self (*dehātmabuddhi*), and so forth. And that [ignorance] is sevenfold, due to the distinctions of: 1. seed-waking (*bījajāgrat*), 2. waking (*jāgrat*), 3. great-waking (*mahājāgrat*), 4. waking-dream (*jāgratsvapna*), 5. dream (*svapna*), 6. dream-waking (*svapnajāgrat*), and 7. deep sleep (*suṣupti*). (288)

In that context, the knowledge that arises immediately after the opening of the eyes of one who has awakened from sleep—being capable of such worldly transactions as engagement and withdrawal—is "waking [consciousness] born from a seed" (bījajāgrat).

The waking state is the cognition capable of worldly transaction, characterized by the notions of "I-ness," "mine-ness," "pot-ness," and so forth, belonging to the individual soul (jīva) which appears as a reflection from the mirror-like Brahman whose nature is pure consciousness. 290.
Awakening characterized by the recollection of past births and so forth, preceded by formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like, is "great waking" (*mahājāgrat*). (291)

Cognition whose objects consist of mental constructs such as those for wealth and so forth is the waking dream; even the perception of two moons and the like is included within this very category. (292)
Dream is a cognition that, upon awakening, is fit to be known as sublated and thus does not deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). ||293||
A dream that has persisted for a long time remains present even when one is awake; such a dream is called "dream-awakening" (*svapnajāgrat*).
Deep sleep is that state of consciousness devoid of mental manifestation, yet imbued with the latent impressions (vāsanā) which serve as the seeds for future pleasure, pain, and so forth. ||295||

In these states, the single number one would appear in various manifestations of form; therefore, having discerned the ground of ignorance with the mind, one should abandon it and take refuge in the ground of knowledge—thus says the King of Yogins. ||296||

Therefore, in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra 2.27 with the Bhāṣya]: "His wisdom has seven stages of culmination. Regarding the word "his": it refers to one for whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen. (1) That which is to be known is that which is to be abandoned; for us, there is nothing else remaining to be known. (2) The causes of what is to be abandoned have been exhausted; there is nothing further among these that remains to be exhausted. (3) Abandonment is directly realized through the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*). (4) The means of abandonment, consisting of discriminative discernment, has been cultivated. (297–298)

Thus: this fourfold liberation belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*), while the liberation of the mind (*cittavimukti*) consists of three [of these]. The intellect (*buddhi*), having fulfilled its function, [ceases]; the qualities (*guṇas*), being without further station, are about to dissolve into their own cause and thus set along with it. (299)

And for those [defilements] that have been dissolved, there is no further arising, due to the absence of any purpose [for them]. Thus, seeing the wisdom of the seven ultimate stages, a person is called "skilled" and becomes "one who is alone" (a *kevalin*). ||300||

Then, for those who practice in this way, meditating for a long time, they attain the state of the disciplined yogi. And since that [state] is to be accomplished through long life, the means for conquering death (mṛtyuñjaya) which achieve it will now be explained. ||301||

And they were addressed by Bhuśuṇḍa, the king of crows, who lives for many kalpas, in response to Vasiṣṭha: "In whose heart the continuous threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), pierced by the fruits of the objects of the senses and their defects, have not ceased... (6.24.5–10) [302]

For him, the tremors and mental afflictions that cause all the creepers of the body to sway do not arise; the rows of serpents that are the five bodily trees, with their hoods of anxiety, do not burn him; the serpent of greed, moving within the midst of his own mind which is reeling from the poison of the five passions and hatreds, does not bite him; likewise, this submarine fire of the ocean of the body, namely anger, does not consume him; and the bodiless god of love does not crush him like sesame seeds in a machine. This is because he has taken refuge in the rest of the mind in some single, supremely pure state.
Death does not seek to slay him. ||303||

P.38 Because of the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth, there is an absence of the causes of death, disease, and the like—namely, the wandering of the vital winds (*pavana*) onto wrong paths and the underlying conditions such as anxiety and indigestion. Thus it has been stated: "The mind, when concentrated in one-pointedness, is not plundered by [such] things as hunger. [304]

In this context, one [object] is Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; the other is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Concentration of the mind upon that Brahman is indeed stated at every step to be the cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. As for the vital breath, however, it shall be discussed in the section concerning *prāṇāyāma*. 305.

Although it yields great fruit, because it is not to be accomplished through strenuous exertion and is thus beloved by the kings of yogis, something regarding the proximate method of *rājayoga* is now briefly stated.

In the heart-lotus, the two named *prāṇa* and *apāna*—the sun and moon of the space of the heart, possessing the nature of fire and water, hot and cold, moving upward and downward, carrying the body, tireless, and endowed with the power of incessant vibration—move through the channels that carry the vital breath during the states of waking and so forth. Their movement is as difficult to perceive as a mere fragment of a lotus fiber. (307)

In that regard, when the sun of prāṇa (the outgoing breath) departs from the heart and reaches the tip of the nose, extending outward to a distance of twelve finger-breadths—that is called "external filling" because it fills the exterior. [308] [External inhalation = inhaling with external air, which extends out to twelve finger-breaths]

When the apāna wind enters from the outside into the interior, that internal filling—the mutual conjunction of the components of prāṇa and apāna—is called "internal filling" (antaḥpūraṇa) because it fills the interior. [Internal inhalation—inhalation within, which is the mutual contact of prāṇa and apāna when apāna enters in]

When the *apāna* wind has subsided within the heart, the state of internal *kumbhaka* lasts as long as the *prāṇa* does not rise upward. When the *prāṇa* has subsided outside, the external *kumbhaka* lasts as long as the *apāna* has not emerged facing toward the person. (310) [Internal and External Retention] Thus, the inward-turning of the *apāna* wind is its external *recaka* (exhalation), because of the expulsion (*recana*) of the externally retained wind by means of turning it inward. (311) [External Exhalation—expelling the external air that has entered the mouth]

Thus, that outward-facing state of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) which occurs from its arising up to the limit of the nose is internal exhalation (*recaka*). Because of the emission (*recana*) of the air held within (*antaḥkumbhita*) by way of being directed outward, these six [stages] arise. [Internal exhalation—exhaling the internal air through the mouth.

Having taken the inward breath (apāna) of the outward breath (prāṇa), there is an upward movement; having taken the outward breath (prāṇa) of the inward breath (apāna), there is a downward movement. And this is twofold. [313]

Thus, the eight modes of movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are to be meditated upon by yogins. Even there, during the phases of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), it is the *prāṇa* and *apāna* themselves that are to be clearly visualized, because they are easily known. During the phase of retention (*kumbhaka*), because those two are difficult to discern, Brahman alone is to be visualized. This very visualization is the generator of the state of liberation. 314.
This was stated by Bhuśuṇḍa in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "O one of great intelligence, these eight are recollected day and night... [Yogavāsiṣṭha 6.26.17, 20].
I have described how, by means of the natural state of the bodily winds, liberation is bestowed.
By withdrawing the mind from external objects and remaining undistracted in this practice,
one attains the state of absolute liberation in just a few days.
For a person practicing this, the mind no longer forms an attachment to external sensory objects, just as a Brahmin does not take pleasure in a dog's mating.
Those of steady intellect who remain firm, having grasped this view—
"Everything that was to be attained has been attained by them; for they alone are truly untiring," and so forth. 318.

In this regard, the *Upadeśasāra* states that during the state of the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and during the state of their steadiness, the mind should be placed with extreme vigilance upon Brahman. (319)

Now, although the means for attaining health will be described in the section on Haṭhayoga, some of them are mentioned here as well because they are easy to perform and yield great results. These have been stated by the venerable Śiva, Ghorakṣanātha, and others in their respective works. (320)
The highly intelligent one who, having placed the tongue at the root of the palate...
One should drink the vital breath; by that, there shall be a complete destruction of diseases.
The wise person who, knowing the method of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, drinks the cool air with the beak of a crow, shall become a vessel for liberation. ||322||
He who, having raised the tongue upward, remains thus for half a moment;
In an instant, the yogi is liberated from disease, death, old age, and the like. ||323||
For that wise yogin who drinks the flavorful wind daily according to the prescribed rule, exhaustion, burning heat, fever, and diseases are destroyed. (324)
Having turned the tongue upward, the lord of yogis who drinks the water of the moon for just one month certainly conquers death. (325)
Having firmly pressed the cavity of the upper teeth according to the prescribed method and meditated upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, one shall become a poet within six months. (326)
One should drink the vital air with the crow's beak during both twilights, meditating upon it at the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī for the pacification of the disease of consumption. 327.
The wise yogi should drink [the elixir] day and night with the "crow's beak" [instrument]; thus he shall indeed possess the power of hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and clear vision. 328.
Pressing his teeth together with his teeth, that wise man, with his tongue turned upward, should drink the air very slowly; thus he quickly conquers death. ||329||
By practicing this four times every day, one overcomes sins and diseases within six months; it is proclaimed in the Yoga treatises that by practicing for a year, one overcomes death. ||330||
The Second Instruction: Now, regarding the ritual manuals (*kalpa*s):
therein, out of compassion for practitioners, that which was spoken by the illustrious Maheśvara to Pārvatī is written down as the *Īśvarī-kalpa*. (1)

[1. Īśvarī-kalpa] It has a black stalk and leaves resembling those of the *tāmbūla* tree, with yellow flowers like gold. It is well known in the world as *nāgadamanī*. This great medicinal herb named *Īśvarī* pacifies poverty, old age, and disease. It is found in abundance in places such as the Puṣkara forest and the Naimiṣa forest. (Its black stalk; its leaf similar to *tāmbūla*; and its yellow flower are mentioned at KCKT 2, p. 7; it is said to remove poverty at KCKT 5a.)

On an auspicious day such as the Puṣya constellation, having first invited Śiva and other deities on the preceding day, she should be accepted; then, after performing the worship of auspicious deities, the feeding of Brahmins, and the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*), it should be worn on one limb at a time—on the head, ear, hand, neck, arm, finger-ring, and waist—or on two or many limbs. Thus worn, it brings all under her control. The sacred scripture (*śruti*) increases [her power]; it destroys obstacles; and it wards off fear of fire, water, lions, snakes, scorpions, poisons, and the like.

It protects from disputes, enemies, dangers, and the like. (Wearing it on the ears, throat, hands, and head is mentioned at KCKT 6cd; wearing it on the arms, rings, and hips is at KCKT 7ab; "it brings all under control" is mentioned at KCKT 7c; fire, water, and lions at KCKT 8cd–9ab; scorpions and snakes at 12ab; disputes, enemies, and dangers are mentioned at KCKT 9b.
One should consume [the medicine] for one year together with ghee and honey. = KCKT 14cd

Freed from all diseases and devoid of wrinkles and grey hair, he shall live for a thousand years, endowed with great splendor and great strength. He wards off weapons; he releases men bound by fetters or those condemned to the stake. Various kinds of poisons and malignant sores are destroyed when smeared with this [substance] along with cow urine.
