By practicing for five years, a man becomes one with a lifespan of a hundred thousand years;
having attained the strength of nine elephants, he may roam the earth at his own will.

Having ground [the substance] with honey, by smearing it upon the penis, a woman becomes submissive. By smearing it upon the vulva, a man becomes submissive to the woman. Likewise, having ground it with cow’s milk and stirred it with ghee, if a husband and wife drink it, they will give birth to a long-lived son. (7) Furthermore—sprinkle the mercury of that [substance] onto tin that has been subjected to *prativāpa* [purification]. (RAK 462cd)
The powder of the root of the *īśvarī* plant, together with tin, arrests [the flow] in three [days].
Moreover:
the mercury of the *nāginī* is seized at that very moment by the first bite of the bee.
Through mardana and svedana, the mercury (rasa) effects the transmutation of all substances;
and with a sixteenth part [of mercury], the mercury penetrates all the metals.
Furthermore—
Having uprooted it along with its roots and leaves, one should combine it with barley-alkali;
then, having rubbed the mercury, one should dry it with the heat of the sun.
Furthermore, one should prepare a paste using the juice of the munivṛkṣa tree.
That [substance], when processed with a twentieth part [of it], pierces all metals.
(11) Now, the purification of copper leaves and so forth: one should smear copper leaves that have been sprinkled with the juice of *nāginī*. (RAK 467ab)
Having caused [the metal] to flow by means of *niṣeka*, the purification of the leaf (*dalaśuddhi*) shall then occur.
(12) The maiden (*kumārī*), *brahmaromā*, and a *pālikā* of *nirguṇḍī* juice—having sprinkled all the metals with these, one should then commence the ritual work. (13)
With that very sixteenth part, pierce the silver and the gold;
having made the lead and the brass equal, combine them with barley and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Having caused it to melt, one should then pour [the liquid] into the fifth buffalo-skin bag;
this pouring is done three times with the juice of *punarnavā* mixed with the juice of *loṇī*,
and likewise dried three times.
One should sprinkle the mercury of the *nāginī* with goat’s urine and milk.
In this manner, the sevenfold silver (*tāra*) should be sprinkled with effort.
O Goddess of the Gods, the wise practitioner should cause the mercury to liquefy together with the silver.
One should apply the ore with a fourteenth part of those two;
thus it becomes a divine gold, possessing the luster of the rising sun.
[One should also employ] *nirguṇḍī*, the milk of *apasnūhī*, mercury, and salts.
In one place, the wise practitioner should grind the mercury and subject it to sudation.
By practicing this for seven nights, the "mouthless" [mercury] swallows the sky.
This should be performed at an auspicious *lagna*, conjunction (*yoga*), and *karana*. [Verses 476–77 of the RAK are missing].
And having worshipped the two Maheśvaras with fragrant flowers and incense,
At the time of his practice, however, his food consists of sixty-day rice with milk. ||20||
Furthermore,
I shall proclaim the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*), by which practitioners attain success:
having taken one *pala* of mercury and likewise one *pala* of quicksilver (*sūtaka*).
Having collected the juice of the *nāginī* plant as well as goat’s urine, the wise one should boil them over a fire;
he should then rub them with a copper leaf.
O beautiful one, he should subject them to heat and continue rubbing for a full day and night.
And that pill shall pierce all metals;
having thus caused it to be melted for seven nights, one who knows the ritual procedure [should act].
O beautiful one, it becomes a piercer of sixty-four [times] in two weeks;
O beloved, it pierces a hundred in three weeks, and it pierces a thousand.
When the fourth week has arrived, it becomes a piercer of a hundred thousand.
When the fifth and seventh [stages] are attained, the mercury becomes a "piercer of the peak" (koṭivedhin). ||26||
When the sixth group of seven has been reached, one becomes a piercer of ten million [targets] with a *guñjā* seed;
O Goddess, in the seventh group of seven, one becomes a piercer of ten million [targets] with a mustard seed.
When the eighth week has arrived, the mercury becomes "piercing by touch" (sparśavedhī).
When the ninth week has arrived, it becomes "illuminating" (udyotanakara).
When the tenth week has arrived, it is called "great mercury" (mahārasa).
When the Great Taste (mahārasa) has been attained, who would not be released from bondage? Thus ends the ritual manual of the renowned Īśvarī known as Nāgadamanī.
[2. The Brahmavṛkṣakalpa] [cf. AK *brahmakalpaḥ*; *brahmavṛkṣatailakalpa*] Now follows the *Brahmavṛkṣakalpa*:
Śrī Maheśvara, having been asked by Kārttikeya for the sake of accomplishing that which practitioners desire—namely, long life, extreme vigor, prowess, wisdom, and so forth—spoke as follows: ||30||

Formerly, when the ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and asuras for the sake of the nectar of immortality, those drops of nectar which emerged and fell due to the blows of churning gave rise to the Brahma-tree, renowned by the name Palāśa. ||31||
One should have the seeds of the Brahma-tree ground into a fine powder; one should then sprinkle them with the juice of *āmalaka* as well as with milk. (32) [p.
And the wise practitioner should diligently cause it to sweat for seven nights.
Then, having pressed it with a machine, one should extract its oil.
And the wise man should rinse his mouth with that oil mixed with milk.
On an auspicious moment, on a holy day, under a favorable lunar mansion, and when joined by benefic planets.
And having worshipped the Lord Śiva with the sounds of "Svasti" and "Puṇyāha," [he departed].
One should first drink that oil in a single drop together with an equal amount of milk; thereafter, according to one's practice, one may drink up to a *kuḍava*. ||35||

He should subsist on a diet of mudga beans, cakes, cow's milk, and boiled rice; he should especially avoid sour and salty foods. He should remain celibate and sleep on a bed of potter’s ashes. There, the practitioner must be protected with great care by his attendants. (36)

But when oil mixed with milk exceeding one *pala* is drunk, then at that very moment fainting occurs. This being so, if milk is given with a cotton wick into the mouth of the practitioner who has been covered with potter’s ash, he regains consciousness after a short while (*muhūrta*). ||37||

Thus, if one drinks a measure of a *kuḍava*, then after seven nights one regains consciousness. During that period, or even for up to twenty-one days thereafter, one should subsist on a diet of milk. Then, once that oil has been digested over the course of seven nights, one attains the fruit [of the practice]. ||38||
One should retain unheard texts through one's intelligence, becoming equal to the teacher.
In strength he was like Indra, and his radiance was equal to the splendor of the sun. ||39||
He has the vision of a vulture, the hearing of a boar, and the speed of Garuḍa.
With hair as curly as bees, she may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars.
(40) Furthermore—
One should drink exactly one pala of the oil together with honey.
Listen as I describe the fruit that results from merely drinking the oil. ||41||
Through practice for six months, this characteristic arises.
Neither by fire nor by water does his death come to pass. ||42||
One becomes both a speaker and a listener of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
One will see treasures hidden in the earth, and all shall come under one's control. ||43||
And a man should beget even a hundred sons who are endowed with intelligence.
Whichever woman he enjoys, she shall possess perpetual youth.
By practicing this for one year, a human being becomes a Vatsa.
By anointing it with his urine and other substances, all iron and other metals become gold.
But this supreme secret was spoken by Rudra himself. ||45||
Alternatively—
one should diligently cause the powder of the Brahma-tree to be prepared.
Having gently steamed it for three days with cow's milk, ||46||
Having pressed it with an oil-press, one should extract the oil from it.
Having mixed it with ghee, one should cause it to be placed within a heap of grain. ||47||
At an auspicious moment, on a very meritorious day, under a lunar mansion conjoined with favorable planets.
After a month has passed, the wise one, having extracted [the essence], becomes pure in body. ||48||
Having ascertained that the digestive fire of the body is very strong, one should consume it at one's ease.
Subsisting on milk or mung bean soup, he should remain in a dwelling free from drafts. ||49||
By practicing this for seven nights, one is sung of together with the kiṃnaras.
He shall live for thousands of years, free from old age and disease.
Possessing the strength of nine elephants, he has black hair and steady eyes.
And furthermore:
one should consume each seed individually together with sesame and sugar.
By practicing for only one month, one obtains the aforementioned qualities. ||51||

Furthermore—having dried the tender leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, one should reduce them to powder. Having prostrated before Śiva and others, one should drink one *prasṛta* measure of that powder with buttermilk at an auspicious hour. When that has been digested, one should eat food devoid of salt, sourness, and fats. If thirsty, one should drink cold milk or water. 52.

By practicing this for only one month, gray hair and the like fall away. In the second month, [hair] resembling that of a bee and so forth grows. One becomes free from all diseases and attains a lifespan of a thousand years. Herein, one may engage in activities and pastimes as one desires. 53.

Alternatively—one should wither the flowers of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree and reduce them to powder. Having mixed that powder, measuring ten *palas*, with twelve *palas* of clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), one should place it in a smooth vessel and set it within a heap of grain for twenty-one days and nights. (54)

Then, at an auspicious moment, having purified his body and worshipped Śiva and the other deities, he should eat according to his capacity up to the size of a *pala*. He should eat *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk. When thirsty, he should drink water mixed with the decoction of *khadira* wood. Within twenty nights, he shall obtain the fruit. 55.
Possessing the prowess of a rutting elephant and valor equal to the wind.
Possessing divine vision and great splendor, his radiance was equal to the flame of fire.
For it is indeed inexhaustible and ageless, entirely free from old age and disease. ||56||

Alternatively—having caused the bark of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree to be ground into a fine powder, one should drink it with milk. One becomes light in diet and has one's senses subdued. By using this for half a month, copper and other metals turn into gold through his urine and feces. His hair becomes like that of a bee, and he becomes long-lived. (57)
And furthermore:
having taken one pala of Brahma-oil, one should cook it together with clarified butter.
A wise person should drink it with an assistant; otherwise, fainting occurs right there.
Then, for one month, he should drink milk; thereafter, he may eat six times a day.
After seven nights, a mortal beholds the earth as full of fissures. ||59||
No shadow of him is seen, and he becomes truly invisible.

The Third Instruction:

Now, for the sake of protecting the body conducive to yoga and for the knowledge of dispassion, creation, and so forth, the physical body is described. In that regard, within the body of each individual person, there are three types, distinguished as gross (*sthūla*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and causal (*kāraṇa*). Among these, the gross body is a specific modification of the five elements—earth and the others—which are endowed with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as smell; it is the delimiting factor for experience. This very [body] is called the "sheath consisting of food" (*annamaya-kośa*). (1)

The subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) consists of seventeen components. These components are: the five vital airs (*vāyu*), namely *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, *samāna*, and *vyāna*; the five organs of perception (*jñānendriya*), consisting of hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, which are respectively presided over by the deities of the quarters, Vāyu, Arka (the Sun), Pracetas (Varuṇa), and Aśvin; the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and finally, the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*), which are presided over by Brahmā (Caturmukha) and Candra (the Moon). Thus, there are seventeen [components]. (Verses 2–4)

The mind (*citta*) and ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) are included within [the categories of] Vāsudeva and Śaṃkara respectively; or, if they are not included, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) consists of nineteen constituents. (5) This subtle body should be examined as follows: Within this [subtle body], the pentad beginning with breath (*prāṇa*), together with the organs of action, constitutes the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*). The mind (*manas*), together with the organs of action, constitutes the sheath consisting of the unmanifest (*mānasa-maya-kośa*). The intellect (*buddhi*), together with the organs of perception, constitutes the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*). (6)

The subtle body itself, when it has become thoroughly cultivated through constant practice, becomes capable of entering the bodies of others and so forth. It possesses the conceit of being an agent and an enjoyer, and it travels between this world and the next.
As it is said in the Sāṃkhya:
"That which was produced first, unattached, fixed, and consisting of the principles from Mahat down to the subtle elements..."
The subtle body (*liṅga*), permeated by the dispositions (*bhāva*), transmigrates without experiencing [objects] for itself.
This [transmigration] is caused by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, through the sequence of causes and their effects;
due to its connection with the omnipresence of *prakṛti*, the subtle body persists like an actor. (8–9)

It is produced first. At the initial creation, it is produced by *pradhāna* as one for each individual *puruṣa*. It is unattached and unimpeded; it penetrates even into stones. It is constant. From the beginning of creation until liberation, it remains as one. Its aggregate consists of everything from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the subtle elements (*sūkṣma*). In this view, it should be understood that the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are also included within the subtle body. 10.

Perfumed by the states (*bhāva*)—namely merit and demerit, knowledge and ignorance, detachment and non-detachment, and power and lack of power—it transmigrates like oil infused with flowers. The meaning is that it first abandons the gross body and takes up a new one. It is called the *liṅga* (the subtle body) because it goes to dissolution (*laya*) into *pradhāna*. The second meaning is as follows: by the power of *prakṛti*, this [subtle body], assuming various forms like an actor in different bodies, produces the sense of ego (*ahaṃkāra*) under the influence of causes such as merit and demerit. *Prakṛti*, which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and is denoted by terms such as "ignorance" (*avidyā*), is the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*) and the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*).

Within these sheaths, the Lord Self is hidden; He is to be heard, reflected upon, meditated upon, and realized. And as to how that Self manifests within each sheath, it has been stated by Sureśvarācārya: "Having entered the sheath consisting of food (annamaya), the Self manifests as one who is stout, a child, emaciated, dark-complexioned, and possessed of the distinctions of caste and stage of life. (14)
"I live even in the vital-sheath (prāṇakośa), yet I am hungry and thirsty;
I am certain and resolute"—thus one thinks within the mental sheath (manomaya-kośa).
Residing in the sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-kośa), one remains with the thought, "I perceive."

In the ego-sense known as the sheath of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*), one rejoices, thinking "I am happy," due to past meritorious deeds and intense meditative practices. Thus, it is enveloped by these five sheaths, as if by five coverings. (16–17)
The Supreme Lord appears as if limited, yet He pervades all;
just as the sun, having entered the water, appears manifold, so too the Lord, having entered bodies, shines forth in many ways. And so forth. 18.

This triad of bodies is also twofold, distinguished as individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*). Here, between the individual and collective bodies, there is both difference and non-difference, like a tree and a forest, or like water and a reservoir of water. Furthermore, consciousness conditioned by the individual gross body is called *Viśva*. (19) Consciousness conditioned by the collective gross body is called *Vaiśvānara* or *Virāj*, because it identifies with all men and because it shines forth diversely. (20)

Consciousness conditioned by the individual subtle body is called *taijasa*, because it identifies with all individual men and because it shines forth in various ways. Consciousness conditioned by the individual subtle body is called *taijasa* because it is conditioned by an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of light. (21) Consciousness conditioned by the aggregate of these [subtle bodies] is called *sūtrātman*, *hiraṇyagarbha*, and *prāṇa*. It is so called because, like the thread of a garland, it is woven through everything; and because it identifies with the five unquintuplicated great elements which possess the powers of knowledge and action. (22)

Thus, consciousness conditioned by the individual causal body (vyaṣṭi-kāraṇa-śarīra) is called the *prājña* (the wise one). This is because, as the illuminator of a single ignorance (*avidyā*), it lacks excessive luminosity and is characterized by a preponderance of non-knowing. (23) Consciousness conditioned by the collective causal body (*samaṣṭi*) is designated as the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), the Cause of the World (*jagat-kāraṇa*), and the Lord (*īśvara*). It possesses attributes such as omniscience, universal lordship, and universal sovereignty, because it is the illuminator of all ignorance. (24)

Thus, for the two consciousnesses conditioned by the respective individual (vyāṣṭi) and collective (samaṣṭi) bodies—namely Viśva and Vaiśvānara, and so forth—there is both difference and non-difference, just as in the case of space delimited by a tree and a forest, or the reflection of space in water and the reflection of space in a reservoir of water; they are different due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), but non-different due to the non-difference in the nature of that which is delimited (upādeya). Among these, the first is the worshipper (upāsaka) and the second is the object of worship (upāsya); through the contemplation of their non-difference, that prior non-difference—which was like a jewel forgotten in the house of one's own home and thus not being utilized—is directly realized through the Vedas, inference, meditation (nididhyāsana), and samādhi.

Thinking "I am the performer of my own duty," those who practice yoga should incessantly contemplate the non-difference between the individual and collective bodies and the consciousnesses inherent within them. When this contemplation has become firmly established, one should contemplate the unity of the entire collection of bodies, just as a great forest is the unity of its intermediate forest-clusters.
(27) One should also contemplate the unity of the consciousness inherent therein, just as the space delimited by a great forest is one with the space itself.

"What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?"—from such scriptural passages as these. Thereafter, or even from the very beginning, by perceiving that everything has consciousness as its material cause and is thus of the nature of consciousness, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. May there be auspiciousness! Now, regarding the body composed of the five elements, the individual qualities of each element were described by the venerable Lord Vyāsadeva to Śukadeva in the *Mokṣadharma*: "O son, listen further to the enumeration of the elements. (29) [And: "bhūtānāṃ parisaṃkhyānaṃ bhūyaḥ putra niśāmaya" (Listen further, my son, to the detailed enumeration of the elements). (30)

The stability, heaviness, hardness, and productivity of the earth; its smell, weight, power, cohesion, support, and endurance. And thus: 30. Stability, heaviness, hardness, and the capacity for production; odor, weight, power, cohesion, support, and fortitude. And likewise—

Through the commonality (*sādharmya*) of stability and so forth, the identity of the body with the earth, trees, mountains, and the like should be meditated upon; the same applies hereafter. For this very reason, through the cognition of difference and non-difference by means of both dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) and similarity (*sādharmya*), the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), which is the cause of liberation, arises.
(31) This was stated by the venerable Śrī Kaṇāda in the Vaiśeṣika scripture:
"From the knowledge of reality through similarity and dissimilarity, the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) occurs. (32)
The essence of water consists of coldness, moisture, fluidity, unctuousness, gentleness, salivation,
and likewise the cooking of terrestrial things.
The qualities of fire are invincibility, light, heat, digestion, and illumination.
Sorrow, passion, lightness, sharpness, and constant upward movement;

the lack of fixed location for wind, touch, the locus of speech, and independence; strength, speed, liberation, the impulse of action, and the sense of self-existence—[these are the qualities of air]. (34–35)
Sound is the quality of space, as well as its pervasiveness and porosity.
It is without support, without foundation, unmanifest, and immutable.
It is also characterized by non-obstruction, the state of being a primary element (bhūtatva), and its various transformations.
Fifty qualities are said to be produced from the nature of the five elements.
(37) Now, the process of the formation of the body born from a womb—
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
Through the oblation, the sun blazes; from the sun comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen.
(Nirukta, 13.2.3)

This food, through internal phlegm (*śleṣman*), becomes semen (*retas*). From phlegm comes lymph-chyle (*rasa*); from chyle, blood (*śoṇita*); from blood, flesh (*māṃsa*); from flesh, fat (*medas*); from fat, sinews (*snāyu*); from sinews, bone (*asthi*); from bone, marrow (*majjā*); and from marrow, semen. (39) This semen, when discharged into the womb, becomes a person. If there is an excess of the male seed (*śukra*), one becomes a male; if there is an excess of the female seed (*śoṇita*), one becomes a female. If both are equal, one becomes a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*). If the male seed is divided, one becomes twin-born (*yama*). (40)

The couple are characterized by the act of killing, and thus the body becomes marked accordingly. That [embryo] remains as a *kalala* for one night; after five nights, it becomes a *budbuda*; after seven nights, a *peśī*; after fourteen nights, an *arbuda*. After twenty-five nights, it is well-established, and after one month, it becomes solid. Within two months, the head is formed. In three months, the neck is designated. In four months, the skin is designated. In the fifth month, nails and hair are designated.

In the sixth [week], the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears come into being. In the seventh, he becomes capable of movement; in the eighth, he determines through the intellect and so forth. In the ninth, he becomes complete in all his limbs.
And it is said: "I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again."
Indeed, thousands of different wombs have been inhabited by me;
various foods have been eaten, and many kinds of breasts have been sucked.
Diverse mothers have been seen, as well as fathers and friends.
Facing downward and being tormented here by my own past deeds, I remain [in the womb].
(43) Having thoroughly practiced Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one realizes the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle.
(44) And then, in the tenth month, one is born. Once born and touched by the external wind, one does not remember birth and death, nor [the fruits of] good and evil at the end. (45)
And Yājñavalkya says:
"In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, agitated by the vital wind;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with the sense organs. (46)
In the fourth month there is stability; in the fifth, the production of blood from the skin and other tissues;
and in the sixth, the emergence of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair.
This embryo is then endowed with mind and consciousness, and is joined with channels, sinews, and arteries.
In the seventh and eighth [weeks], he possesses skin, flesh, and memory;
[there is] the sinew which binds the bones, the channel through which the wind flows, and the vessel that carries wind, bile, and phlegm.
Furthermore, his vital essence (*ojas*) rushes back and forth between the placenta and the fetus.
In the eighth month from conception, the fetus is born and released from its vital breaths (prāṇas).
Regarding the nature of *ojas*, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"That which resides in the heart is pure, slightly red, and yellowish."
The body is reckoned as being composed of *ojas*; through its destruction, it meets with destruction.
By this [it is understood that] stability and instability, which are the causes of life and death, should be known to depend upon the stability of that *ojas*.
When, in the ninth or tenth month, [the fetus] moves due to the vital winds (*māruta*), [it is born].

Like an arrow with fever being drawn through the opening of a machine, he whose body is composed of sinews, bones, skin, and so forth, having been born through the opening of that machine, does not remember his former state when touched by the vital wind (vāyu). Two [faults] arise from the non-bestowal of the heart: the fetus may incur a defect.
Therefore, one should do what is pleasing to women, even at the cost of disfigurement or death.
(53) The single heart of the fetus and the single heart of the pregnant woman constitute the "two-heartedness" (*dvaihṛdya*) desired by a woman who possesses two hearts.
(54) That body consists of many types [of parts] through its divisions, such as the snake and so forth. (55)

For instance: the serpent [nature] consists of sharpness, fearfulness, ferocity, and fickleness in one's dwelling, conduct, and behavior; the bird [nature] consists of excessive desire, constant hunger, impatience, instability, and so forth; the rakshasa [nature] consists of being narrow-minded, violent, envious, and outside the bounds of dharma; the piśāca [nature] consists of eating leftovers, sharpness, recklessness, lust for women, shamelessness, and so forth; and the preta [nature] consists of lack of sharing, laziness, envy, a disposition toward suffering, greed, and wretchedness. (56)

Now, the characteristics of those dominated by *tamas* are as follows: dullness of intellect, sluggishness, constant preoccupation with sexual intercourse, and the desire to act—these belong to the "beastly" (*pāśava*) type. Instability, ignorance, cowardice, a longing for water, and mutual aggression—these belong to the "fish-like" (*mātsya*) type. Delighting in staying in one place, constant eating, indulgence in pleasure, and being devoid of virtue, desire, and wealth—these belong to the "vegetable-like" (*vānaspatya*) type. In this manner, other types should also be understood according to the scriptures and worldly renown. (57)

Thus, having understood the nature of men and their bodies, one should perform actions appropriate to that nature. For action that follows one's own duty quickly attains success. One who abides in their own nature becomes happy; it should be understood and considered that there is no fear for one who remains within their own nature, and so forth. (58) And that body has six limbs: four branches, the trunk as the fifth, and the head as the sixth. (59)

Now, the secondary parts (*pratyaṅga*): the head, abdomen, back, navel, forehead, nose, chin, bladder, and neck are each single units. The ears, eyes, eyebrows, lips, cheeks, armpits, breasts, testicles, sides, buttocks, knees, arms, thighs, and so forth, are each double units. Likewise, the skin, the layers (*kalā*), the tissues (*dhātu*), the wastes (*mala*), and the humors (*doṣa*). The liver and spleen; the lungs and water-carrying vessels; the heart and the stomach; the intestines, kidneys, channels (*srotas*), tendons (*kaṇḍarā*), networks, cords (*kūrca*), ropes (*rajju*), sutures (*sīvanyā*), unions (*saṃghāta*), cranial seams (*sīmanta*), bones, joints (*sandhi*), ligaments (*snāyu*), muscles (*peśī*), veins (*śirā*), arteries (*dhamanī*), and vital points (*marman*). 60.

Therein, there are seven layers of skin (tvac), seven membranes (kalā), seven constituent elements (dhātu), three impurities (mala), and three humors (doṣa). The liver (yakṛt) and the spleen (plīhā) are each mentioned as one. There are seven receptacles (āśaya), distinguished by the receptacle of wind (vātāśaya), the receptacle of bile (pittāśaya), the receptacle of phlegm (śleṣmāśaya), the receptacle of blood (raktāśaya), the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya), the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), and the receptacle of urine (mūtrāśaya). For women, the womb (garbhāśaya) is the eighth. (61) There are nine channels (srotas): the ears, eyes, nostrils, abdomen, and penis. For women, there are three additional ones: two in the breasts and one for the flow of nutrient fluid (rasavaha). There are sixteen large tendons (kaṇḍarā), four in each of the hands, feet, neck, and back. (62)

Among these, the nails are the terminal growths of the tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the hands and feet. The penis is the [terminal growth] of the tendons of the neck. The buttocks are the [terminal growth] of the tendons of the back. There are sixteen networks (jāla): four each in the flesh, vessels, ligaments, and bones; they are situated at the wrists and ankles. (63) There are six tufts (kūrca): two in the hands, two in the feet, and one each in the neck and the penis. There are four large muscular cords (māṃsarajju): two on either side of the spinal column for the purpose of binding the muscles—one external and one internal. (64)
There are seven sutures in the head, five in the tongue, and one each in the penis and the scrotum; these must be avoided when using a surgical instrument.

(65) There are fourteen groups of bones: three each in the ankles, knees, and groins; one each in the two feet and the two arms; and one each in the sacrum and the head. Within each group, there are eighteen bones. There are fourteen cranial sutures. (66)

There are three hundred and sixty bones. According to the Vedic school and the opinion of Śākalya, there are three hundred. Of these, one hundred and twenty are in the limbs; one hundred and seventeen are in the hips, back, abdomen, and chest; and sixty-three are above the neck. Thus, there are three hundred [and sixty]. (67) In that regard, there are three in each finger, making fifteen. There are ten in the palms, ankles, and wrists. There are two in the shanks. There is one each in the heels, knees, and thighs. Thus, there are thirty bones in each limb. (68)

There are four in the pubic region, the anus, and the hips; one in the sacrum; thirty-six on each side; eight on the chest; two in the parts known as *kṣa*; ninety-seven [in total so far]. There are nine in the neck; four in the throat-arteries; two in the jaws; sixty-nine [in total so far]. There are thirty-two teeth; three in the nose; one in the palate; one each in the cheeks, ears, and temples; six in the head; sixty-three [in total so far]. Thus, there are three hundred [bones]. These are of five types, distinguished by being skull-bones (*kapāla*), collar-bones (*rucaka*), young bones (*taruṇa*), ring-shaped bones (*valaya*), and needle-shaped bones (*nalaka*). Seventy.

In their knees, hips, shoulders, cheeks, palate, temples, and head, they are designated as *kapāla* (skull-bones). The teeth are *aruca* (rings). In the nostrils, ears, neck, and eye-sockets, they are *taruṇa* (tender). In the hands, feet, sides, back, belly, and chest, they are *valaya* (circles). The remaining bones are designated as *nalaka* (reeds).
(71) Just as trees stand firm by means of the internal pith, so too are the bodies of embodied beings certainly supported by the pith of the bones. (72)

There are two hundred and ten joints (*sandhi*) in total. Among them, those in the limbs (*śākhā*), the jaws (*hanu*), and the pelvis (*kaṭī*) are movable; elsewhere they are fixed. There are sixty in the limbs, fifty-nine in the trunk (*koṣṭha*), and eighty-three in the neck and upwards. (73) There are three joints in each finger, and two in the thumb; thus, there are fourteen in the hands. There is one each in the knee, the ankle, and the groin; thus, there are seventeen in each leg. There are three in the pelvic bones (*kaṭikapāla*), and twenty-four in the spinal column (*pṛṣṭhavaṃśa*). (74)

There are exactly that many [channels] on each side; eight in the chest; exactly that many in the neck; three in the throat; eighteen in the channels connected to the heart and the kloma; thirty-two at the roots of the teeth; one in the nose; two in the circular openings of the ears; one each in the sockets of the eyes, the cheeks, the ears, and the temples; two in the joints of the jaws; two above the eyebrows; two in the temples; five in the cranial plates; and one on the crown of the head. (75)

There are nine hundred sinews (*snāyu*). Of these, six hundred are in the limbs; thirty-two are in the trunk; and seventy are above the neck. There are six sets of ten in each finger. There are thirty [sinews] in the *kūrca* and the ankles; just as many in the shanks; ten in the knee; forty in the thigh; and ten in the groin. Thus, there are one hundred and fifty in each leg. There are sixty in the pelvis; eighty in the back; sixty in the two sides; thirty in the chest; thirty-six in the neck; and thirty-four in the head. Thus, the total is nine hundred. (76)

Like a boat laden with fruit and bound by many ropes, the body becomes firm when bound by sinews. There are five hundred muscles (*peśī*). Of these, four hundred are in the limbs; sixty-six are in the trunk; and thirty-four are above the neck. (77)

There is one [vein] in each finger and toe. There are twenty in the soles of the feet and between the ankles and knees. There are five in the knee and twenty in the thighs. There are ten in the groin. Thus, there are one hundred in each limb. There are three in the anus, one in the penis, and another in the perineal seam. There are two in the testicles. There are five each in the buttocks. There are two at the head of the bladder. There are five in the abdomen. There is one at the navel. There are five long ones each in the upper part of the back and the thighs. There are six in the sides. There are ten in the chest. There are seven counted for each of the collarbones and shoulders. (78)

There are two muscles in the heart and the stomach; six in the liver, spleen, and kidneys; four in the neck; two in the ears; four on the forehead; and one in the head. Thus, there are five hundred muscles. Encased by these muscles, the vessels, ligaments, bones, joints, and articulations of the body become strong. In women, there are twenty additional muscles: ten in the breasts, four in the birth canal, three situated at the opening of the womb, and four in the uterus. (79) The female reproductive tract is shaped like a conch-shell whorl and is described as having spiral curves.
In its third coil, however, the bed of the fetus is established.
It has the appearance of the mouth of a rohita fish.

There are seven hundred channels by which this body is nourished—like a field by irrigation ditches or a garden by water-carrying conduits—and it is sustained by them through actions such as contraction and expansion. From their root at the navel, they spread upwards, downwards, and transversely. Of these, there are forty principal vessels: ten carry wind (vāta), ten carry bile (pitta), ten carry phlegm (śleṣman), and ten carry blood (rakta).
Among them, those carrying *vāta* and located in the seats of *vāta* number one hundred and seventy-five (81).

Similarly, those carrying *pitta* and so forth, located in the seats of *pitta* and so forth, are likewise that same number. Among these, there are twenty-five *vāta*-carrying vessels in each limb (*śākhā*). There are thirty-four in the trunk (*koṣṭha*). Of these, eight are situated in the pelvis (*śroṇi*), while [the remainder] are supported by the anus and the penis (82).

Two each on the two sides; six on the back and as many (six) on the belly; ten on the chest; forty-one above the collarbone (*jatru*); of these, fourteen are in the neck; four in the two ears; nine in the tongue; six in the nose; eight in the two eyes. Thus, there are one hundred and seventy-five channels carrying wind (*vāta*). This same division applies to those carrying bile (*pitta*) and the others as well; the only difference is that of these, ten are in the eyes and two are in the ears.

In this context, when the winds and other elements move without being deranged through their respective vessels (*sirā*), they produce many beneficial qualities; however, when deranged, they produce defects (*doṣa*). There are twenty-four vessels (*dhamanī*) originating from the navel. Although these are essentially the same as the *sirās*, they are presented in the scriptures as distinct entities due to the difference in their functions. Of these, ten course upwards. Carrying specific [sensory] particulars—such as sound, form, taste, smell, exhalation, inhalation, yawning, sneezing, laughing, speaking, and weeping—they sustain the body. (85–86)

These [channels], having reached the heart, become threefold; thus there are thirty. Among them, two by two carry wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), blood (śoṇita), and nutrient fluid (rasa); thus there are ten. One perceives sound, form, taste, and smell through eight [channels].
One speaks with two and makes noise with two. One sleeps with two and awakens with two. Two are the carriers of waste products (āsrava). Two carry breast milk in women and semen in men. (87–88)

These [ten vessels] support and pervade the body above the navel; they do not perform the function of moving upward. However, there are ten that move downward. They carry urine, feces, semen, menstrual blood, and so forth, and they nourish the body with the essence of food and drink from the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya). || 89 ||

These arise in three ways within the stomach and the large intestine; thus, there are thirty [channels]. Of these, two each carry wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), blood (*śoṇita*), and nutrient essence (*rasa*); those are ten. Two are located in the intestines and carry food. Two carry water. Two are situated in the penis and bladder and carry urine. Two carry semen. Two are situated in the large intestine and anus for the purpose of evacuation. These same two, in women, carry the menstrual flow (*ārtava*). Two are connected to the thick intestine. Two expel speech. (90)

There are eight others that convey sweat laterally; four of these move transversely. Each of these is divided into a hundred thousand branches, so they cannot be numbered. By them this body is latticed, bound, and stretched out. (91) Their openings are connected to the pores of the hair, through which they carry away sweat. They also distribute the essence of food and other substances internally and externally, as well as the potencies of massages and ointments. Through them alone, sensations such as touch and pleasure are perceived. (92) Now, the locations of the vital points (*marmasthāna*):

These total one hundred and seven. In each of those branches, there are exactly forty-four [marmas]: eleven in each of the arms and legs; twelve in the abdomen and chest; fourteen in the back; and thirty-seven in the neck and above. Among these, the marmas of the leg-branch are: chidra, talahṛdaya, kūrca, śiras, gulpha, meḍhra, basti, jānu, āṇī, ūrvī, lohitākṣa, and vitapa—making five [in the leg]. (93)

Likewise, the other thigh-marmas are: the *bāhu*, *kṣipra*, *tala*, *hṛdaya*, *kūrca*, *śiromani*, *maṇibandha*, *indrabasti*, *kūrpara*, the two *ūrvī*, the two *lohitākhyā*, the *kakṣadhara*, and the *kaṭīndhara*. The same applies to the other arm. (94) In the abdomen and chest, however, they are: the *guda*, *basti*, *nābhi*, *hṛdaya*, *stanamūla*, *rohitā*, *palāpa*, the two *asta*, and the two *vaṃsau*. In the back and waist, they are: the *taruṇa*, *kukundara*, *nitamba*, the two *pārśvasandhi*, the two *bṛhatī*, the *aṃsaphalaka*, and the two *aṃsa*. (95)

There are four vessels (dhamanīs) above the collarbone; eight *mātṛkā*s; two *kṛkāṭikā*s; two *vidhura*s; two *phaṇa*s; two *apāṅga*s; two [vessels] carrying wind (*vātāvaha*); two *utkṣepa*s; two *śaṅkha*s; one *sthapanī*; five *sīmanta*s; four *śṛṅgāṭaka*s; and one *adhipati*. These are the vital points (*marmāṇi*). (96) Because of the convergence of flesh, vessels, ligaments, and bones, the life-breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) reside in them by their very nature. Therefore, those who seek liberation must restrain these [breaths] within them. (97)
When these [marmas] are struck, one reaches the states that will be described hereafter. Among them, those that take life immediately are the fiery (āgneya) ones.

When the qualities of fire (agni-guṇa) have been rapidly exhausted, they destroy [life]. And they are: the throat, the dhamani, the mātṛkā, the śṛṅgāṭaka, the apāṅga, the sthaphaṇika, the kakṣa, the base of the breast, the stanarohita, the adhipati, the śaṅkha, the guḍa, the hṛdaya, the basti, and the nābhi marmas. Those that take life after a lapse of time are the lunar (saumya) and fiery (āgneya) ones.

When the qualities of fire (agni) have been gradually exhausted, they deplete the qualities of soma over the course of time. These vital points (marman) are: the chest, the sīmanta, the talas, the eyes, the penis, the bladder, the hips, the two taruṇa joints, the sides, the two bṛhatīs, and the buttocks;
these are indeed those that cause death after a lapse of time. 100.
The Vāyavya [marmas] are those that remove the arrow but take away life. As long as the vital air remains obstructed within the opening of the arrowhead, so long does one live;

however, as soon as the arrow is extracted, the life-force residing in the marma-site departs. These include the two *utkṣepas* and the two *sthapanīs*, which cause impairment; for Soma, due to its stability and coolness, provides support to the life-force.
The *lohitākṣas*, the two knees, the two *urvīs*, the two *kūrcas*, the two *viṭapas*, and the two *kūrparas*.
The *kakundhara*, *kakṣandhara*, *vidhura*, and the two *sakṛkāṭika* [are mentioned].
The *aṃsa*, *aṃsaphalaka*, *apāṅga*, *nīla*, *manya*, and *phaṇa* are likewise [listed]. They say that the *āvartas*, occurring in pairs, produce deformity. 103–104.
Those belonging to the fire and wind [elements] are particularly painful;
one should know that these eight—the two ankles, the two wrists, and the two *kūrcaśiras*—are specifically cause-makers of pain for the wise man. 105.
Now, the individual vital points (*marmasthāna*) are described:

among them, between the big toe and the second toe is the *kṣipra* vital point. One pierced there dies from convulsions (*kṣepaka*). In the middle of the sole of the foot, following the sequence of the middle toes, is the *talahr̥daya* (sole-heart) vital point; one pierced there dies from pains. 106.

The ankle (gulpha) is at the junction of the shank and the foot; there, pain occurs, as does stiffness of the foot or lameness. Below both sides of the ankle joint is the "kūrca-head" (the tendons of the instep). There, pain and swelling occur. Above and on both sides of the *kṣipra* vessel is the "kūrca" (the calf muscle); there, the foot experiences spinning and trembling. 107.

The *indrabasti* is located midway between the heel and the middle of the calf; there, death results from loss of blood. The knee (*jānu*) is at the junction of the calf and the thigh; there, lameness occurs. Three finger-breadths above the knee on both sides is the *aṇī*; there, an increase in emaciation and stiffness of the thighs occur. (108)

In the middle of the thighs is the *ūrvī* [marman]; there, due to the filling of the marrow-cavity with blood, one dies from cough and dyspnea. At the end, from the depletion of blood, there is wasting of the thigh (*sakthi-śoṣa*). Above the *ūrvī*, between the groin-joint and the root of the thigh, is the *lohitākṣa*. There, through the loss of blood, hemiplegia (*pakṣāghāta*) occurs. (109) Between the groin and the testicles is the *viṭapa*. There, lameness or diminished semen results. These are the *marman*s of the thighs. The same applies to the arms. This is the distinction: the *gulpha*, *jānu*, and *viṭapa* do not occur elsewhere; instead, those [corresponding] locations in the arm are the *maṇibandha*, *kūrpara*, and *kakṣadhara*. (110)

Among those, at the wrist-joint (*maṇibandha*) there is *kaṇṭha*; at the elbow (*kūrpara*) there is *kuṇi*. Between the chest and the armpit is *kakṣadhara*; there, [wounding] causes hemiplegia (*pakṣāghāta*). Thus, there are forty branch-vital points (*śākhāmarmāṇi*). (111) Now, the vital points of the abdomen and the chest: for the arms as well, it is the same; this is the distinction. Among them, the vital point named *guda* is connected to the large intestine (*sthūlāntra*) and serves to expel wind and feces; if pierced there, death occurs instantly. Inside the waist, where flesh and blood are scant, is the bladder (*basti*), the reservoir of urine; there too, death occurs instantly, except in the case of a wound caused by a urinary stone (*aśmarī*). (112)

In that case as well, if it is pierced on both sides, one does not survive; if pierced on one side, one survives. Or, if pierced on one side, there occurs a wound with a discharge of urine. The navel is the origin of the vessels located between the two receptacles of digested food (the stomach and the large intestine); there, death is instantaneous. (113) The heart is between the two breasts; there too, death is instantaneous. Two finger-breadths below the breasts, at the root of both, is the *stanamūla*; there, one dies due to the abdominal cavity being filled with phlegm (*kapha*). Above the nipples of the breasts is the *stanarohita*; there, one dies due to the abdominal cavity being filled with blood, accompanied by cough and dyspnea. (114)

Below the two shoulder-tops (aṃsakūṭa), on the upper portions of the sides, are the apalāpas; death results from blood located in the portion of pus there. (115) Now, the vital points of the back (pṛṣṭhamarmāṇi):

therein, on both sides of the spinal column (pṛṣṭhavaṃśa), corresponding to each hip-basin (śroṇikāṇḍa), are the kaṭīkataruṇa bones. There, due to the loss of blood, one dies pale, discolored, and with impaired form. On the outer part of the sides and buttocks, on both sides of the spinal column, are the kakundaras; there, there is loss of sensation to touch and impairment of movement in the lower body. (116)

The *nitamba* (hips) are the two coverings over the *śroṇi-kāṇḍa* (buttock regions), situated on the sides opposite each other; death occurs there due to the wasting of the lower body and weakness. The *jaghana-pārśva-sandhi* (groin-hip joint) connects the lower sides with the middle of the flanks, extending obliquely and upward from the *jaghana*; death occurs there because the abdominal cavity becomes filled with blood. 117.

On both sides of the spinal column, at the base of the breasts, are the *bṛhatī* [marma-s]; there, one dies from complications arising from excessive hemorrhaging. Above the back, on both sides of the spinal column and connected to the *trika*, are the *aṃsaphalaka* [marma-s]; there, numbness and wasting of the arms occur. Between the upper arm and the neck, at the binding point of the shoulder-blade and the shoulder, is the *aṃsa* [marma]; there, stiffness of the arm occurs. (118) Now, the *marma-s* located above the clavicle (*ūrdhvajatrūgata*)—

There are four vessels (dhamanīs) on both sides of the throat canal: two *nīla* and two *manyā*. When [the wind] affects them alternately, there occurs muteness, distortion of the voice, and death. The *kṛkāṭika* are the joints of the head and neck; when [the wind] affects them, there is instability and upward tilting of the head. The *vidhurau* are located below and behind the ears; when [the wind] affects them, there is deafness. The *phaṇau* are located internally on both sides, blocking the channels of the nasal passage; when [the wind] affects them, there is loss of the sense of smell. The *apāṅgau* are located externally below the outer corners of the eyes between the ends of the eyebrows; when [the wind] affects them, there is blindness or impairment of vision. 119–120.

Between the eyebrows and above them, in the middle of the ears and the forehead, are the two *śaṅkhas*; death occurs there immediately. Above the two *śaṅkhas*, at the ends of the hair, are the two *utkṣepas*; one lives there as long as the arrow-head remains embedded, but dies once it has been extracted. (121) Between the eyebrows is the *sthaphaṇī*; in that case, it is like the *utkṣepas*. There are five joints on the head divided by the *sīmantas*; death there occurs through madness, fear, or loss of consciousness. (122)

Among the vessels that nourish the nose, ears, eyes, and tongue, there is the confluence of vessels at the head; these are the four *śṛṅgāṭaka* vital points (*marman*), and there too death is instantaneous. Furthermore, above the interior of the skull, where the vessels and joints converge, is the *adhipati* point covered with hair; there too death is indeed instantaneous. Thus, these constitute one hundred and seven vital points. 123.

Now, this is the measurement: the thighs, the heads, and the sides with the armpits are each measured at one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) above the base of the breasts. Know that the wrists and ankles are two finger-breadths; the knees, along with the elbows, are three. They say the heart, bladder, pubic region, anus, and navel are four [finger-breadths]; on the head they are five, and on the neck ten and two. These are equal in size to one's own closed palm; know that the remaining parts are half a finger-breadth in circumference.

"Jānusaparam" means that one should know [the distance] including the second knee to be three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). There are four *śṛṅgāṭakas*. There are five *sīmanta*s. In the throat there are ten, and those two [additional ones], making twelve. There are eight *mātṛkā*s. There are two *nīla*s and two *manye*s. (126) "Those are measured by one's own hands," etc.; the meaning is that they are four finger-breadths in measure. Know that the remaining fifty-six vital points (*marman*) are measured at half a finger-breadth. However, some say that these fifty-six *marman* are equal to the contracted palm of one's own hand, measuring four finger-breadths. (127)

Others, however, state that there are two at the base of the breasts, two at the ankles, four at the *indravasti* (the perineum), and two at the wrists—these ten measure two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*) each. There are two knees, four others [at the elbows], and two at the forearms; thus, these eight [measure one finger-breadth each]. (128) In the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*:

"From that time forward, she should avoid physical exercise, strenuous exertion, sexual intercourse, over-nutrition, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, grief, fear, riding in vehicles, suppressing natural urges, squatting in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture, and bloodletting. (129)

In that same work, the symptoms of pregnancy are stated as follows: "Immediately upon conceiving, there is fatigue, debility, thirst, throbbing of the thighs, the continued presence of semen and blood, and a tingling sensation in the vagina," and so forth.
(130) Furthermore, Yājñavalkya says: "His bodies are sixfold, and the six layers of skin sustain them."

There are six limbs, and likewise, with the bones, there are three hundred and sixty. These belong to that self which is born from a womb; generally, bodies are also born from eggs. They consist of the transformation of the essence of food being cooked by the fire situated within their respective sheaths, and are of six types according to the distinction of blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
(131–133) He says this very thing:

Together with their locations, there are sixty-four teeth and twenty nails; the digits of the hands and feet also consist of these, and their locations number four. (134) The Locations: There are thirty-two bones situated in the regions at the roots of the teeth; together with them, there are thirty-two teeth. Thus, [the total for the teeth and their locations] is sixty-four. The nails are twenty; the bone-like structures at their bases are also twenty. Thus, [the total for the nails and their locations] is forty. Of those bones, beginning with the nails, there are seventeen in the two hands and the chest. Thus, [the total for the hands, chest, and nails] is twenty-three. (23) Thus, [the total count] is three hundred and sixty. (360) (135)
Likewise, fragrance, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
while the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ear are the sense organs.

"The root *ṣiñ* means 'to bind'; therefore, [the senses] are called *viṣayas* because they bind one to their objects. Thus it has been said. (136) One should know that the hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the feet are indeed the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), while the mind (*manas*) is of a dual nature. (137)
The navel, the spleen, the rectum, the testicles, the blood, the two temples, as well as the head, the shoulders, and the heart—these are the abodes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
He now elaborates upon these abodes of the *prāṇas*: [138]
The omentum, the two kidneys, the pericardium, the liver, the spleen,
the small intestine, the large intestine, the bladder, the rectum,
the stomach, the heart, the colon, and the anus. (139)
The abdomen and the two rectal regions (guda)—this is declared to be the breadth [of the body].

(140) *Vapā* is well-known [as the omentum]. *Vasā* is the fat of the flesh. *Avahanana* is the *puppuṣa* (the pulmonary cartilage). *Plīhā* is well-known in Āyurveda; these two are shaped like masses of flesh and are located in the left side of the belly. *Yakṛt* (the liver); *kālikā* and *kloman* are masses of flesh, and they are located in the right side of the belly. (141) The two *vṛkkau* (kidneys) are masses of flesh situated near the heart. *Basti* is the bladder, the receptacle for urine. *Purīṣādhāna* is the receptacle for feces. Inside the outer ring of the anus, there are two inner rings of the anus; those two are the rectal regions (*guda*) and the abdominal cavities (*koṣṭha*). (142)

The *kānīnike* are the two eyelids. The *śaṣkulī* and *karṇapatraka* are the two earlobes (*karṇapālī*). The teeth are two or eight; the *dantapālī* are the two rows of teeth. The *kakundare* are the two hollows of the loins (*jaghanakūpaka*). The *vaṅkṣaṇa* is the joint between the loins and the thighs. The two *vṛkkau* (kidneys) have been mentioned previously; they are produced at the joints of the phlegm (*śleṣma*). (143) The *upajihvikā* is the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*). The *sphijau* are the two buttocks (*kaṭiprotha*). The *piṇḍikā* are the fleshy parts of the calves and thighs. Including the two fleshy parts of the feet, there are these four locations. Thus, there are one hundred and four [parts]. (144)

Furthermore, there are sixty bones in the fingers; two on each side [of the feet], and four in the ankles (4). There are four bones in the *aralikā* [knees], and the same number in the shanks (*jaṅghā*). For each of the twenty fingers, there are three bones; thus, there are sixty bones connected to the fingers. In the feet, the two posterior parts are the heels (*pārṣṇī*), and there are two bones for them. In the ankles, there are four. Thus, there are six in the arms, measuring one *arali*, and four in the shanks as well; thus, there are seventy-four (74) (146).

One should point out two bones each arising at the knees, the cheeks, the surfaces of the thighs, the shoulders, the palate, the *tālūṣaka*, and the surfaces of the hips. The knee (*jānu*) is the joint of the shank and the thigh; the cheek (*kapola*) is the *galla*; the thigh (*ūru*) is the *sakthi*. Its surface is the shoulder (*aṃsa*), which is the root of the arm. (147) Between the ear and the eye, below the region of the temples and so forth, is the *tālūṣaka*—the palate (*kākuda*). The hip is the *kakudminī*; its surface is the pelvic surface. In each of these locations there are exactly two bones; thus, there are fourteen. (148)

There is one bone called the *bhaga*, likewise forty-five on the back, fifteen bones in the neck, one in the collarbone (*jatru*), and likewise one in the jaw (*hanu*). There is one in the private parts; forty-five on the back; fifteen in the neck; and in the two breasts there is the joint of the collarbone (*jatru*) and the sub-collarbone (*pratijatru*). (149) Each jaw and the chin is one each; thus, [these] make sixty-four. At its base are two [bones], as well as the forehead, eyes, cheeks, and the nose. The ribs together with the sockets (*sthālaka*) and the *arbuda* bones number seventy-two. (150)

At the root of that jaw (hanu) are two bones. The middle region of the forehead, extending from the eyes to the temples, is called the *gaṇḍa*; there, too, are two pairs of bones each. The *nāsāvyañjakāsthīni* are the bones located in the region below the armpits (*kakṣādhaḥ*). (151) The *pārśvakas* are the bones supported by those *sthālakas*, along with the specific bone-types known as *arbudas*. Together with these, the *pārśvakas* number seventy-two. When added to the nine previously mentioned, they total eighty-one. (152) There are two *śaṅkhakas* and four *kapālas* of the head.

The chest consists of seventeen bones; this is the summary of the bones of a person. (153) The *śaṅkhakas* are the specific bones located in the region between the eyebrows and the ears. There are four [bones] of the head: the region of the chest, the two *galaśuṇḍikās*, the joint between the base of the jaw and the throat, and the *śīrṣaśiras*. (154) A *pravaṭa* is any depressed area on the body, such as the base of the neck or the armpits. Likewise, there are four *vartmas*, which are the two white [scleral] areas on each side of the pupil of the eye. (155)
The pair of eyes, the pair of ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the anus, and the generative organ—these nine apertures are the abodes of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
(156) There are exactly seven hundred vessels (sirā), nine hundred sinews (snāyu), two hundred arteries (dhamanī), and five hundred muscles (peśī). (157)

There are forty vessels connected to the navel that carry *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*; branching out in various directions and pervading the entire body, they number seven hundred. Likewise, there are nine hundred *snāyu* (ligaments) that bind the joints of the limbs and their subdivisions. There are twenty-four *dhamanī* (arteries) originating from the navel that carry the vital airs (*prāṇa* and so forth); through their various branches, they become two hundred.

The *peśīs* (muscles) are fleshy in form and connected to the major and minor limbs, such as the calves and so forth; there are five hundred of them. Regarding these very vessels—veins and the rest—the author states another number due to the abundance of their branches:
"One should know that the total number of the series of veins and arteries is twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred, and fifty-six. (161)
Furthermore:
Three hundred thousand hairs on the beard and head are to be known as belonging to embodied beings;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) and two hundred joints. 162.

This is the count for the combined beard and head hair. There are two hundred bone-joints. However, the joints of the tendons, veins, and so forth are infinite; as for the body hairs, there are fifty-four crores (540 million). Furthermore, sixty-seven and a half lakhs (6,750,000) are counted by the openings of perspiration through which the vital winds pass—this is the meaning. Although this is difficult to know because it is beyond the range of the eyes and other senses, it has been stated according to the perspective of the scriptures; the sense is that whoever understands this is fortunate. (163–164) He now states the measurements of the bodily fluids and so forth:
Nine añjalis of rasa (nutrient fluid) are to be known, and ten of water;
seven of feces, and eight of blood are proclaimed.
Six of phlegm, five of bile, and four of urine as well. (165)
There are three parts of fat, two of marrow, and one part of fat; but the marrow alone is in the head. There is as much phlegm as there is dust, and just as much semen.
He who seeks liberation must understand that Brahman is thus unstable. (166–167)

There are ten *añjali*s of water as the cause for the cohesion of the earthly atoms [of the body]. Such is the measure of the essence of the transformed food (*rasa*). Likewise, at the head, the measure of the marrow, phlegm, and the essence of semen is exactly half an *añjali*.
(168) This refers to a body with balanced humors (*dhātu*); however, there is no fixed rule for one whose humors are unbalanced.
As it is said in the Āyurveda:
Furthermore, there is a diversity of bodies because they are not fixed;
likewise, there is no fixed measure for the humors, tissues, and wastes.
Here, he states the nature of that which is to be meditated upon:
Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is a lunar orb,
and within that stands the Self, motionless like a lamp.
Having known that which is to be known here, he is not born again;
for [that is] the meaning of "the light of the Self residing in the *suṣumnā* should be realized.
Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses free from other objects—

The Self that resides in the heart like a lamp is the Lord who is to be meditated upon (dhyeya). This very state of being the object of meditation for the Self consists in the turning away of the mental fluctuations from external objects toward the Self through their suppression—like the one-pointedness of a lamp whose light is confined within a pair of reed-shields. Regarding what is to be reflected upon during the time of meditation, he says: "The recollection of past objects: who is the cause of dreams and so forth? Who is this person adorned with birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and the rest? Even this [person], though consisting of objects such as sound and the like, is [perceived] by means of the mind, action, and speech. (174)

Now, specifically, the anatomy relevant to *prāṇāyāma* as stated by Yājñavalkya is described: In that regard, for almost everyone, the body measures ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) according to one's own fingers. From that, the *prāṇa* extends twelve finger-breadths.

(175) And that [prāṇa] should be held within the center of the body, unified with the fire situated in the middle of one’s own body, by one who desires immortality and other such states. The location of the fire, however, is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis. (176)

The heart of humans is triangular and has the luster of molten gold; that of animals is square and situated in the middle of the belly; and the orb of birds is in the middle of the chest. Starting from there, nine finger-breadths above is the location of the *kanda* (the bulbous root).

The *kanda* is four finger-breadths in width and height, shaped like an egg, and adorned with skin and other tissues. In its center is the navel-cakra, which serves as the foundation for the body. In that cakra, impelled by merit and demerit, the individual soul (*jīva*)—mounted upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) below and situated within a web of channels—wanders like a spider.

Above that, the Kuṇḍalinī power resides horizontally and vertically within the ether; she consists of the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti) and is coiled eight times. Constantly obstructing the flow of air, water, food, and so forth, she remains forever situated around the sides of the *kanda*. (179–180)
Having thus completely enveloped the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with the mouth,
at the time of yoga, she— blazing intensely in the form of a serpent within the space of the heart— awakens by means of the *apāna* wind together with the fire. 181.
Then the vital breath (vāyu), together with its companion, proceeds through the *suṣumnā*.
The channel situated in the middle of the *kanda* is celebrated as the *suṣumnā*.
Around it, within this wheel (*cakra*), reside those known as channels (*nāḍīs*). 182–183.

There, within the *kanda*, seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍīs*) have arisen; among them, fourteen are primary: 1. Iḍā, 2. Piṅgalā, 3. Suṣumnā, 4. Sarasvatī, 5. Vāruṇā, 6. Pūṣā, 7. Hastijihvā, 8. Yaśasvinī, 9. Viśvodarā, 10. Kuhū, 11. Śaṅkhinī, 12. Payasvinī, 13. Alambuṣā, and 14. Gāndhārī. Of these, the first three are the most important; even among those, the Suṣumnā is the supreme, the sustainer of the universe, and the bringer of liberation. (184)

And that [Suṣumnā] is situated at the crown aperture (brahmarandhra) in the head, together with the bone located in the middle of the back, like the string of a lute upon the neck of the lute; it rests within the bulb (kanda). To its left is the Iḍā, in which dwells the nectar-filled moon;

to its right is the Piṅgalā, in which dwells the poison-filled sun. These two alone, consisting of darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas), fashion night and day. But the Suṣumnā, the consumer of time, consists of goodness (sattva) and has Fire as its presiding deity. Sarasvatī and Kuhū are situated on either side of the Suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā are located behind and in front of Iḍā [respectively].
Viśvodarā is situated between Kuhū and Hastijihvā.
Just as Svadhā is established in the middle of Kuhū, Vāruṇā is likewise established.
In the eastern portion of the *suṣumnā*, the *kuhū* is situated as far as the penis;
it should be known to extend downward and upward, belonging to Varuṇa and reaching everywhere.
And the *yaśasvanī* is held to belong to Yama, extending as far as the big toe of the foot. (189)
Know from me, O my beloved, that Piṅgalā goes upward to the right, reaching the end of the nose (190).
To the right of Piṅgalā, Pūṣā reaches the end of the eye;
likewise, O Gārgī, Payasvinī is held to reach the end of the right ear (191).
Likewise, Sarasvatī is established above the tongue;
Śaṅkhinī goes upward from the left ear to the tip of the trunk of the lordly elephant.
Gāndhārī is situated behind Īḍā, reaching to the corner of the left eye.
The *iḍā* is situated on the left side, ending at the left nostril.
Likewise, the *hastijihvā* is held to extend to the big toe of the left foot.
The channel called *viśvodarā*, however, is situated in the middle of the abdomen. (193–194)
O highly fortunate one, Alambuṣā is situated with her face turned downwards in the middle of the navel.
From these [channels] others have arisen, and from those [others], yet other vessels;
just as it is on the leaf of an Ashvattha tree, so too are the vessels upon the petals of a lotus. (195)
O one rich in asceticism, within all these channels (nāḍīs), the following are to be known:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
These ten winds move through all the channels (nāḍīs).
Among these, the five beginning with prāṇa are primary; among those, prāṇa and apāna are primary, and of those two, prāṇa alone is the most primary.
[It resides] between the mouth and the nose, in the center of the heart, and in the region of the navel.
Some say that the abode of the vital breath (prāṇa) is even in the big toe.
The one known as prāṇa resides both below and above the kuṇḍalī, surrounding it;
dwelling within these three [channels], it becomes manifest like a lamp.
Some indeed say that the abode of the *apāna* wind is in the anus, the penis, the thighs, and the knees;
others say it is in the abdomen, the testicles, the hips, the shanks, and the navel.
However, the *apāna* wind stands between the anus and the base of the genitals.
In these locations it constantly shines like a lamp:
Vyāna resides in the ears, the middle of the eyes, the throat-tube, and the ankles;
it also stays in the nose, the throat, and the region of the buttocks—of this there is no doubt. (201–202)
Udāna resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and hands.
Samāna is situated pervading all the limbs, having spread throughout the entire body.
It distributes all consumed flavors throughout the body together with the digestive fire.
Moving through the seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍī-mārgas),
the single Samāna wind alone remains pervading [the body] along with fire;
together with the fires, it is present everywhere throughout the entire physical frame, including its limbs and minor parts.
The five winds, beginning with *nāga*, reside within the skin, bones, and other tissues.
Having equalized the water, food, and even the bodily fluids located in the stomach,
the *prāṇa* wind, situated in the center of the abdomen, separates them one by one.
Having placed water above the fire and food and other substances upon the water,
one should oneself reach the *apāna* [wind]; together with that very wind,
it proceeds to the flame there, and by means of that, it enters once more into the center.
Impelled by the apāna wind,
O best of Brahmins, the fire then gradually blazes within one’s own body in its own seat.
There, the fire is then impelled by the prāṇa along with its flames.
Furthermore, the water situated within the interior of the stomach makes the food, along with its condiments, extremely hot;
then the fire cooks it by means of that heated water. (210–211)
Sweat and urine would be water, and *rasa* would take the form of semen;
the feces would be food, O Gārgī, and the *prāṇa* would perform its functions separately [in each].
Together with the *samāna* wind, it distributes the *rasa* into all the channels.
Pervading the body in the form of breath, the wind moves within it.
All the winds continuously perform the excretion of feces, urine, and so forth, by means of the nine apertures of the body. (213–214)
Exhalation, inhalation, and coughing are proclaimed as the function of the *prāṇa* [vital air].

The evacuation of feces, urine, and so forth is the function of the *apāna* [downward-moving air]. The activities of giving, taking up, and moving about are called the function of the *vyāna* [pervasive air]. (215)
That which causes the elevation of the body and so forth is declared to be the *udāna* action.
From *devadatta*, however, comes lethargy (*tandrā*), while yawning and the like arise from *dhanañjaya*.
Having thus understood the arrangement of the channels (*nāḍī*) in relation to the functions of the arrangement of the vital airs (*vāyu*).
Perform the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana) according to the path prescribed by the rules.

Now, the anatomy useful for specific meditative contemplations (bhāvanā), as sung in various Upaniṣads, accepted by the great yogins who perceive that truth, and set down in writing by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya and others in their respective works, is here set forth.

In this regard, although all sacred sites (tīrtha) as well as even those with water flowing against the current have been established by the knowers of that [truth] as being composed of Brahman, nevertheless, for the sake of one engaged in practice whose primary contemplation concerns pilgrimage, something specific is now stated. 219.

Ayodhyā is in the head; Mathurā is in the heart; Māyā is in the *mūlādhāra*; Kāśī is between the eyebrows; Kāñcī is in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; Avantī is in the *maṇipūra*; Dvārāvatī is in the throat; Prayāga is at the tip of the nose; the Gaṅgā is in the *iḍā* [nāḍī]; the Yamunā is in the *piṅgalā*; and the Sarasvatī is in the *suṣumnā*. In the other *nāḍīs*, all rivers such as the Narmadā and others are present. Therefore, in each respective location, that particular sacred ford (*tīrtha*) should be meditated upon, either through the relationship of container and contained or by way of non-difference. (220)

And thus there are two *śirasīs*. From below the throat down to the navel is one; from below the navel down to the feet is another—these constitute the three *grāmas*. In the hairy regions such as the head, beard, heart, and armpits, there are fourteen *araṇyas*. In the hairless regions such as the forehead and so forth, there are nine vowels (*svaras*). Furthermore, near the *puryaḥ* and so on, there are the *upapuryaḥ* and so on; thus the body consists of all the *tārthas*. 221.

Now, for the sake of the procession of the deities within the body, the deities are thus designated: Consciousness and Bliss are the Person (Puruṣa) in the form of Śiva; the qualities such as Sattva and the rest are Nature (Prakṛti) in the form of Śakti. Because everything is derived from these two as its material cause, all is composed of them. 222.

Thus, Vāsudeva resides in the *citta*; Caturmukha in the *buddhi*; Śaṅkara in the *ahaṃkāra*; Candra in the *manas*; the Quarters (*dik*) in the ears; Vāyu in the skin; and Sūrya in the eyes. Among these, the Person-form who is in the right eye is the Lord (Īśvara) whose nature is Indra; he who is in the left is the Goddess (Īśvarī) whose nature is Indrāṇī. And in the middle of the eyebrows, from the meeting of those two, one should meditate upon them there in the form of the radiance of the eyes. They are the divine couple. 223.

And thus, Varuṇa is in the tongue; the two Aśvinīkumāras are in the nose; Agni is in speech; Indra is in the hands and in valor and so forth; Upendra is in the feet; Yama is in the anus; and Prajāpati is in the generative organ.

(224) In each respective location, that particular deity should be meditated upon through the relationship of support and supported, or the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary, or as non-different [from oneself]. And in this way, there arises the perfection of the respective functions and their fruits. (225) Now, for the purpose of meditating on the fourteen worlds within the body—which is the cause for achieving the state of full I-consciousness—those [worlds] are described. (226)

At the soles of the feet is Pātāla; at the heels and forefeet, Rasātala; at the two ankles, Mahātala; at the two shanks, Talātala; at the two knees, Sutala; at the two thighs, Vitala and Atala; at the hips, Mahītala; at the navel, Bhūrloka; at the abdomen, Bhuvarloka; at the chest, Svarloka; at the neck, Maharloka; at the mouth, Janaloka; at the forehead, Tapoloka; and at the crown of the head, Satyaloka. Furthermore, one should contemplate the goddess as being composed of everything, with Śakra and the other deities located in the arms and other limbs, by means of her own essential existence. (227)

Now, describe those [phonemes] as they are stated in the *Bhuvaneśvarī-stuti*: "Ā is the first head; then A is the face; I and Ī are the two eyes; U is the water of the ears; Ṛ and Ṝ are the two nostril-pits; and the two phonemes following them are the two cheeks. (228)

The upper and lower rows of teeth are the eight pairs of diphthongs in sequence; the root of the tongue is the prominent bindu, while the visarga is the Lord located in the throat. The letters beginning with *ka* are the right arm, and the subsequent group of consonants is the left arm.
O Ambikā, the letters *ṣṭa* and *stā* correspond respectively to your two feet;

*pa* and *pha* to your two sides; *vaṃ* to the lineage born from your back; *śa* to the navel; *tha* to the heart; *da*, *dha*, and *na* to the three vital breaths (*prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *vyāna*); *ya* and the following seven letters to the seven constituent elements (*dhātus*); *sa* with *para* (the letter *ha*) to the vital winds; and *kṣa* to your wrath.
The practical meaning is that one should meditate upon those phonemes at the locations specified for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.
Thus: "O Śivā, this body of yours, composed of phonemes, pervades the three worlds;
I, through such contemplation, recite [the mantra] by superimposing the syllables upon its various limbs. (232)

Having become manifest in bodily form at the close of day, the sciences worship him with their heads—the forms of the lotus—bowed down by sinners, their palms upturned and eager to grant a vision [of him].

(233) Now, the six *cakras*: Therein, the location of the *kanda* is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis. Above that is the triangle of *Kāmarūpa*, possessing the luster of molten gold.

(234) To the left of that triangle is the *Iḍā*; to the right is the *Piṅgalā*; in the middle is the *Suṣumnā*. In the center is the *Citriṇī*, composed of colors; from the arrangement of those colors, the production of the lotus-shaped wheels (*cakra*) occurs as follows: (235)

First, above the form of desire (kāmarūpa), there is the wheel named Mūlādhāra. It is golden in luster. It is adorned in the center by a pericarp-shaped lotus in the form of the earth, which is square with four corners, possesses fifty-six pairs of Śiva and Śakti, and is endowed with the seed-syllable *laṃ* and presided over by Gaṇeśa and others, together with Brahmā and Sarasvatī. It has four petals consisting of the qualities of control (*vaśya*).

In its center is the self-manifested (svayambhū) Śivaliṅga, radiant in form and facing downward, its mouth sealed and encircled by the Kuṇḍalinī, which is of the nature of consciousness, possesses the luster of lightning, and stands in the form of three and a half coils.
Meditated upon, this brings about the attainment of all yogic enjoyments and powers, victory over the earth and other elements, and the favor of Brahmā, Gaṇeśa, and the other deities.

As for the location of Kuṇḍalinī at the navel mentioned by Yājñavalkya, that is intended so that she may be easily understood by the yogi through a slight manifestation when she has become grossified by moving upward; for even there, she exists in this very form. (238) Thus, the locations of the earth element and the others in the heart and other places mentioned by Gorakṣanātha and others are merely alternative views.
