In the view of the yogis, [the elements] exist everywhere; however, they are perceived in specific locations due to the causal complex consisting of meditation and so forth. Therefore, everything is true, since all accomplishments arise from meditation. (239)

Thus, the fact that the presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the power of consciousness (*citkalā*) in the heart is well-known from the Vedas and other sources is not contradicted; for although she has risen from the *mūlādhāra*, she becomes manifest in the heart.

(240) In this very way, even in other Yoga scriptures, that which appears as contradictory should be understood as non-contradictory through the grace of the Guru. This is the direction [of the teaching]. (241) Above that, at the base of the *liṅga*, is the wheel named *svādhiṣṭhāna*. It possesses a luster equal to a fine ruby (*maṇikya*). It is endowed with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, presided over by Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī and others, and consists of fifty-two couples. (242)

In the center, it is adorned with a supreme pericarp that is white, shaped like a half-moon, and composed of water; it possesses six petals consisting of the letters *va*, *bha*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, and *la*. For those who meditate upon it, this lotus causes the pleasure of Viṣṇu and bestows victory and other blessings. (243) Next, in the navel is the wheel named Maṇipūraka. It has the brilliance of lightning and is presided over by Śaṅkara together with Pārvatī, accompanied by the seed-syllable *Raṃ*; it contains sixty-two pairs [of deities]. (244)

It is adorned in the center by an excellent pericarp in the form of light, shaped like a triangle with the radiance of the rising sun; it consists of the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, has ten petals, and for those who follow their own nature, it brings about the joy of Bhavānī and Śaṅkara, as well as spiritual victory and other benefits.

(245) Now, in the heart is the wheel named Anāhata. These deities are established upon the support of the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and the sixteen transformations; thus, it is renowned in the Āgamas and other scriptures by names such as "the sixteen-spoked" and "the sixteen supports. (246)

And that [wheel] is smoke-colored. It is adorned in the center by a six-cornered [hexagon] associated with the seed-syllable *maṃ*, presided over by Īśvara together with Prakṛti, possessing fifty-four couples, and marked by the Śiva-liṅga named Bāṇa; it has an excellent pericarp in the form of air. It consists of twelve petals composed of the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*. For those who are naturally inclined toward liberation, it effects the conquest of Prakṛti, Īśvara, and Vāyu. This is the wheel named Viśuddha in the throat. And that is white, associated with the seed-syllable *aṃ*. (247)

It is adorned in its center by a supreme pericarp, which has the nature of the sky, possesses the luster of pure rays, and is encircled by seventy-two pairs of deities presided over by Sadāśiva in his form as Ardhanārīśvara. It consists of sixteen petals representing the letters of one's own [alphabet], and it always brings about the joy of Sadāśiva and victory for those who contemplate it. (248)

Between the eyebrows is the wheel named Ājñā. It is shaped like a pearl and is adorned in its center by an excellent pericarp in the form of a mind, which has sixty-four male and female deities, possesses the form of the syllable *haṃ*, and is presided over by the individual soul (*jīva*) together with ignorance (*avidyā*). Its petals consist of the two phonemes *ha* and *la*. It is characterized by another Śiva-liṅga known as Bhairavānanda. For those who possess self-nature, it is the cause of self-pleasure, mental joy, and so forth. (249)

The region of earth extends from the feet up to the knees; it is characterized by the previously mentioned qualities, such as being associated with the seed-syllable *laṃ* and presided over by Brahmā. Similarly, the region of water extends from the knees down to the anus. The region of fire extends from the anus up to the heart. The region of air extends from the center of the heart up to the midpoint of the eyebrows. The region of ether extends from the midpoint of the eyebrows up to the crown of the head. This is stated in the *Yājñavalkya-gītā*, because [the elements] are accepted as pervading all parts of the body everywhere. (250)

This should be understood as non-contradictory because the defects of those respective entities are logically established. At the crown of the head is the thousand-petaled lotus; that is the abode of the Guru, the Supreme Self, who possesses the radiance of the moon. Above that is the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra); above the forehead is the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva); and above that is primordial nature (prakṛti). 251.

It has been explained that the place of the Puruṣa is in the thousand-petaled [lotus]. Now, rising from the center of the bulb (kanda) near the unstruck (anāhata) [cakra], there is a lotus named Dahara, which has eight petals, a stalk twelve finger-breadths long, and a width of four finger-breadths; though its face is downward, it should be conceived as facing upward.
Therein, impelled by the prāṇa and apāna breaths, bound by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of past karma, and incapable of discernment, the individual soul (jīva) wanders day and night.

In that regard, the sequence of rotation is as follows: first, on the left half of the eastern petal, beginning from the base and extending to the tip of the leaf, one rotates for thirty breaths while relying upon the element of space (*ākāśatattva*). For sixty breaths, the element of air (*vāyutattva*); for ninety breaths, the element of fire (*tejastattva*); for one hundred and twenty breaths, the element of water (*vāritattva*); and for one hundred and fifty breaths, the element of earth (*pṛthvītattva*). (254)

Thus, in one half of the petal, there are four hundred and fifty breaths (*śvāsa*). Likewise, in the other half, starting from the tip of the petal down to the base, first there are one hundred and fifty breaths, which is the earth element (*pṛthvī-tattva*). Then, one hundred and twenty breaths are the water element (*vāri-tattva*). Ninety breaths are the fire element (*tejas-tattva*). Sixty breaths are the air element (*vāyu-tattva*). Thirty breaths revolve by resorting to the space element (*ākāśa-tattva*). Thus, on the complete petal, there are nine hundred breaths.

In this very way, during the rotation through the eight petals, there are seven thousand two hundred breaths (*śvāsa*). By such a rotation, it revolves three times in a day and night. (257) As it has been said: "The upward rotation occurs here day and night; therefore, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths. Gorakṣanātha said:
(258) "Twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths] in a day and night."
"The individual soul (jīva) constantly mutters the mantra 'haṃsa, haṃsa.
By the letter *ha* it goes out; by the letter *sa*, it enters again," and so forth.
(259) Sixty such breaths constitute one ghaṭikā. To illustrate: in the time it takes to pronounce ten long syllables (*gurvakṣara*), approximately one breath occurs for an ordinary person. (260)

Six breaths constitute one *pala*. Three hundred and sixty breaths constitute one *ghaṭikā*. Sixty *ghaṭikās* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*). Three hundred and sixty days and nights constitute a year.

(261) Thus, it should be stated that for each individual, the years and so forth are distinct due to the diversity in the duration of the exhalation of breath. For this very reason, there is an increase in lifespan through *prāṇāyāma*s. For this very reason, even yogins who possess a lifespan of a *kalpa* are said to have a lifespan of a hundred years. (262)

This is because one hundred years of his [the cosmic being’s] breath constitute our own kalpa. Even the astronomers and experts in the science of longevity follow this very sequence. For this reason, at times it must be synchronized with the sequence of the common year. (263) Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the individual soul (*jīva*), revolves within the heart-lotus by relying upon the five elements, so too is this "heart-wheel" (*hṛdayacakra*) drawn for the sake of knowledge. Now, whatever state of mind arises through the breath moving in the petals of the directions starting from the east, such is the case. (264) The movements of the breath in each respective location are described here for the purpose of knowledge. (265)

And likewise, in the *Haṃsopaniṣad*: "I am he, the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*), resembling ten million suns; his activity is eightfold. On the eastern petal is the thought of merit (*puṇya*); in the southeast (Āgneya) arise sleep, laziness, and so forth; in the south (Yāmya) is the thought of cruelty; in the southwest (Nairṛtya) is the intention toward sin; in the west (Vāruṇī) is play; in the northwest (Vāyavya) is the intellect regarding coming and going and the like; in the north (Saumya) is pleasure and delight; in the northeast (Aiśānya) is the giving of wealth; in the center is detachment (*vairāgya*); in the filaments is the waking state (*jāgrat*); in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is dreaming (*svapna*); in the stalk (*liṅga*) is deep sleep (*suṣupti*); in the abandonment of the lotus is the fourth state (*turīya*)," and so forth. (266)

In the *Samarasāra* as well: "When the wind moves through the petals of the directions starting with Indra (the East), one should become angry for the sake of battle; when it moves through the petals starting with Agni (the Southeast), one should be intent on enjoyment; when it moves through the petals starting with Yama (the South), one should be intent on pleasure;

when it moves through the petals starting with Nirṛti (the Southwest), the mind should be inclined toward compassion; when it moves through the petals starting with Varuṇa (the West), one should be intent on bestowing gifts upon kings; and when it moves through the petals starting with Vāyu (the Northwest), one should move for the sake of supreme joy. (267)

[This state] belongs to the Supreme, which consists of the mass of the bliss of Brahman. For this very reason, yogins who have perfected their practice, immediately after the movement of the element of space (*ākāśatattva*), when the flow of breath occurs between two petals during the interval of conjunction with another petal, and when the awakening of the bliss of Brahman has manifested for a mere moment, they stabilize the mind in such a way that the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by the breath, becomes steady within the space between those two petals.
Thereafter, the awakening of the bliss of Brahman occurs incessantly. (268)

For this very reason, yogins who seek the qualities of Indra and others—characterized by sovereignty and so forth—steadily fix the vital breath (śvasana) specifically upon the petals corresponding to Indra and the rest. The means for steadying it therein is as follows: one must incessantly resort to the aforementioned mental modifications (manovṛtti) corresponding to those respective world-protectors (dikpāla), such as "I am Indra," at the same time that the breath circulates through those respective petals. As long as the mental modification conforming to Indra and the others is maintained, the individual soul (jīva), conjoined with the breath, remains fixed precisely on the petal of the direction belonging to that particular deity.

In this very way, as long as the mental state (*manovṛtti*) persists—characterized by the qualities of the elements beginning with space that are about to be described—the individual soul (*jīva*) remains in that very same state for that duration of time. This is the essence of the Guru’s instruction (verse 270). Now follows the examination of the flow of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with space, according to the Guru’s instruction. As stated in the *Gurupadeśasāra*: "The examination of the flow of the principles beginning with space is explained according to the Guru’s instruction" (verse 271).

When the individual soul (jīva), impelled by the breath and relying upon the reality of space (ākāśatatva), wanders like a hawk in flight bound by the specific latent impressions (vāsanā) of past actions, then the breath exiting through the nostrils—neither hot nor cold to the touch, circular in shape, and extending even twelve finger-breadths in length—becomes a wondrous variegated color, assuming red, white, black, and other hues as it spreads its reach over the palm of the hand placed at the tip of the nose.

And when a mirror is placed at the tip of the nose, the transformation of the soiled shadow produced by the connection with the breath—which gradually undergoes contraction within the center of the mirror—clearly manifests as a circular shape and a variegated color. || 272 ||

Thus, when the air-element is being carried [in the breath], this wind is neither hot nor cold to the touch and is light. It has a hexagonal shape, measures nine finger-breadths, and is perceived as moving obliquely from the tip of the nose to the palm of the hand and other such places; it arises with a smoky color. As before, when the reflection on a mirror is contracted, its hexagonal shape and smoky color are clearly observed. (273)

Thus, when the fire element (*tejas-tattva*) flows, the breath becomes warm, red, triangular in shape, six finger-breadths in length, and its touch is felt on the upper part of the palm or other areas placed at the tip of the nose. Furthermore, the redness and triangularity of the reflection in a mirror are perceived. (274) Likewise, when the water element (*jala-tattva*) flows, the breath becomes cool, white in color, and crescent-moon shaped. Its movement extends for less than six finger-breadths. Its touch is felt on the lower part of the palm or other areas placed at the tip of the nose. Moreover, the crescent-moon shape and white color of a dirty reflection in a mirror are observed. (275)

In the flow of the earth-element (*pṛthvī-tattva*), the breath is neither hot nor cold, yellow in color, and four-cornered; its movement becomes manifest in the middle of the palm of the hand placed at the tip of the nose and so forth. That the reflection in a mirror is four-cornered and yellow in color should be understood through such instructions from the Guru.
(276) Now, as an incidental point, something else is also stated:

thereafter, for five *ghaṭikās*, the right channel (*dakṣiṇa-nāḍī*) flows under the names of the Sun and so forth. Then, starting from the fourth [unit] up to the sixtieth, first the right channel flows, and then the left channel (*vāma-nāḍī*). (277)

Thus, by five *ghaṭikās*—comprising eighteen hundred breaths (1800)—the movement through one *nāḍī* via the circulation through two petals occurs according to the stated sequence; this is appropriate at the time of the commencement of a lunar day (*tithi*) if it indeed happens so.

Then, auspiciousness arises on that lunar day. Conversely, if the opposite occurs, the result is the opposite. Furthermore, in the flow of the lunar channel (*cāndravahe*), auspicious acts such as royal audiences become fruitful. However, in the flow of the solar channel (*sūryanāḍīvahe*), inauspicious acts such as battle, killing, and eradication (*uccāṭana*) succeed.
As it is said in the *Samarasāra*: [The verse from the Samarasāra follows here.]
When the Moon flows [in the left channel], activities such as visiting kings, observing omens, entering houses, wearing turbans, consecrations, and marriage ceremonies will be auspicious.
However, when Saturn flows [in the right], activities such as bathing, sexual union, enjoyment, and warfare will truly result in inauspicious fruits.

This, however, must be considered: if it is the time for eating, cohabitation, and so forth while the Vāmanāḍī (left channel) is flowing, one should perform them during the time the Dakṣiṇanāḍī (right channel) is flowing; for even if the breath is restrained in the left, it flows through the right channel.

In this very manner, by restraining the right channel through such means as lying on the right side, one should bring the breath flowing in the right channel into the left channel and establish the time for its flow in the left channel. (282) Thereby, [the yogi] accomplishes travel, subjugation, the cessation of summer heat, and so forth. If the yogi always causes the breath to flow through the right channel at night and through the left channel during the day, then he conquers Time.
(283) For at night, due to the cold and other factors, and during the day, due to the movement of the sun and other factors, he is not overcome [by Time]. Furthermore—

When the *arka* (fire) element flows through the *hari-helayā* channel, it is no wonder that a certain individual slays many; for, having cast his enemies and even his own army into the void (*śūnya*) on the side of the vehicle, he scatters a hundred thousand foes in an instant. (284) The meaning is this: when the fire element (*tejas-tattva*) flows through the right channel (*dakṣiṇa-nāḍī*), then even a single warrior, like Śrī Kṛṣṇa, slays many enemies. Furthermore, by placing the enemy army in the direction of the void channel (*śūnya-nāḍī*) while keeping his own army in the direction of the flowing [fire] channel, one who fights—even if alone—slays a hundred thousand enemies. (285)
Now, the inquiry:
In the case of the question, if the Moon flows through the left channel, victory is declared with certainty;
if the Sun is in the right channel, one achieves victory with difficulty; and if there is a flow in both [channels], there is loss. (286)
If the vowels are uneven when the Sun [is predominant] and even when the Moon is spoken of, then victory is certain.

(287) Now, its application to the enjoyment of pleasure and so forth, which is dear to those who indulge in worldly life, is also described. When the watery element flows in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) of the woman and the fiery element flows in the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*) of the man, then, while sexual union is being performed, she melts like butter through contact with fire.
(288) As it has been said:

If, at the time of sexual union, the moon or the sun (dyumaṇi) flows from a woman or a man like fire, then she becomes a torrential stream of the water of passion for men; moreover, if she is empowered by the power of the peacock’s butter (śikhinavanītā), she acts like Śakti. Thus, the method of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa) is also described.

If, while she is asleep, one should inhale the moon situated in the channel of her own hot-rayed [sun] breath, then she will remain under his control until death; and she repeatedly drinks the sun’s channel along with the moon. (290) If a man, by means of his own right channel, inhales the breath flowing through the left channel of a woman lying upon her bed, then she becomes subject to him for as long as she lives. (291)

And thus, if a woman drinks the breath situated in the right nostril of a man through her own left nostril, then she brings her lover under her control for as long as she lives; this is the meaning. (292)

Therefore, whether one is a seeker of yoga or a seeker of worldly enjoyment, desiring liberation, heaven, sensual pleasures in this world and the next, omniscience, long life, strength, nourishment, excellence, and so forth, as well as health and other such capacities; or desiring stability of the mind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the rest; or being free from desire and seeking the knowledge of Brahman—one should, with focused attention and preceded by meditation on Maheśvara, fix the mind upon the vital breath when it has become steady and is joined with the downward breath (*apāna*) as it exits through the two nostrils and enters the interior of the body. Furthermore, the five elements should be examined according to the previously mentioned method of investigation. May there be auspiciousness! (293)
Thus ends the third instruction, titled "Instruction on the Body" (*śārīropadeśa*), in the work named *Yuktabhavadeva*, composed by Sanmiśra Śrī Bhavadeva, son of Sanmiśra Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva of Mithilā.
Om! Salutations to the lotus feet of the Guru.
The Fourth Instruction.

Now, the eight limbs of the King of Yoga, which is the nature of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) samādhi, are described. These consist of the forms of restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and conceptual samādhi (*savikalpaka-samādhi*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra]:

"From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the illumination of knowledge leading up to discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). Restraint, observance, posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and samādhi are the eight limbs. (YS 2.28–29)

Among these, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of malice toward all beings in every way and at all times. Regarding violence (*hiṃsā*), first of all: it is threefold—namely, that which is committed, caused to be committed, and approved. Furthermore, because it is motivated by greed, anger, and delusion, each of these is again threefold. Greed and the others are also threefold, according to whether they are mild, moderate, or intense. Thus, there are twenty-seven varieties. (3)

Furthermore, these [degrees] are threefold: mild-mild, medium-mild, and intense-mild; likewise, mild-medium, medium-medium, intense-medium, mild-intense, medium-intense, and intense-intense. Thus, there are eighty-one varieties. (4) When non-violence is firmly established, all living beings abandon hostility in his presence. Truth consists of speech and thought that accord with reality and are beneficial to others. When this is firmly established, his speech becomes unfailing. (5)

Theft (*steya*) is the unauthorized appropriation of another's property; non-theft (*asteya*) is its prohibition—this is the remainder [of the definition]. When non-theft is firmly established, there is the appearance of jewels. (6) Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the secret organ and the organs of generation. When celibacy is firmly established, there is the attainment of vigor (*vīrya*). (7) These *yamas*, however, when not limited by species, place, or time, constitute the great vow (*mahāvrata*) of universal sovereignty. For instance, the thought "I must not commit violence against a Brāhmaṇa or others" is limited by species (*jāti*); this applies to ordinary people. (8)

For the sovereigns among great yogis (*mahāyogisārvabhaumānām*), however, no injury whatsoever should ever be committed against anyone, anywhere, or at any time. This means that their vow of non-injury (*ahiṃsā-vrata*) is unconditioned by caste, place, or time. The same should be inferred for truthfulness and the other virtues. (9) As stated in the *Yājñavalkya-gītā*:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, and uprightness..."

Forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten *yamas*. (10) Among these, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is characterized by not inflicting suffering upon any living being at any time or in any way through thought, word, or deed; it is also the realization that the Self is omnipresent and that "He alone am I. (11) Truthfulness (*satya*) is generally speaking according to the facts; however, even speech that is not factual may be truth when intended for the protection of a Brahmin’s life or similar purposes. It is also the realization that the Supreme Brahman is the ultimate truth and nothing else. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the absence of desire for the property of others through thought, word, or deed. (112)
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the renunciation of unordained sexual intercourse. In the *Agnipurāṇa*: "The abandonment of sexual intercourse is celibacy, and it is eightfold:
recollection, verbal expression, dalliance, looking, secret conversation, intention, determination, and the actual accomplishment of the act. (13)
The wise declare this eightfold sexual conduct to be rooted in the practice of celibacy; otherwise, such action is fruitless. Or, celibacy consists in service to the teacher. 14.

Compassion (*dayā*) is the favoring of all living beings. Integrity (*ārjava*) is being of one and the same nature whether engaged in worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) or in renunciation (*nivṛtti*). Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is equanimity toward the pleasant and the unpleasant. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the stabilization of the mind in the face of loss of wealth, separation from kinsmen, and so forth. Moderation in food (*mitāhāra*) consists of eating wholesome food while abstaining from one-fourth of the stomach’s capacity.
As it is stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "One should consume very unctuous and sweet foods, having abandoned one-fourth [of the stomach's capacity]. (15)
That which is eaten for the sake of pleasing Śiva is called "moderate diet" (mitāhāra).

They declare that pungent, sour, bitter, salty, hot, green vegetables, *sauvīra* vinegar, oil, sesame, mustard, liquor, fish, goat meat, beef, curd, buttermilk, horse-gram (*kulattha*), jujube (*kola*), oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), garlic, and similar things are unwholesome (*apathya*).
Furthermore, a man should avoid food that has been reheated, is dry, or is unwholesome.
He should avoid the company of wicked people and the frequenting of fire, women, and roads.
He should abandon practices that cause physical distress, such as bathing at dawn or fasting. (18)
Gorakṣanātha says: "Oil, āmalaka, and mustard—these are the brothers of Time. As it is said in the Bhārata:

The consumption of oil-cakes, *rukṣa* (dry) substances, and the like has been prescribed for one seeking physical strength (*bala*). This is for the purpose of prohibiting the consumption of oily foods and the like that produce intense desire, which are contrary to the practice of *rājayoga*.

(19) However, in *haṭhayoga*, where physical strength is required for the various types of *prāṇāyāma*, *mūlabandhas*, and the collection of *mudrās* to be described hereafter—which serve as natural means for subduing desire and the like by ensuring the upward flow of vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*)—it should be understood that only moderate eating of nourishing, non-indigestible, and strengthening substances such as milk and clarified butter is recommended.
(20) And so it is said in the *Śivayoga*:
Wheat, rice, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, and other excellent grains; milk, ghee, sugar-candy, fresh butter, white sugar, and honey;
ginger, patola, fruits, and the five types of leafy vegetables such as mung beans; and divine water—these are the wholesome diet for the lords of sages.
All leafy vegetables are harmful to the eyes, except for these five specific vegetables which are beneficial for vision.
Jayantī, vāstuka, matsyākṣī, meghanāda, and punarnavā [are beneficial].
(22) A yogi should partake of food that is excellent, very sweet, unctuous, derived from cow products, nourishing to the bodily constituents, agreeable to the mind, and wholesome. (23)
Whether young, old, or very aged, diseased or even weak,
one who is untiring attains perfection in all yogas through practice.
Excessive eating, over-exertion, idle chatter, and rigidity in observances [are obstacles].
Association with people and fickleness— through these six, yoga is destroyed.
Through enthusiasm, daring, fortitude, knowledge of reality, resolve,
and the abandonment of association with people— through these six, yoga is perfected.

At the initial stage of practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended; once the practice has become firm, such strict adherence to rules is no longer required. And so forth. (27) Purity (*śauca*) is twofold: external purity is achieved through earth and water; internal purity consists of the knowledge of the self and the sacred sciences (*adhyātma-vidyā*). External and internal purity are both attained through the remembrance of Hari (*hari-smaraṇa*) and other such means. (28)
And thus says the Smṛti: "Whether impure or pure, even if one has reached every possible state, whoever remembers the Lotus-Eyed One becomes pure both externally and internally," and so forth. (29)

In compassion (*dayā*) and so forth as well, the attainment of being a source of sustenance for all beings and other qualities should be inferred by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) in accordance with the restraints (*yamās*).
Thus ends the fourth instruction on the restraints in the *Śrīyuktabhavadeva*. [End of] Yuktabhavadeva.
The fifth instruction: Now, regarding the observances (niyama) in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra]:

Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (*niyamas*). Purity (*śauca*) is external, produced by earth, water, and so forth, through the removal of impurities; internal purity is the cleansing of the impurities of the mind. From purity arises a sense of revulsion toward one's own body and a lack of association with others.
From contentment arise purity, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, fitness for the vision of the Self, and so forth.
(2) Contentment is the lack of desire for more than the means already at hand.

From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness. Penance consists of the *kṛcchra* and other such disciplines. From penance comes the purification of the body and the senses through the destruction of impurities. (3)
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the scriptures concerning liberation. Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of all actions to the Supreme Lord, the teacher of all.
(4) As it has been said:
"Whether lying on a bed, sitting, or walking on a path, one who is composed and whose web of discursive thoughts is exhausted [should practice]."

"Beholding the destruction of the seed of saṃsāra, one becomes eternally disciplined and an enjoyer of the enjoyment of immortality. (5) "From devotion to the Lord comes the realization of the inward-turned consciousness as well as the absence of obstacles; thus [is] the perfection of samādhi. So it is said.

But when the mind is inclined toward violence and the like, then one must cultivate the perception of fault in violence and the like, and the perception of merit in non-violence and the like, in accordance with the scriptures, worldly renown, and the instruction of the guru. By this means, the mind desists from violence and the like. As it is said in that very same work: "When there is obstruction by discursive thoughts (vitarka), one should cultivate the counter-measures (pratipakṣabhāvanā). The meaning is: the counter-measures consist in reflecting that discursive thoughts—such as violence, whether committed, caused to be committed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; whether mild, moderate, or intense—have suffering and ignorance as their ultimate fruits. 6.
In the *Yājñavalkyagītā*:
"Austerity, study of the Vedas, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation, and vows. (7)

These restraints (*niyamas*) have been described; all of them are to be observed individually. Among them: austerity (*tapas*) is the emaciation of the body through practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. Contentment (*santoṣa*) is satisfaction with whatever is obtained by chance. Faith (*āstikya*) is conviction in the treatises on Dharma. Charity (*dāna*) is the bestowing of wealth, food, and so forth—acquired by righteous means—upon those who ask for it. Worship of the Lord (*īśvarapūjana*) is the adoration of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others with a gracious disposition.
(8) It is stated in that very same [text]: "A heart free from passion and the like, and speech free from faults such as falsehood..."

Or alternatively: "That which is free from violence and the like should be performed; this is the worship of the Lord. (9) For the twice-born, it is the hearing of the Vedānta; for women and Śūdras, it is the hearing of the Purāṇas and the hearing of the Siddhānta. Modesty (*hrī*) regarding actions forbidden by the world or the Vedas; faith and resolve (*śraddhā-mati*) regarding those things enjoined by the Guru and the Vedas and so forth; and the practice of mantras through speech or mind is *japa*. (10) The undertaking of means for the sake of dharma or for the sake of self-realization is *vrata*. Here too, as before, the corresponding attainment (*siddhi*) should be inferred. (11)

This has been stated by the Blessed One in the Bhāgavata: Non-violence, truthfulness, faith, non-attachment, modesty, lack of accumulation, faith in the scriptures, celibacy, silence, steadfastness, forgiveness, and fearlessness. (12)
Purity, recitation, austerity, fire-offerings, faith, hospitality, worship of Me, pilgrimage to sacred fords, desire for the welfare of others, contentment, and service to the teacher— these,
along with the [eight] restraints (yamas), are both remembered as the twelve observances (niyamas). 13.
"O dear one, those who have taken refuge in men indeed milk them according to their own desires.

(14) One devoted to Me should constantly practice the restraints (*yama*), but occasionally employ the observances (*niyama*). Likewise, practices such as austerity (*tapas*) and fire-offerings (*homa*) should be performed when they are known to be conducive to yoga during the stage of practice; however, when they are known to cause distraction from yoga, they should not be performed.
(15) This has been stated in the *Gītā*:
"For one who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.

(Gītā 6.3) This is the summary: non-violence and the other [observances] must be practiced at all times. Regarding the various types of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) taught in many scriptures, even when there is some apparent contradiction between them, they ultimately resolve into no contradiction whatsoever, because their intended purpose is the understanding that both are to be performed. May there be auspiciousness! (17)
Thus ends the fifth instruction, titled "Instruction on Observances," as regulated by the illustrious Maithila Sanmiśra Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva.
The sixth instruction is "The Possessed Bhavadeva."
Now, as for the postures (āsanas):

since there are eighty-four lakh species of living beings, there are that many distinct postures. From among them, some which have been extracted by the Teacher of the World, the venerable Maheśvara, as being the most essential, are here written down. 1.

And these are fifteen types, distinguished as: 1. Svastika, 2. Gomukha, 3. Vīrāsana, 4. Padma, 5. Siṃhāsana, 6. Bhadra, 7. Muktāsana, 8. Mayūrāsana, 9. Kūrmāsana, 10. Kukkuṭāsana, 11. Uttānakūrmāsana, 12. Dhanurāsana, 13. Matsyendrapīṭha, 14. Śavāsana, and 15. Paścimatānāsana and so forth.
(2) Regarding this, the individual definition for each is stated in the *Yājñavalkya-gītā*:
"Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs..."
With the body straight and sitting comfortably, that is declared to be the *svastika* posture.
Having placed the ankles of the two feet on the sides of the perineum— specifically,
the right ankle on the left side of the perineum and the other (left) ankle on the right side— [one assumes this posture].

And this is declared to be the Svastika, which destroys all sins. Thus ends the Svastikāsana (4). One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right; it is like the face of a cow. Thus ends the Gomukhāsana (5).
One should bind the two thumbs with both hands in reverse order, O best of Brahmins, having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs;
this becomes the *padmāsana*, which is honored by all. Thus ends the description of *padmāsana*. (6)

Placing one foot upon one thigh and likewise the other thigh upon the other [foot], this is declared to be the *vīrāsana* (hero’s posture). Thus ends the description of the *vīrāsana*. Then, one should place both ankles below the scrotum on either side of the perineal seam (*sīvanī*).
With the right ankle over the left and likewise the other [left ankle] over the right,
having placed both hands upon the knees and extended the fingers,
one should gaze at the tip of the nose with an open mouth and a well-composed mind.

This is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), which is always honored by yogis. Thus ends the description of the lion-throne (9). One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineal seam;
then, having firmly bound the feet against the sides with the hands, one should remain perfectly motionless.

This Bhadrasana (Auspicious Posture) destroys all diseases and poisons. Thus ends Bhadrasana, number ten. Pressing the subtle seam [of the perineum] with the left ankle, and placing the right ankle over it, this is known as Muktāsana (the Liberated Posture).
This very posture is described as Siddhāsana in another text:
"Having placed the left ankle above the penis, and likewise having placed the other ankle upon that, this is Muktāsana. Thus ends Muktāsana. 12.
Firmly supporting the earth with the palms of both hands, one should place the elbows at the sides of the navel;
with the head and feet raised, one remains poised in the air like a staff. (13)
This is the Peacock Posture (Mayūrāsana), which destroys all sins. Thus ends the Mayūrāsana.
All internal diseases and poisons are destroyed [by it]. (14) —From the Haṭhapradīpikā.

Restraining the anus with the two ankles in reverse order, one who is composed—this is known as the tortoise posture (*kūrmāsana*), so the knowers of yoga understand. Thus ends the tortoise posture (15).
Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), one places the hands between the knees and the thighs.

Having placed [the hands] on the ground and established the *kukkuṭāsana* situated in the sky—thus is *kukkuṭāsana*. (16) Remaining in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture, having bound the neck with both arms, one lies face upward like a tortoise; this is *uttānakūrmaka*. Thus is *uttānakūrmāsana*. (17)

Holding both big toes with the hands up to the ears and drawing the bow, it is called the Bow Pose (dhanurāsana). Thus ends the Bow Pose. 18. Placing the right foot at the base of the left thigh and encircling the knee with the right arm [is the next pose].
Standing with the body turned back while holding [the arms], this is the glorious Matsyanātha-āsana.
(19) The Matsyendrapīṭha awakens the belly; it is a weapon that shatters the circle of fierce diseases.
It bestows the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī and steadiness of the staff-like body upon men who practice it. This is the Matsyendrapīṭhāsana. (20)
Lying on the ground face up like a corpse is the corpse posture (*śavāsana*). The corpse posture removes fatigue and brings rest to the mind. Thus ends the corpse posture (21).
Having stretched out the two feet on the ground like a staff and grasping the pair of feet with both arms—
Placing the forehead upon the knees, one should perform this; they call it *paścimatāna*. Elsewhere it is said:
"Thus, *paścimatāna* is the foremost of postures; it causes the breath to flow backward. This is the *paścimatāna* posture. (22)

In the *Pātañjala*, there are these aphorisms: "Now, the seat (āsana). Therein, the seat is that which is firm and pleasant. It is attained through relaxation of effort and meditative absorption on the infinite. Thereby, one is not afflicted by dualities. (Yoga Sūtras 2.46–48). The meaning of this is as follows:

That particular configuration of the body by which one is able to remain steady, comfortably, and for a long time is indeed *āsana*. And that [is achieved] through the cessation of effort. It bestows infinite happiness. It is accomplished through the concentration of the mind (*manodhāraṇā*). When that is perfected, there is no longer subjugation by the pairs of opposites, such as cold and heat. 24. Thus ends the sixth instruction, titled "Instruction on Posture" (*āsana*), in the *Yuktabhavadeva* composed by Bhavadeva, son of the illustrious Kṛṣṇadeva, who was associated with the people of Mithilā. *Yuktabhavadeva*.
The Seventh Instruction: Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma),
it has been described in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra]:

When that [posture] is established, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). It has the external, internal, or stationary modes of operation; it is observed by means of place, time, and number, and thus becomes long and subtle. The fourth [type] transcends the objects of the external and internal [breaths]. Thereby, the veil over the light [of consciousness] is destroyed, and the mind attains fitness for the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*). Thus [ends the first sūtra]. The meaning is as follows: when the posture is established, the drawing in of the external air is inhalation (*śvāsa*); the expulsion of the internal air is exhalation (*praśvāsa*). The cessation of their movement—the absence of both—is breath control. "It has," and so forth. (2)

Where there is an absence of movement preceded by exhalation, that is the external [breath]. Where there is an absence of movement preceded by inhalation, that is the internal [breath]. The third is the state of suspension (*stambha*), where both cease simultaneously through a single effort. (3) All three of these are observed by those who know the [measurements of] space and so forth: "The range of this breath is this much; its duration is this long; its count is this many," in terms of the first, second, and subsequent *udghātas* (expiratory impulses). (4) Thus, they are observed through soft, medium, and superior counts and so forth. When practiced in this way, it becomes long and subtle.

The third [type of prāṇāyāma] is the absence of movement preceded by the observation of the objects and locations of inhalation and exhalation; the fourth is that preceded by the observation of those same [objects]. This is the distinction. (5) For one thus practicing prāṇāyāma, the veil over the light—consisting of delusion, the net of illusion, evil karma, and so forth—is destroyed. As it has been said: "There is no austerity superior to prāṇāyāma; from it comes the purification of impurities and the like. (6) Therefore, the mind becomes stainless and fit for concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Śrī Gorakṣanātha, however—
When the breath moves, the drop moves; when it is still, the drop becomes still.
The yogi attains the state of a pillar; therefore, he should restrain the vital air.
As long as the wind is bound within the body, for that long the mind remains free from affliction.

As long as one has not seen [the light] between the eyebrows, from where could there be fear of death? (8) With little exertion and effort, those devoted to breath-control—yogins and sages alike—should practice the restraint of the vital breaths. (9)

The *haṃsa* moves thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) outward through the left and right channels; therefore, it is called *prāṇa*. When the entire network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), which is filled with impurities, attains purification, [the breath becomes pure]. 10.
At that very moment, the yogi becomes capable of restraining the vital breath.
Having assumed the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*), the yogi should fill the breath through the moon (the left nostril);
having retained it for as long as possible according to his capacity, he should then exhale through the sun (the right nostril). 11–12.

Having meditated upon the orb of the moon, which resembles flowing nectar and is like the white of cow’s milk, one who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma) shall become happy. Drawing the vital breath (prāṇa) through the sun [channel] and slowly filling the abdomen, one should perform the practice.
Having retained [the breath] according to the prescribed method, one should exhale again through the moon.
Having meditated upon the solar orb situated at the navel as a mass of blazing, flaming fire, the yogi who practices prāṇāyāma shall become happy. (14–15)
If one should drink the breath in limited measure through the iḍā and exhale more through the other,
then having drunk the air through the piṅgalā and retained it well, one should release it through the vāmā;
for those meditating upon the two orbs of the sun and moon according to this method—

The clusters of channels of those who practice self-restraint become purified after two months. From the purification of the channels, there arises the ability to retain the breath at will, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (*nāda*), and freedom from disease, and so forth. (16–17)

And this breath control (prāṇāyāma) consists of a triad of forms: inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). Among these, in the case of breath control performed with mantras, it should be done by the twice-born (dvijāti) with the syllable *oṃ* and so forth; however, by women and Śūdras, it should be performed with Puranic mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu, Śiva, or others. (18) This has been stated in the Yājñavalkya-gītā:
"The chanting (japa) during the restraint of breath for a Kṣatriya is said to be like that of the twice-born."

"O Gārgī, for Vaiśyas endowed with dharma, for women, Śūdras, and ascetics, the wise declare that at the time of restraining the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃyamana), there is a mantra devoid of the Praṇava, ending in 'namaḥ', or the Śiva-mantra, or the Vaiṣṇava-mantra. Thus [it is said]. (19–20)

In that regard, inhalation (*pūraka*) is [measured] by a certain duration; retention (*kumbhaka*) is four times that, and exhalation (*recaka*) is twice that. For example, one should perform them according to practice in this sequence: sixteen *oṃ* sounds for inhalation, sixty-four for retention, and thirty-two for exhalation, and so forth.
Gorakṣanātha, however, says:
"There should be ten *oṃ*s in inhalation and sixteen in retention."
Ten *oṃ* sounds during exhalation (*recaka*) are said to constitute one *prāṇāyāma*.

In reality, however, one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) slowly according to one's capacity. The standard rule is that one breath (*śvāsa*) is equal in duration to the pronunciation of ten long syllables (*gurvakṣara*). One should continue for as long as time exceeds that [standard measure].

Breathing for that long a duration brings about an increase in one's lifespan. Therefore, with every inhalation and exhalation, there is an increase in life. Likewise, during sexual exertion and similar activities, because the breath rises even during the time it takes to utter ten short syllables, there is a loss of life with every breath. (24) However, when the breath lasts for the same duration as the utterance of ten long syllables, there is neither an increase nor a decrease in life. It was stated previously that the lifespan is determined by years composed of such breaths. One should stabilize the *prāṇa* according to one's capacity or according to one's practice, but never by exceeding one's capacity or practice. (25)
And so Gorakṣanātha says:
"By the practice of prāṇāyāma performed correctly, there is the destruction of all diseases;
by the practice of yoga performed incorrectly, there is the arising of all passions. (26)
Hiccups, dyspnea, as well as cough, and pain in the head, ears, and eyes—various diseases such as these arise from the derangement of the wind (vāyu).
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger may be brought under control gradually and slowly. (27)
Otherwise, like a wind that is not properly cultivated, it destroys the practitioner.
One should exhale the breath when it is properly regulated, and one should fill [the lungs] when it is properly regulated;
one should likewise restrain [the breath] when it is properly regulated—in this way, one shall attain perfection.
Now, that same [author] states this sequence of the practice:

"The yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and having paid homage to the Guru and Śiva, with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and alone, should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma). (30)
Having drawn up the apāna wind, one should unite it with the prāṇa.
When raised upward by the śakti, one is liberated from all sins.
Having blocked the nine gates and having firmly retained the breath after inhaling it—

Having led [the breath] into space together with the fire of the apāna and impelled by the śakti, one who is endowed with meditation on the Self should, according to this method, certainly place it upon the crown of the head;
for as long as it remains there, he is praised by a multitude of great beings. (32)
"Thus, *prāṇāyāma* becomes the fire that consumes the fuel of sins;
it is always described by yogins as the great bridge across the ocean of worldly existence. Thus [ends the section on] Śivayoga. 33.
In a very beautiful hermitage, the yogi, assuming the lotus posture (padmāsana),
should sit upon his seat and practice breath control (pavanābhyāsa) during the morning,
at midday, at sunset, and at midnight. 34.
In this manner, one should perform twenty-one *jṛmbhakas* four times.
Regarding the *jṛmbhakas*, which are types of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
the wise do not practice them immediately after eating or when one is excessively hungry.
The practitioner should consume [food] in very small amounts many times a day;
he should perform the *jṛmbhaka* breath-retentions daily at the previously mentioned times.
Thereby, the yogin will attain power according to his desire in the retention of the vital air (*vāyu*).
When the wind can be retained at will, the Jṛmbhaka [power] is certainly accomplished.
Once the Jṛmbhaka is mastered, what cannot a yogin achieve here?
In the first, inferior stage of Jṛmbhaka, it arises within one's own body.
When perspiration arises, one should perform massage with it;
otherwise, the constituent element (dhātu) of the yogi is destroyed within the body.
During the middle stage of yawning, trembling occurs, and during the frog-like stage, leaping takes place.
Then, through even greater practice, the best of practitioners— the yogi— though remaining in the lotus posture, leaves the earth and ascends into the sky. At that time,
it should be known that the perfection of the vital winds has been attained, which destroys the delusions of saṃsāra.
For that duration, one should observe the restraints prescribed for yoga.
(42) Little sleep occurs, and excrement and urine are produced in small quantities;
freedom from dejection and freedom from disease belong to the yogi who perceives reality. (43)
Sweat, saliva, and worms do not arise at all;
nor do phlegm, bile, or wind [disturbances] exist within the body of the practitioner.
Then, through the power of practice, the yogi shall attain the siddhi of Bhūcarī (the Earth-walker). 44.
By the striking of the hand, death occurs for those creatures that are difficult to subdue.
(45) There are many obstacles here—terrible and hard to ward off;
nevertheless, the yogi should accomplish [the goal] even when his life-breaths have reached the throat.

"One should mutter the Praṇava long for the sake of pacifying obstacles," and so forth. (46) Therefore, the practice here, according to the consensus of all authorities, is as follows: One who is intent on performing the duties prescribed by the Guru—consisting of the desireless and optional rites according to one's own caste and stage of life; who is free from excessive attachment; and who is practicing yoga in a delightful place such as a penance grove, a temple, the bank of a river, or a mountain cave, which is adorned with fruits, roots, water, shade, and sunlight, and is devoid of all persistent calamities, wicked people, and the like. (47)

In a very beautiful monastery built by others or by oneself, on a soft seat covered with cloth, deerskin, and *kuśa* grass—neither too high nor too low—one should sit in the *padmāsana* or other postures. Having paid homage to the Guru, Gaṇeśa, Baṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and others, and having performed the stages of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth, during the three junctions (*sandhyā*) and at midnight, being neither overly hungry nor overly full, while contemplating the non-difference between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), one should practice *prāṇāyāma* with great attentiveness, discerning the movement of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and other vital breaths. (48–49)

In that context, when *prāṇāyāma* is performed with the *praṇava*, during the phases of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), there sequentially appear the Sandhyās of the East and other directions, who are the embodiments of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; whose names are Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī; whose essential forms are the vowels *a*, *u*, and *m*; whose colors are red, white, and black; who ride upon swans, Garuḍas, and bulls; who represent the stages of childhood, youth, and old age; and who hold a staff, a discus, a trident, and so forth—these being the meanings of the syllables *a* and the others. (50)

The three gods, the three worlds, the three states, the three Vedas, the three fires, and so forth—all these various manifestations of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) are to be meditated upon as being of a threefold nature. However, Brahman, which consists of consciousness and pervades all directions and times, expressed by the entire *praṇava*, is to be meditated upon as eternally present. (51) In this manner, when the breath is being led into the *iḍā* [left nostril], the moon is to be meditated upon; in the *piṅgalā* [right nostril], the sun; and in the *suṣumnā*, the fire whose form is Brahman. One should perform a massage of the limbs with sweat produced from exertion, mixed either with cow-dung ashes or alone. (52)

One should consume wholesome food and the like; avoid unwholesome things such as women, travel, and fatigue; and drink small amounts of milk and other liquids in various ways until the mastery of the vital air (*vāyu*) is achieved. When the vital air can be established wherever one wishes it to be at ease, then it should be known as conquered.

(53) In that regard, when the *prāṇa* and other airs are to be conquered, one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) by contracting [the body] into their respective locations, retention (*kumbhaka*) by holding it there, and exhalation (*recaka*) by expanding [the body]. One should also perform meditation on their respective forms and the recitation (*japa*) of their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*). (54)

In that regard, the locations of *prāṇa* are the tip of the nose, the heart, the navel, the big toes, and so forth; its color is green; its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *yaṃ*. Upon mastery of it, there arise intensity of the digestive fire, steadiness of breath, mastery over all the vital airs (*vāyu*), lightness of the body, and other such qualities. (55) The locations of *apāna* are the back of the neck, the spine, the anus, the heels, and so forth; its form is black; its seed-syllable is *aiṃ*. Upon mastery of it, there arise the healing of wounds and fractures, the kindling of the digestive fire, the reduction of fat, and the destruction of mental afflictions (*ādhi*). (56)

The locations of the *samāna* breath are the heart, the navel, all the joints, and so forth. Its form is white; its seed-syllable is *vaṃ*. Upon its mastery, the fruit is the same as that of mastering the *apāna*. 57. The locations of the *udāna* breath are the heart, the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, the crown of the head, and so forth. Its form is red; its seed-syllable is *raṃ*. Upon its mastery, one attains the desired departure [from the body] by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*). Furthermore, there is unimpeded movement through water, mud, thorns, and the like. 58.

The locations of *vyāna* are all the skin-surface (*tvak*). Its form is like that of a bow made of bamboo. Its seed-syllable is *laṃ*. Upon its mastery, there occurs invulnerability to cold, heat, and other such extremes, as well as luster and freedom from disease. (59) Thus, wherever pain arises in a limb, for the sake of pacifying it, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention) of the vital air (*prāṇa* and the others) by means of stability achieved through specific contractions of that particular limb. Thereby, its pacification occurs. In this manner, the air held in the big toe, calf, knee, thigh, anus, and penis leads to swift movement and strength. (60)

Likewise, when held at the navel, it serves to destroy fever and other ailments; at the stomach, for the purification of the body; at the heart, for the sake of knowledge; in the *kūrma* channel, for the cutting off of disease and old age; at the throat, for the destruction of hunger and thirst; at the tip of the tongue, nose, and so forth, for the perception of taste, smell, and the like; and at the crown of the head, for the attainment of supreme bliss—and so on. (61) This should be inferred by oneself from the previously mentioned Vedic statements, logical reasoning, and the instructions of the Guru. This meaning has been clarified in the *Yogaśāstrasāra*, which is rooted in the *Adhyātmopaniṣad*. (62) [The five vital airs are] Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna.
One who knows the locations, colors, seed-syllables (*bīja*), and functions [of the breath] should conquer [the vital energy] through *prāṇāyāmas*.

(63) "Functions" (*kriyā*) refer to the activities of the vital energies (*prāṇa*) and so forth, such as inhalation and exhalation. "Result" (*artha*) refers to the fruit of victory. The "seed-syllables" (*bīja*) are *yaṃ*, *aiṃ*, *vaṃ*, *roṃ*, and *loṃ*. The vital energy (*prāṇa*) moves from the tip of the nose to the heart, the navel, and finally to the big toe; it is green in color. Victory over it is achieved either through the practice of its coming and going, or by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
(64) Through the practice of its coming and going, [one should focus on] the heart, the navel, and the big toe.

Through the application of the nose and other locations, by repeatedly filling and emptying [the breath], there should be the practice of inhalation and exhalation; furthermore, from the *kumbhaka* (retention), there is *dhāraṇā* (fixation). The *apāna* wind is black in appearance and resides in the throat, the back, the end of the spine, and the heels.
Victory [is attained] through the yoga of one's own station by means of repeated exhaling and inhaling.
(66) I consider the back of the neck to be the two channels. The end of the back is the anus. The heels are the two posterior parts of the feet.
(67) The *samāna* wind is white; it resides in the heart, the navel, and all the joints.
By means of the yoga of one's own station, through repeated exhaling and inhaling, the *udāna*—
which is red and situated in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head—
should be brought under control by regulating its upward and downward movements. (68–69)
He describes the practice of going and coming:
"By means of the yoga of drawing [the breath] through the nose, one should establish it in the heart and other locations;
having forcibly drawn it up and repeatedly blocked the path, one should bring it under control. (70)
The Vyāna wind, which pervades the entire skin and resembles Indra’s bow (the rainbow),
is to be conquered through the practice of Kumbhaka by means of the sequence of contraction and expansion.
This applies to the winds Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna.
The seed-syllables *yaṃ*, *aiṃ*, *vaṃ*, *roṃ*, and *loṃ* should be meditated upon in their proper sequence.
When mastery over the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is attained, there arises intensity of the digestive fire, the conquest of long-drawn breaths and disease, and lightness of the body. (72–73)

The meaning is that the breath is long, uninterrupted, and steady. Because the *prāṇa* is primary, by its conquest, there is also the conquest of the other winds bound to it. (74) In the conquest of the *samāna* and *apāna*, there is the healing of wounds and fractures, the kindling of the digestive fire (*udarāgni*), a reduction of fat, and the destruction of diseases. (75)
Through the conquest of the udāna breath, there is the ability to ascend and the absence of obstruction by water, mud, and the like.
Through the conquest of the vyāna breath, there is non-attachment to cold and heat, as well as beauty and freedom from disease.
In whatever place a debilitating disease may arise, [one can overcome it]. 76.
To pacify that [distraction], one should always hold the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the other winds there.
Thus, having practiced for mastery over the prāṇa and the others,
one should constantly practice concentration (dhāraṇā) and the rest at every moment for the sake of steadying the mind.
He states the sequence of retention (dhāraṇā): Seated in the aforementioned posture, having slowly exhaled the breath, one should fill [the body] up to the big toes via the left channel (iḍā). (79)
First, having restrained the mind in the big toe, then in the sole of the foot;
then in the heel, the ankle, the calf, the knee, the thigh, and also in the anus;
[then] in the penis, the navel, the abdomen, and also in the heart, the throat, and the tongue. (80)
Then, upon the palate, the tip of the nose, the eyes, the eyebrows, the forehead, and finally the head— thus,
by means of the sequence of rays, while fixing it with the mind,
one should lead it from place to place until one brings it to the City of Brahmā.
Then, by that same process, he should gradually lead [the breath] down to the tips of the big toes.
Having led it as far as the navel-lotus, he should then exhale the air.
(83) Regarding the verse beginning with "nābhau": by that [process], the air, having filled all the channels through the openings of every channel situated at the navel, fills the entire body. (84)

When the breath is held sequentially at the big toe, the calf, the knee, the thigh, the anus, and the genitals, it leads to swift movement and strength. When held at the navel, it destroys fever and other ailments; when held in the abdomen, it purifies the body.
For the sake of knowledge, [one should place the mind] in the heart; for the destruction of disease and old age, in the *kūrma* channel;

for the destruction of hunger and thirst, in the throat; for the perception of taste, on the tip of the tongue; for the perception of smell, on the tip of the nose; for the perception of form, in the eyes—and so forth. (86–87)
In the *Yājñavalkyagītā*:
"For one performing *dhāraṇā* on the feet, all diseases born of wind (*vāta*) are destroyed.
For one who constantly performs *dhāraṇā* on the earth-element portion and the water-element portion [of the body], [all diseases born of wind are likewise destroyed]. (88)

Diseases born of phlegm (kapha) and those born of wind (vāta) likewise perish constantly for one who always performs concentration (dhāraṇā) on the portion of space and the portion of wind. All diseases produced by the three humors (tridoṣa) certainly perish.

"By the very restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), there is the pacification of those defects for human beings. (90) And this prāṇāyāma is of eight kinds. As it is stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*, after declaring that "the state of *unmanī* is characterized by the steadiness of the mind [which arises] from the steadiness of the vital air": (91)
To achieve that, those who know the methods perform various types of breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*).
Through the practice of diverse *kumbhakas*, one attains manifold accomplishments (*siddhi*).
These are: *sūryabheda*, *ujjāyī*, *sītkārī*, and likewise *śītalī*.

The Bhastrikā, Bhrāmarī, Mūrcchā, and Kevala are the eight types of Kumbhaka. At the end of the Pūraka, the Bandha known as Jālandhara should be performed; at the end of the Kumbhaka and at the beginning of the Recaka, the Uḍḍiyānaka should be performed.
By quickly contracting the lower body and constricting the throat,

and by applying a backward pull on the middle [of the body], the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the central channel. Having raised the downward-moving breath (apāna) upward, one should lead the vital breath down from the throat.

The yogi, liberated from old age, shall become sixteen years of age. (96) Because of the preeminence of *kumbhaka*, its specific varieties have been described; it should be understood that the varieties of *prāṇāyāma* are defined precisely by these divisions of *kumbhaka*. (97) Now, [the practice of] *sūryabhedana*:
Then, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) on a comfortable seat,
the yogi should slowly draw in the external air through the right channel (dakṣanāḍī),
from the hair to the tips of the nails, and retain it until the point of restraint (nirodha). 98.
Then, the wise practitioner should slowly exhale the breath through the left nostril.
This purifies the skull, destroys wind-related disorders, and removes the defects caused by worms.
This practice, known as Sūryabheda, should be performed again and again. (99–100)
Now, regarding *ujjāyī*:
having restrained the mouth and slowly drawn the breath through both nostrils, one fills it so that it reaches from the throat down to the heart. 101.
As before, one should retain the breaths and then exhale through the *iḍā*.
This removes phlegm and heat, increases the radiance of the digestive fire in the body, and wards off defects residing in the channels, the abdomen, and the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (102)
Whether walking or standing, this *kumbhaka* is called *ujjāyī*.
Now, as for *sītkārī*:
one should always produce the sound *sīt* with the mouth and perform a yawn through the nose.

Through such practice of yoga, one becomes a second Kāmadeva (the God of Desire), common to the circle of Yoginīs, and the agent of creation, maintenance, and destruction. Neither hunger nor thirst, neither sleep nor laziness arises. (104–105)
By this method, one shall truly become a lord of yogis upon the earth in the mandala, possessing a body that acts at will and free from all calamities.
This very thing was stated by Gorakṣanātha:
He who constantly drinks the *prāṇa* through the root of the palate by means of the tongue—
within half a year, all his diseases shall be destroyed. (107) Now, [the practice of] Śītalī:
Having drawn in the air through the tongue as before, and following the retention (kumbhaka), the wise practitioner should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils.
[This cures] disorders such as abdominal tumors and spleen disease, as well as fever, bile, hunger, and thirst. (108)
Furthermore, this kumbhaka named Śītali indeed destroys [fever and other ailments].
Now, the Bhastrikā:
one places both soles of the feet upon the thighs.
The lotus posture (padmāsana) is truly the destroyer of all sins.
Having properly assumed the lotus posture, with the neck and abdomen held straight, one should carefully close the mouth and exhale the breath through the nose. 110–111.
Just as it resonates within the heart, throat, and palate,
one should forcefully fill the breath slightly up to the heart-lotus (112).
Then one should exhale again in that same manner, filling it again and again.
Just as the bellows of smiths are moved with great force,
even so one should move the vital air (pavana) residing within one's own body by means of the intellect.
When fatigue arises in the body, then one should exhale through the solar channel (sūryanāḍī).
Just as the abdomen becomes full, one should hold [the breath] firmly in the middle of the nose with the two index fingers, excluding the thumbs, while remaining light like air.
Having performed the *kumbhaka* as before, one should exhale slowly through the *iḍā*.
It pacifies wind, bile, and phlegm; it increases the digestive fire of the body;
it awakens the Kuṇḍalinī; it destroys all defects, bestows happiness, and is auspicious;
it removes the obstructions of phlegm and other humors located within the opening of the Brahma-nāḍī. (116–117)
This kumbhaka known as *bhastrā* must specifically be performed for the purpose of piercing the three knots produced in the body correctly. (118) Now,
the *bhrāmarī*:
The *pūraka* [inhalation] has the resonance of a rushing stream, the *bhṛṅganāda* [humming] is the *recaka* [exhalation] very slowly;
through such practice of yoga, a certain play of bliss arises in the minds of the lords of yogis. (119) Now, regarding fainting (*mūrchā*)—

At the end of the inhalation (pūraka), having firmly applied the Jālandhara band, one should slowly exhale; this is called Mūrchhanā, which bestows the bliss of mental absorption (manomūrchā). With the belly filled by the internal wind set in motion from its base, [one should practice].
Even in the bottomless [ocean], one floats easily like a lotus leaf.
This very [practice] is also the floating *kumbhaka*. (121) Now, the *kevala* [kumbhaka]:

Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is said to be threefold, consisting of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka). Retention is considered to be of two kinds: combined (sahita) and pure (kevala). In the combined retention, after exhaling, inhalation should be performed slowly.
One should practice this combined method until the state of *kevala-siddhi* (absolute perfection) is attained.
That which consists of the retention of breath, having abandoned both exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), is called *prāṇāyāma*; it is indeed *kevala-kumbhaka* (the absolute retention).

When kevala kumbhaka, devoid of both exhalation and inhalation, is mastered, there is nothing in the three worlds that remains difficult for him to attain. One who is capable of retaining the breath at will through kevala kumbhaka [achieves all things].
One correctly attains the state of Rājayoga; there is no doubt in this.
Without Haṭha, Rājayoga does not succeed, and without Rājayoga, Haṭha does not succeed. Therefore, one should practice the pair until both are accomplished.
At the end of the exhalation of the breath, one should perform the retention (*kumbhita*) and make the mind free from affliction.
By practicing yoga in this manner, one shall attain the state of *rājayoga*.
From retention comes the awakening of the *kuṇḍalinī*, and from the awakening of the *kuṇḍalinī* [liberation] occurs.
The *suṣumnā* becomes unobstructed, and the perfection of *haṭha* arises.
(129) Leanness of the body, brightness in the face, the manifestation of the internal sound (*nāda*), and clarity of the eyes;
freedom from disease, mastery over the vital drops (*bindu*), stimulation of the digestive fire, and purification of the channels—these are the signs of the perfection of *haṭha*. (130)

Haṭhayoga is the means for stabilizing the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth through forceful exertion and persistence. It is said to be of eight types, consisting of the aforementioned and the following: the eightfold *prāṇāyāma*, the six *karmas*, and the ten *mudrās*.

(131) These specific forms of *prāṇāyāma*, such as *sūryabhedana* and others, should be properly understood through the instruction of a guru and practiced by those seeking various fruits according to their capacity. (132)

If, however, these [specific winds] cannot be distinguished, one should nevertheless bring the *prāṇa*—together with the external air—into the heart through the mouth or the nostrils; then, by contracting the lower passage and so forth, one should draw the *apāna* upward and retain it within as much as possible. One should place the tongue against the uvula (*tālughaṇṭikā*) or other upper locations, mutter the *praṇava*, and mentally perceive Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, pervading all directions and times. Then, one should exhale very slowly.

Again, as before, having filled [the body] through the upper and lower openings, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention). "One should practice especially during the three junctions of the day and at midnight"—this is the essence of the instruction.
Thus it was said by Sureśvarācārya:
"The contraction of the *apāna* and the restraint of the *prāṇa*."
"The placement of the tongue upon the uvula is the practice of yoga.
(134) Thus ends the instruction on the eightfold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) within the *Yuktabhavadeva* [treatise] on the instruction of breath control.
Now, the four stages of yoga are described:

As it has been stated in the *Śivayoga*: "The stages of yoga are fourfold: namely, the initial stage (*ārambha*), the stage of effort (*ghaṭa*), then the stage of mastery (*paricaya*), and finally the stage of perfection (*niṣpatti*). (135)

In that regard, when the purification of the *nāḍīs* has occurred through the previously mentioned fourfold *prāṇāyāma* and other practices, the stage of "commencement" (*ārambhāvasthā*) arises. Its characteristic marks are the fragrance of the body, its luster, and so forth. (136) Now follows the stage of "pot-like concentration" (*ghaṭāvasthā*):
the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the *nāda* and *bindu*, and the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
Because it functions by uniting [the breaths], it is indeed called *ghaṭa* (the pot).

One who is capable of holding the breath for the duration of a single watch (*yāma*) through practices such as *prāṇāyāma* attains the state of *ghaṭa*. In this state, there arise the mastery over the three worlds, the attainment of desired perfections, the perfection of speech, the power of moving at will, far-sightedness, far-hearing, subtle vision, the ability to enter another's body, the power to transform excrement and urine into ointments, the alchemy of gold (*svarṇasiddhi*), invisibility, and so forth.
When the supreme state of *ghaṭa* has been attained by the practitioner of breath-control...
Then, in this wheel of saṃsāra, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish. (139) Now, the stage of proficiency:
when the breath of the yogis becomes motionless at will.
Then, through practice, the state of familiarity (*paricayāvasthā*) arises for the yogin.

(140) In this state, the vital air (*vāyu*), having abandoned the sun and moon and become steady, takes hold of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), pierces the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), and moves within the void of the *suṣumnā*. Then, by means of that action, the yogin beholds the triple peak (*trikūṭa*) of karmas. (141)

And one should destroy that [karma] by means of the recitation of the *praṇava*, the manifestation of the body (*kāyavyūha*), the enjoyment of experiences, and so forth. Fixing the mind and the vital air (*pavana*) for five *ghaṭikās* at each of the cakras, beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, is *dhāraṇā*. One should practice that. When, in each respective place, one sequentially contemplates earth and the other elements, it brings about mastery over those particular elements.
(142) Furthermore:
"The wise person who thoroughly practices *dhāraṇā* upon the five elements..."
Even by the nectar of a hundred Brahmās, death does not exist for him.
(143) In this state, concealing his own power, he should remain like one who is mad; he should accomplish his own task through a secret process.
(144) Now, the stage of completion—
Then, through the very process of practice, the perfection of yogis shall come to be;
by which they, having severed the seeds of karma from time immemorial, may drink the nectar of immortality.

(145) In this state, there occurs samādhi at will, liberation while living, and the heroism of peace. Furthermore: "Having seized the consciousness, the vital air, and the power of action, [the yogi] becomes swift."
"Having swiftly conquered all the *cakras*, it dissolves into the power of gnosis (*jñānaśakti*).
(146) Thus ends the instruction on the four stages within the teaching on breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Now, if the practitioner becomes filled with phlegm, impurities, and the like, he should then perform the six actions (*ṣatkarma*). These have been described in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:"
One who is filled with fat, phlegm, and so forth should perform the six practices;
however, another whose humors are in equilibrium should not perform them.
These are *dhauti*, *basti*, *neti*, *trāṭaka*, and likewise *naulika*. (147)
These six practices are declared to be the "pot-illumination" (kapālabhāti).
This set of six practices, which is the cause for purifying the body, is always performed by yogis who bestow various extraordinary qualities; it must be kept secret. (148–149)
Now, regarding *dhauti*:
one should slowly swallow a wet cloth four fingers wide; then one should withdraw it. This washing [of the esophagus] is the practice of *dhauti*. (150)
Spleen disease, asthma, leprosy, and the twenty types of phlegm diseases—by the power of the *dhauti* practice, these surely vanish; there is no doubt. Now, the procedure for *basti*.
In water reaching up to the navel, with the nozzle inserted into the anus while seated in the utkaṭāsana posture, one should perform the contraction of the base (ādhāra);
that is the basti-karma (enema therapy), which cleanses [the system].
It also cures abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīhodara), and diseases arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha.

By the power of the enema treatment (bastikarma), all diseases are destroyed. When practiced regularly, the water enema (jalabastikarma) bestows luster upon the tissues, the senses, and the internal organs; it grants beauty and a radiant glow, and it eliminates the accumulation of all morbid humors (doṣas). (153–154)
This indeed is the *gajakaraṇī*. As it has been said:

"Expelling the substance within the abdomen while forcing the *apāna* wind up through the throat-pipe, whereby the path of the wind is brought under control through gradual practice—this is called *gajakaraṇī* by those who know *haṭha*. (155)
Now, regarding the practice of *neti*:
one should insert a well-lubricated thread measuring one *vitasti* into the nasal passage and draw it out through the mouth; this is called *neti* by the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (156)

It is indeed the purifier of the skull and the bestower of divine vision; it certainly conquers diseases arising above the collarbone and other ailments—this is most certain. (157) Now, the *trāṭaka* [practice]:

With steady gaze and composed mind, one should look at a well-defined object until tears fall; this is known as *trāṭaka* by the teachers. It is a crusher of all diseases and a shatterer of drowsiness and other such ailments. (158)
The Trāṭaka should be guarded with effort, like a casket of gold.

(159) And that steady gaze is of three kinds: Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Agocarī. Among these, that which is restrained from all other directions and gazes at the ground extending from the tip of the nose through the entire body down to the tips of the feet is Bhūcarī. (160)
