That which visualizes the space between the eyebrows or the orbs of the sun and moon is khecarī. That which gazes only at the tip of the nose or the region of the navel is agocarī, because it moves only slightly. It is like the expression "rice-gruel without salt. (161) Now, as for *nauli*:
with the force of a rapid whirling motion, one churns the abdomen from left to right.
Bending the shoulders, one should perform this *nauli*; it is praised by the masters of the Gauḍa tradition.

It always kindles a weak digestive fire, promotes digestion, provides nourishment, and bestows bliss. Indeed, this *nauli* is the pinnacle of Haṭha practices, for it dries up all defects and diseases. (162–163)
Now, Kapālabhāti:
When exhalation and inhalation are performed with great intensity using a bellows-like motion like that of blacksmiths, it is known as Kapālabhāti;
it dries up the defects of phlegm (kapha). (164)
Having eliminated grossness through the sixfold actions and transcended phlegm, fat, and impurities, one should then perform *prāṇāyāma*; it is accomplished without effort.
By means of *prāṇāyāmas* alone, all impurities are dried up.
However, some teachers do not approve of other practices [such as *trāṭaka*].

But *trāṭaka* and the like must be performed by everyone because they yield infinite fruit; the tradition holds that other [practices] possess those very defects. When *trāṭaka* is performed at the tip of the nose, the power of the breath-light (*niḥśvāsabhāsikā śakti*) arises. By means of this, the wind—characterized by its respective forms—is seen at the tip of the nose like the orb of the moon. And through that form, the principles (*tattvas*) such as space (*ākāśa*), appearing in smoky, green, red, white, and yellow colors, are discerned. Furthermore—

First, at the tip of the nose, it is seen in the shape of a peacock’s tail like a parasol; then, by the instruction of the Guru, that very [light] manifests in the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and so forth—this is the general direction [of the practice]. (168) Thus ends the instruction on prāṇāyāma and the instruction on the six acts (ṣaṭkarman).
Now, the ten mudrās are described:

In this regard, what has been stated in the *Śivayoga*, the *Gorakṣaśataka*, the *Haṭhapradīpikā*, and other works is written here in accordance with all [authoritative traditions]. (169) Among these, in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Just as the central pillar is the support for the earth, including its mountains and forests,"
Indeed, Kuṇḍalī is the foundation of all Yoga Tantras.
When Kuṇḍalī, who was asleep, awakens through the grace of the Guru, then all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced. (170–171)
The state of emptiness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the great cavity, the great path,
the cremation ground, *Śāmbhavī*, and the central path— these are synonyms.
Therefore, with every effort, one should awaken the Goddess.
One should practice the mudrās while sleeping at the opening of the Brahma-door (the mouth).
These are: Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvedha, Khecarī, Uḍḍiyāna, Mūlabandha, and likewise Jālandhara-bandha. (173–174)

Viparītakṛti, Vajrolī, and Śakticālana— this indeed is the tenfold collection of mudrās, the most excellent among mudrās, perfectly proclaimed by Ādinātha, and bestowing the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭaiśvarya). (175)
It is beloved even by all the lords of the Siddhas and difficult for even the gods (maruts) to attain.
It must be guarded with great effort as it destroys old age and death;
it should never be spoken of to anyone, just like the secret sexual union of a woman of noble family.
Therein, in the Mahāmudrā posture, one should press the vulva with the left foot,
extend the right leg, and hold [the body] firmly with both hands. 178.
Having placed the binding upon the throat, one should hold the breath upwards.
Just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff, so too the Kuṇḍalinī power suddenly becomes straightened. 179.
Then that state of death arises, resting upon two cloths (dvipaṭāśritā).
Thereafter, one should exhale very gradually indeed, and not with force.
This is truly the Mahāmudrā, as it is perceived by the great adepts (mahāsiddhas). (180–181)
The defects arising from the great afflictions, such as death and so forth, are worn away;
and the most excellent among the wise call that very state the Great Ocean (Mahāmudrā).
Having practiced with the lunar portion, one should then practice with the solar portion.
One should release the mudrā when the number has reached its equivalent.
In this state, whether wholesome or unwholesome, flavorful or flavorless,
even if terrible poison has been consumed, it is digested like nectar.
Consumption, leprosy, constipation, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and other such ailments—
these diseases of one who practices Mahāmudrā go to their destruction.
This Mahāmudrā, which brings about great accomplishment for men, has thus been described.
It must be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone.
(186) This is the meaning:

having pressed the region of the *yoni* located between the anus and the genitals with the root of the left foot, having extended the right leg, and having grasped the tips of the feet with both hands; having restrained the nine apertures and performed the *jālandhara-bandha*, characterized by the contraction of the throat and head; and having fixed the mind upon Brahman or the vital air (*vāyu*), one should draw the air upward and downward and hold it above the heart.

Thus, when the wind-retention (vāyudhāraṇā) is being performed, the agitated Kuṇḍalinī, together with the apāna and prāṇa breaths, comes to rest within both nostrils. Therefore, one should exhale very slowly in order to prevent their movement from becoming excessive. Then, as before, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to one's capacity.

Then, having pressed the region of the *yoni* with the right foot and holding the extended left foot with both hands, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) exactly as before—simultaneously and for the same number of times. In this way, it becomes the *Mahāmudrā*.
(189) Now, the *Mahābandha*: one should place the heel of the left foot at the location of the *yoni*.
Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh,
then having filled the breath, one should firmly press the chin [against the chest],
contract the perineum, and fix the mind in the center.
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, the wise person should exhale the wind;
there, he should raise the two "royal teeth" (the upper and lower lips) with the tongue.
This indeed is the Great Bond (Mahābandha), which bestows great spiritual accomplishments.
He is skilled in liberating one from the great bondage of the noose of Time (Kālapāśa).
Indeed, he awakens the upward movement of all the channels (nāḍīs);
he maintains the confluence of the three rivers (Triveṇī) and leads the mind to Kedāra. 193–194.

The meaning is this: after *mahāmudrā*, *mahābandha* is performed. Having left the foot that was placed at the site of the *yoni* during *mahāmudrā* exactly as it was, one places the other extended foot upon its thigh. Contracting the anus and the site of the *yoni*, one causes the *apāna* to move upward and the *prāṇa* to face downward; joining them with the *samāna*, one performs *kumbhaka* (retention) in the heart, abdomen, and so forth, and then exhales slowly. Just as before, one should perform an equal number of *prāṇāyāmas* on both the left and right sides. 195.

One should place the mind in the *suṣumnā* and also perform the contraction of the vessels of the throat; or else, one should lift the two *rājadanta* teeth at their root with the tongue—thus the *mahābandha* is accomplished. (196) Now, the *mahāvedha*:
"The *mahāmudrā* and *mahābandha* are fruitless when devoid of the *vedha*."

Just as a woman endowed with beauty and grace [is incomplete] without a man, so it is for the yogi. Established in the great bond (mahābandha), having performed the inhalation (pūraka) once, he should arrest the movement of the vital winds by means of the silent throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā). || 197–198 ||
Placing both hands on the ground, one should slowly strike the buttocks;
drawing up both shanks, the vital air (vāyu) quickly vibrates.
A connection between the moon, sun, and fire arises, leading to the attainment of nectar.
When the state of death has arisen, one should then expel the breath;
this is the "Great Piercing" (Mahāvedha), which, when practiced, bestows great accomplishment.
It destroys wrinkles, gray hair, and disease, and is cultivated by the most excellent practitioners.
Having pierced [the knots] with this piercing (*vedha*), that bull among yogis pierces the knots by means of the *suṣumṇā* path and reaches the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

This is the intended meaning: after the *mahābandha*, the *mahāvedha* is performed. By means of that, one who is established in the *mahābandha* unifies the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, fills the abdomen, obstructs the movement of the wind by constricting the throat and so forth, and places both hands upon the ground.
One should gently strike with the wind alone the fleshy region below the navel, characterized as the buttocks (*sphica*). In this way, the "Great Piercing" (*mahāvedha*) occurs.
(203) The three bonds (*bandhatraya*) are a great secret that destroys old age and death; they increase the digestive fire and bestow qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest. (204)
It is performed eight times, every watch and day after day—always accumulating a store of merit and shattering the flood of evil.
For those who possess the perfect training, this initial practice is thus quite brief. (205)
At the outset, one should practice the avoidance of fire, women, and travel on roads.
(206) Now, as for Khecarī:
the tongue is inserted into the hollow of the skull and turned backwards.
The gaze directed between the two eyebrows is the *khecarī* mudrā.
(207) This is the intended meaning:

having sat upon a comfortable seat and fixed the gaze firmly between the eyebrows, one should diligently join the tongue in a reversed position within the hollow of the throat known as the "well of nectar" (*sudhākūpa*), which is situated above the uvula; there, while meditating on Kuṇḍalinī—the embodiment of all deities—one should drink the nectar falling from the lunar orb with the tongue held in that very spot, accompanied by a hissing sound (*sasītkāra*). In this way, the *khecarī* mudrā is accomplished. (208)
If one remains for half a moment with the tongue turned backward,
the yogi is liberated in an instant from disease, death, old age, and the like.
For him there is no disease, no death, no sleep, and no thirst or hunger.
There shall be no fainting for him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā.
He is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma;
he is not constrained by time, for whomsoever possesses the Khecarī Mudrā. (210–211)
Since the mind moves in the void and since the tongue moves in the void,
this Khecarī Mudrā is saluted by all the Siddhas.
By whomsoever the opening above the uvula is sealed with Khecarī, [by him all is attained].
Not even a drop of his semen is lost when he is embraced by a passionate woman.
Having turned the *kalā* away from him, one should join it upon the path of the triple-way (*tripatha*).
That becomes the *khecarīmudrā*, and it is called the *vyomacakra*.
That wise knower of yoga who performs the drinking of soma with his tongue turned upward undoubtedly conquers death within half a month;
for that yogi, the body is perpetually filled with the digits of the moon.
"Even when bitten by Takṣaka, the poison does not spread within him.
Gorakṣanātha also said:
"That which has flowed from the sixteen-petaled lotus at the crown of the head and been forcibly obtained from the *prāṇa*..."
With the face turned upward and the tongue restrained, one should contemplate the supreme power (*parā śakti*) within the cavity.
That yogi who drinks the nectar-stream—the pure water consisting of the essence of its surging waves—lives supremely, free from defects, with a body as delicate as a lotus fiber. (217)
If the tongue, dripping with nectar, constantly kisses the tip of the uvula— whether it tastes like salt, pungent, sour, milk, honey, or clarified butter—
it effects the removal of diseases, crosses the waters of old age, and brings forth the realization of the scriptures.
For him there shall be immortality endowed with the eightfold supernatural powers, including the power of attracting celestial women.
There is but one seed-syllable consisting of creation, one mudrā which is Khecarī,
one God who is without support, and one state which is Manonmanī.
The wise declare that this mouth of rivers is like the hollow at the base of Mount Meru which enters into Pātāla;
from the moon, essence flows from its body, and by that, death comes to men.
One should perform that excellent practice, for otherwise there is no perfection of the body.
(220) By one desiring the perfection of Khecarī, the tongue must be made to grow through cutting, moving, and milking. (221) Now, the Uḍḍiyāna-bandha—from the Śivayoga:
One should perform this expansion intensely both above and below the navel;
for this is the Uḍḍiyāna Bandha, which destroys the flood of all suffering. The yogi who performs it daily, four times every day, [attains liberation].
The purification of that navel occurs by which the vital air (marut) becomes pure.
This is its meaning:

having firmly contracted the navel from both above and below, one should perform *kumbhaka* on the breath according to practice; this is *Uḍḍiyāna*. Having assumed a firm posture and placing the feet near the region of the ankles with both hands, while pressing the *kanda* located near the navel, one should apply a backward contraction (*paścimatāṇa*) in the abdomen such that the air does not enter the junction of the belly; thus the *Uḍḍiyāna-bandha* is accomplished, which destroys old age and death. (223–224)
Now, regarding the *mūlabandha*, it is said in that same [text]:
"Having firmly pressed the anal passage with the root of the foot and well-restrained, one should forcibly draw up the *apāna* and gradually lead it upward. (225)

This *mūlabandha* has been described as the destroyer of old age and death. It effects the union of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths, the cessation of urine and feces, and likewise the unification of the *bindu* and *nāda*. (226)

By the grace of this *bandha*, the yogi, having conquered the wind in the sky and remaining in the *padmāsana* posture, departs from the earth. (227) Having pressed the anus with the heel and repeatedly contracting it, one should draw the *apāna* upward; thus the *mūlabandha* is formed. (228)
Now, the Jālandhara-bandha:
Having bound the network of vessels in the throat, one should place the chin upon the heart.
This is declared to be the Jālandhara-bandha, difficult even for the gods to attain. (229)
For the water from the sky does not descend below once it has bound the network of vessels;
therefore, Jālandhara-bandha destroys the flood of ailments in the throat.
When Jālandhara-bandha, characterized by the contraction of the throat, is performed...
The nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the wind become agitated.
By means of this binding, the wise man drinks the nectar himself;
having attained immortality, he rejoices throughout the three worlds.

Having constricted the throat, one should place the chin upon the heart; thus the Jālandhara-bandha is formed. By this means, the nectar flowing from the moon does not fall into the fire-mandala situated at the navel, but instead spreads through the body via the tongue—this is the intended meaning. (233) Now, the Viparītakṛti:
placing one's head on the ground, one should lead both feet toward the sky.
This reversal of action is concealed in all tantras.
He who performs this constantly for even a single *yāma* through practice drinks the nectars and does not perish even at the time of universal dissolution. (234–235)
This very point was stated by Gorakṣanātha:
"The navel is above and the palate is below; the sun is above and the moon is below.
This practice called 'the reversal' (viparītakaraṇī) is understood through the mouth of the Guru. (236)

Having placed the two feet upward and the head upon the two hands below, one assumes this inverted posture (*viparītākṛti*). This should be practiced for a mere moment on the first day, for a slightly longer time on the second day, and so on, until it is maintained for the duration of a *yāma* (three hours). While this is being performed, the practitioner must ensure that ample food is provided; otherwise, the increased digestive fire (*jāṭharānala*) will consume the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Wrinkles and gray hair are no longer seen after six months and a half. He who practices this daily for even a single *yāma* becomes a conqueror of time (*kālajit*). (237–238)
Now, as for Vajrolī:
having attained the bliss of Brahman, it was taught by the Lord Gorakṣanātha for the sake of householders and renunciants who are still attached to the pleasure of sexual union.
(239) I shall describe Vajrolī, which has been kept secret by all yogis.
By which yogis, having abandoned the rules prescribed for yoga, attain perfection.
(240) In this matter, I consider two things difficult for anyone to obtain: first, milk; and second, a woman who remains under one's own control. (241)
Listen to the practice of Vajrolī; I shall speak of this supreme secret.
A woman attains happiness, and a man achieves perfection.
Having placed the beautiful woman in a secluded place, she should be left naked.
Having himself become naked, he should lie upon her as she lies on her back;
he should perform the *kumbhaka* breath-retention and the woman should exhale gently.
Firmly embracing her from behind—where there is no vulva—he should not insert the lingam into the vulva.
Therefore, one should then practice drinking from each other's lips;
and having embraced one another, they should continue until perspiration arises.
If the vital essence (vīrya) should slip outside, then one should rub it back in with the sweat.
If the seminal drop does not slip while embracing a passionate woman, one should insert the penis into the womb;
or, in such a way that the drop might fall externally, once it has fallen, one should rub the area thoroughly with perspiration-water. (246–247)
In this manner, one should practice for three days, performing it three times every day;
then, by means of the tongue-tube (*rasanāla*), the yogi should gradually perform the blowing (*phūtkāra*) for the purpose of circulating the vital air (*vāyu*), as much as his capacity allows. (248)
Then, at the time of sexual union, one should draw up the falling drop;
having pressed the vajra-kanda and restrained the vital breath (māruta),
one should draw back the moving drop and fix the mind right there.
Through such practice, the drop (bindu) never falls into the womb;
in this way, one whose self is united with yoga may even enjoy a passionate woman who has restrained her passions—hundreds of times, there is no doubt of this. (251)
Thus, when the *bindu* has become stable, one conquers death in every way.
Death results from the falling of the *bindu*; life comes from the retention of the *bindu*.
And only when it has thus become stable does one conquer death, not otherwise. (252–253)
If a woman should thus extract the semen through practice,
her body attains stability by means of the yoga of vajrolī practice. (254) I shall now describe the gradual sequence of practice for women, step by step.

If the semen located at the external penis should flow out due to the passage of time, one should contract the mouth of the *ṭiṇṭikā* and insert the *maṇi* there. One should then draw it back up by means of that very path using the vital air (*vāyu*). (255–256)
Then the semen (*retaḥ*) never goes to destruction.
And in the case of women, that drop (*binduḥ*) in the *mūlādhāra* attains the state of the *nāda*.

(257) This yoga succeeds for the meritorious, but certainly not for the envious. This is the intended meaning: in a windless pleasure-chamber, one should engage in dalliance with the beloved in various ways. (258)

One should forcibly draw up the falling drop by means of the *apāna* breath together with the sound "huṃ huṃ," pause for a short time, and then experience pleasure. When it can no longer be retained, one should rub the body with the sweat along with the drop that has slipped outside. (259) Having performed this three times each day for three days, one attains mastery over the *bindu*. A woman should likewise draw up her *rajas*; she should make her breath gentle, minimize the emission of semen, and perform the cool *kumbhaka* breath-retention. (260)
It is stated in the *Gorakṣaśataka* and in the *Śivasaṃhitā*:

"First, the wise man, having carefully and according to rule drawn up the menstrual blood from the woman's womb with effort, should cause it to enter his own body through the channel of the *liṅga*. (261)

Having awakened one's own *bindu*, one should begin the movement of the *liṅga*. If by chance it moves upward, it should be bound by the *yonimudrā*. Holding the *bindu* as it falls onto the left path, one should restrain the *liṅga*.
The yogi should know [this] through the guru’s instruction by means of the syllable *huṃ*.
Having forcibly contracted the *apāna* wind, he should draw up the *rajas*.
By this method, the yogi quickly attains the perfection of yoga. (263–264)
The yogi who worships the lotus feet of the guru consumes the essence of the cow (gavya).
The *bindu* should be known as consisting of the moon, and the *rajas* likewise as consisting of the sun.
One must effect the union of these two and cause them to enter one's own body.
When there is a union of me, the power of the drop (bindu) and the dust (rajas), then for yogins who possess the means of practice, a divine body arises.
Death occurs through the falling of the drop; life comes from the retention of the drop.
Therefore, one should perform this retention of the *bindu* with great effort.
In this world, one is born and dies by means of the *bindu*; there is no doubt about this.
Having understood this, the yogi should always practice the retention of the *bindu*.
When the *bindu* is mastered through great effort, what on this earth cannot be accomplished?
By the greatness of its grace, one attains similarity to me;
the *bindu* brings about the pleasure and pain of all beings as they exist. (269–270)

This yoga, which destroys old age and death for those wandering in saṃsāra who are deluded, brings happiness to yogins; it is the most excellent of all. Through practice, a human being attains perfection even while engaged in worldly enjoyments.
In time, even when the goal has been accomplished, success is attained upon the earth.
Having indeed enjoyed all pleasures without exception through this yoga, it is certain that by means of this, every accomplishment for yogis occurs with certainty. (272–273)
He who, at the time of voiding his own urine, forcibly draws it upward with the breath and then releases the urine little by little again,
and practices this daily according to the method instructed by the Guru— 274.
For him, the perfection of the *bindu* occurs, which bestows all perfections.
He who practices daily for six months according to the instruction of the Guru—his *bindu* does not perish even during sexual union with a hundred women. (275–276)
When his jewel-like *bindu* is perfected, what on this earth is not accomplished?
By its grace, even that which is difficult for me to attain becomes easy.
Even if the great *bindu* has moved, even when the fire has been reached. (277)
Bound by the *yonimudrā* and by means of the *śakti*, the *haṭha* ascends upward.
(278) The drop (*bindu*) flows in two ways: white and likewise red.
They call the white the semen (*śukra*) and the red the great dust (*mahārajas*). (279)
The *rajas* (dust), resembling liquid vermilion, is situated in the place of the sun;
the *bindu* (drop) is situated in the place of the moon. The unification of these two is very difficult to attain.
Śiva is the *bindu* and *rajas* is Śakti; the *bindu* is the moon and *rajas* is the sun.
Only through the union of both is the supreme state attained.
Driven by the wind through the movement of *śakti*, the great pollen reaches the state of oneness with the *bindu*; then the divine body comes into being. (281–282)
Semen joined with the moon and the menstrual flow united with the sun—
he who knows their state of equal flavor and oneness is a knower of Yoga.
(283) He by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by Khecarī.
Not even a drop of his semen is lost, even when he is embraced by a passionate woman.
This is the most secret of secrets; it has never occurred before, nor will it ever happen again.
Therefore, this must always be guarded with great effort by the wise.
Thus it is stated in the Śivasamhitā as part of the Śivaśataka.
Furthermore, in the Śivayoga:
"One should gradually discharge urine, drawing it upward again and again."
For one who practices daily according to the path taught by the Guru,
there shall arise the perfection of the *bindu*, which bestows all perfections.
By practicing this for six months, even when enjoying the company of a hundred women, there is no emission of the *bindu*.

Furthermore, at the time of voiding feces, one should press the vaginal region with the fingers; in this way, the retention of urine is to be practiced. Likewise, at the time of urinating, the retention of feces is to be performed gradually by contracting the anus.

(288) One should practice in this manner until both [functions] occur spontaneously according to their respective times for urine and feces. Even for one practicing this, the perfection of the *bindu* (seminal essence) occurs. This perfection of the *bindu* and so forth is intended only for the ignorant; however, for the wise, it is as stated in the *Gītā*:
(289) "The man who moves about, having abandoned all desires and being free from longing..."

Free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism, he attains peace. This, my dear, is the state of Brahman; having attained it, one is no longer deluded. Abiding even at the time of death in this state, one reaches the extinction of Brahman (brahmanirvāṇa).
Vajrolī itself, when possessing certain specific characteristics, becomes Amarolī and Sahajolī. Thus it is said in the Śivayoga:
"Sahajolī, Amarolī, and Vajrolī do not differ;
by whatever means possible, one should diligently retain the *bindu*. (292)
If, by chance, there occurs the union of the moon and the sun within the *bhaga*, this is called *amarolī*;
the yogi should dry it with the stalk and, having drawn up his own *bindu*, should bind it with the *yonimudrā*. (293)
This Sahajolī has been proclaimed as hidden in all the Tantras.
(294) There may be a difference due to a difference in terminology, but in its effect, the three modes of proceeding are equal. Thus, the upward leading of one's own *bindu* is Vajrolī.
The mantra of Vajrolī is: *ŪM JRĀM PHAṂ KRUṂ LLUṂ JAṂ JAḤ SVĀHĀ*. (295)

The upward movement of the *bindu* that has united with the blood in the *bhaga* is *amarolī*. The binding of the *bindu*, whether accompanied by blood or alone, within one's own body is *sahajolī*; such is the distinction.
(296) Now, regarding the activation of the *śakti* in the *Śivayoga*:
"One should awaken the firm *kuṇḍalī*, who is asleep in the *ādhāra*-lotus."
Drawing up the apāna wind and forcefully contracting [the anus],
the wise man who performs this "shaking of the śakti" daily will experience an increase in digestive fire and the destruction of diseases. (297–298)

Abandoning sleep, the female serpent (the *śakti*) shall indeed ascend quickly. For one who diligently performs the movement of the *śakti* according to the prescribed method for a period of two *muhūrtas*, spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) is not far off. (299)
Kuṭilāṅgī, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī, Śakti, Īśvarī, Kuṇḍalī, and the goddess Arundhatī—these words are synonyms.

(300) The drawing up of the apāna wind, the contraction of the anus, and the movement from the mūlādhāra constitute the "activation of the śakti" (śakticālana). This group of ten mudrās is extremely secret and generates manifold siddhis; it is certain that among these, the mastery of even a single one brings about perfection. (301)
Thus concludes the instruction on the ten mudrās.

This is the seventh instruction, titled "The Instruction on Prāṇāyāma with its Auxiliaries," in the *Yoganibandha* named *Yuktabhavadeva*, composed by Śrī Bhavadeva, son of Kṛṣṇadeva and a native of Mithilā.
The Eighth Instruction.
Now, withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
it consists of the drawing back of the senses from their respective objects.
As it is stated in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra]:

Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the drawing back of the senses from their respective objects, like darkness over the mind’s own nature when it is not in contact with its objects. From this follows the supreme mastery over the senses.

This is the meaning: withdrawal is the resting of the mind within itself, as if in the darkness of its own nature, when the eyes and other senses are no longer in contact with their respective objects. (1)

Because of that, through the mind's state of being devoid of activity, there occurs the cessation characterized by the non-perception of form and so forth; this is the conquest of the senses (*indriyajaya*). Regarding this, some say that the conquest of the senses is the absence of addiction to form and the other objects. Others say it is the application of the senses to those [objects] according to one's own will. Still others say that the conquest of the senses is the cognition of objects that is free from pleasure and pain, occurring when passion, hatred, and the like are absent. [This is achieved] through one-pointedness of consciousness (*citaikāgryāt*). 3.

Jaigīṣavya maintains that the non-perception of external objects is itself the conquest of the senses. It should be understood that this supreme subjugation of the senses arises from the cessation of the mind (*cittanirodha*). There are four types of this withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).

(4) Among them, one consists in the stabilization of the senses—while they are operating upon objects with the notion of being objects—by means of the notion of Brahman, wherever that notion of Brahman may be fixed.
(5) This has been stated by Gorakṣanātha:

The withdrawal of the senses, such as the eyes and so forth, from their respective objects in due order— that is called *pratyāhāra*. Just as the sun, situated at the third hour [of its course], withdraws its radiance.
The yogi situated in the third limb likewise [subdues] mental modification.
According to the view that yoga consists of six limbs beginning with posture (āsana), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) constitutes the third limb.
Just as a tortoise certainly withdraws its limbs among its members, [so does the yogi withdraw his mind].
In this way, the yogi withdraws the senses into the self.
Whatever—whether unpleasant or pleasant—the yogi skilled in yoga hears with his two ears, having realized that each of those is the self, he withdraws it [into the self]. 8–9.

Whether it be impure or pure, whatever the knower of yoga perceives with the eye, having realized that each is the Self, he withdraws [the mind from it]. Whether it be odorless or fragrant, whatever he smells with the nose...
Recognizing each of those as the Self, the knower of yoga withdraws them.
Whether it be the untouchable or the touchable, whatever he touches with his skin, recognizing each of those as the Self, the knower of yoga withdraws them. (11–12)
"Whether it be non-greed or greed, whatever [object] the tongue resorts to, the knower of yoga, recognizing that as the Self, withdraws [the senses] from it. And so forth.

(13) The second [type of renunciation], however, consists in performing with the mind those actions that ought to be done, even when they have been externally abandoned because they distract from yoga.
And so it is said in the Yājñavalkya-gītā:
"Those obligatory rites which are abandoned by embodied beings—
by performing them within the self through the mind, without external [rituals]," (14)
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is also an excellent means for the practice of yoga.
When practiced by yogis, that which is praised in pratyāhāra is as follows:

the third [type] consists of withdrawing the vital air from one location and holding it in another, starting from the big toe up to the crown of the head, across the eight vital points (*marmasthāna*). Thus is its nature. 15–16.
This too is stated in that very same [text]:
"The retention of the vital air within the eighteen vital points (marmasthāna) by drawing it from one place to another is called pratyāhāra. (17)
"O Gārgī, the Aśvins, the best of divine physicians, always declare the vital points (marmas) in the body for the sake of success in yoga and liberation.
I shall describe them all exactly as they are; listen, O lady of virtuous vows. (18)
The two big toes, the two ankles, and likewise the middle of the calves;
the base of the thighs, the two knees, and the middle of the two thighs;
the root of the anus, and then the middle of the body and the penis. (19–20)
O Gārgī, O bull among sages, [the points are] the navel, the heart, likewise the pit of the throat, the root of the palate,
the root of the nose and the mouth, the circles of the eyes, the space between the eyebrows,
the forehead, and the crown of the head.
These are the vital points (marmas), and their measurements are as follows:
from the big toe to the ankle is four and a half finger-breadths;
from the ankle to the middle of the calf should be known as ten finger-breadths.
From the base of the shank to the base of the altar (citi) is eleven finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
O lady of beautiful hips, from the base of the altar to the knee should be two finger-breadths.
The lords of sages say that the middle of the thigh from the knee is nine finger-breadths.
Likewise, O Gārgī, from the middle of the thighs to the root of the anus is nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From the root of the anus to the middle of the body is two and a half finger-breadths.
Likewise, from the middle of the body to the penis is likewise two and a half finger-breadths. (25–26)
From the genitals to the navel, O Gārgī, it should be known as ten and a half finger-breadths (daśāṅgula).
From the navel to the heart, O lady of beautiful countenance, it is fourteen finger-breadths.
And from the center of the heart, the pit of the throat is said to be six finger-breadths.
From the pit of the throat and from the root of the tongue, [the distance] is four finger-breadths;
the location of the eyes is held to be half a finger-breadth from that root.
Know that the space between the eyebrows of the self is half a finger-breadth from that.
From the forehead, that which is known as the ether is held at a distance of three finger-breadths.
Having mentally projected the vital air (*vāyu*) into these locations, one should maintain it there.
For one who performs *pratyāhāra* by drawing [the breath] back from each location to its source, [this practice is prescribed].
All diseases perish and enjoyments indeed succeed for him.

(31) The fourth [type], however, is as follows: having drawn the wind held in the *kumbhaka* from the head down to the big toe, sequentially from one place to another, its retention in different locations; such is its nature.
(32) This too is stated in that very same [text]:
Holding the breath with the intellect as prescribed in the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, one should draw the wind from the thumb through the center of the head like a full pitcher,
and then hold it again at the forehead, drawing it from the aperture of space (*vyomarandhra*).
O fair-faced one, having drawn the wind from the forehead, one should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa) between the eyebrows;
from between the eyebrows, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue;
having drawn it as far as the root of the tongue, one should block it in the hollow of the throat.
From the base of the throat to the center of the heart, from the heart to the navel region;
from the center of the navel again to the penis, and from the penis to the abode of fire (the anus);
then from the middle of the body to the anus, O Gārgī, and from the anus to the root of the thighs.
One should restrain it from the root of their thighs into the space between them; from there, from the knees into the base of the anus; likewise from there, from the middle of the calves;
from the calves into the base of the ankles; and from the ankles into the big toes of the feet.
The wise person who, having drawn [the breath] from place to place, should thus retain it,
becomes a soul purified of all sins and shall live as long as the moon and stars exist.
Having drawn the vital air through the two channels (nāḍīs), one should cast it into the sides of the Kuṇḍalinī.
If one should hold [the breath] simultaneously, one is also liberated from the disease of worldly existence.

(40) Thus, having drawn the vital air through both nostrils, one should hold it in the space of the heart, the abdomen, or between the eyebrows; this results in the pacification of all diseases, long life, the realization of Brahman, the destruction of sins, merit, the non-arising of suffering, and supreme bliss.
(41) Having fixed the breath of the self within the *suṣumnā* between the eyebrows...
"Perform restraint [of the breath] there as long as the mind remains dissolved.

(42) When the nectar flows from the lunar orb located at the *viśuddhi-cakra* and falls into the solar orb situated at the navel, one should first apply the *jālandhara-bandha* and then, by means of the *viparītākṛti-mudrā*, place the tongue at the root of the palate. Withdrawing [the senses] through the tip of the tongue, the retention of that [nectar] within one's own body is also indeed *pratyāhāra*. (43) As Gorakṣanātha has said:
The sun draws back the stream consisting of lunar nectar;
that drawing back of it is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).

Thus ends the eighth instruction, named "Instruction on Pratyāhāra," in the work titled *Yuktabhavadeva*, composed by Śrī Bhavadeva, the son of Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva, who was associated with the people of Mithilā. 8.
The Ninth Instruction by Yuktabhavadeva:
Now, on Dhāraṇā (Retention).
In the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra]: "Dhāraṇā (concentration) is the binding of the mind to a place.
This is the meaning:

1. For one whose mind is endowed with qualities such as self-restraint (*yama*) and the rest, the prolonged fixing of that mind—which is of the nature of consciousness and bliss—upon Brahman, within the great space of the heart-space through the unification of the two spaces, at a specific location such as the knees and so forth, is called *dhāraṇā*.

2. And that [concentration] is fivefold in the body. To explain: from the feet up to the knees is the region of Earth, accompanied by the seed-syllable *laṃ*. Having meditated there upon the Self as Brahmā, four-faced, the creator of the universe, together with his Śakti, and having fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) there along with the mind for five *ghaṭikās*, one conquers the Earth.

3. Thus, having meditated upon the region of water from the knees down to the anus as being endowed with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, and having visualized there Nārāyaṇa—white-complexioned, wearing yellow garments, four-armed, accompanied by Lakṣmī, and possessing a pure smile as one's own form—and having held the breath in the mind for five *ghaṭikās*, one conquers water.

4. Thus, [having meditated] from the anus up to the heart as the region of fire endowed with the seed-syllable *raṃ*, and having visualized there Rudra—three-eyed, serene, with ashes as body-unguent, and accompanied by Pārvatī—and having held the mind along with the breath there for five *ghaṭikās*, one conquers the fiery elements.

Thus, from the heart up to the space between the eyebrows is the locus of air, accompanied by the seed-syllable *yaṃ*. Having meditated upon Īśvara there—possessing all powers and having Māyā as His body—as one's own self, and having held the mind together with the vital breath for five *ghaṭikās*, one should conquer the air. By conquering the air, one conquers space, just like the air. 5.

From the midpoint between the eyebrows to the crown of the head is the locus of space (*ākāśa*), accompanied by the seed-syllable *haṃ*. Having meditated there upon Mahādeva, who is of the nature of space, five-faced, three-eyed, with ten arms raised with weapons, moon-crested, and having Umā as his half-body, and having held the mind along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for even a moment, one becomes liberated and conquers space. 6.

Thus there are five [stages]. Here, when the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) is to be performed within this *dhāraṇā*, one should dissolve the earth together with Brahmā and the others as previously described—water into water, fire into fire, air into air, space into space, and space into the Self, which is the Supreme Brahman, the bliss of consciousness—and then fix the mind, along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), upon that subtle element (*tanmātra*). (7) Furthermore, during emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), one should produce air from the element of space, fire from air, water from fire, and the earth of the aforementioned form from water; then, one should incessantly fill it with the nectar of the knowledge of Brahman. (8)

In the state of stability (*sthiti*), however, one should contemplate the earth and other elements exactly as they are, as being identical with the *ātman* which is Brahman, the presiding deity of each; as long as one contemplates them in this manner, once they have been so contemplated, they become subject to one's own control. Regarding this, some maintain that the location of the fire (*śikhisthāna*) is from the genitals up to the navel. [Verse 9] However, because the location of the fire within the body has been described as being between the anus and the penis in such passages as "the location of the fire in the middle of the body has the luster of molten gold," it is not thus. The venerable Yājñavalkya [says so].
[Verse 10] But Śrī Gorakṣanātha says:

He has stated that the heart, the throat, the root of the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) are the locations for the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) on earth and the other elements. (11) The Gurus maintain that all these positions are fruitful because of the primacy of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Furthermore, the previously mentioned results—such as "all diseases born of wind (*vāta*) perish when one performs *dhāraṇā* in the feet"—should also be understood here. (12) These meditative concentrations on earth and the other elements are named: 1. the Paralyzer (*stambhinī*), 2. the Dissolver (*drāviṇī*), 3. the Incinerator (*dahanī*), 4. the Confuser (*bhrāmiṇī*), and 5. the Desiccator (*śoṣiṇī*). (13)
And so Gorakṣanātha says:
"The paralyzing, the liquefying, the burning, the whirling, and likewise the drying—these are the five types of dhāraṇās for living beings. (14)
Through action, mind, and speech, the five dhāraṇās are difficult to attain.
Having constantly realized this, the yogi is liberated from all sufferings. 15.
Thus ends the ninth instruction, titled "The Instruction on Dhāraṇā," in the *Śrīyuktabhavadeva*. 9.
The tenth instruction by Yuktabhavadeva:
Now, meditation (dhyāna).
And that has been stated in the *Pātañjala*:

"Dhyāna is the one-pointedness of the mental modification (*pratyaya*) therein. In that place, the one-pointedness of the mental modification which takes the object of meditation as its support—a continuous flow of similar modifications untouched by other mental modifications—is called *dhyāna*.
1. Gorakṣanātha, however, says:
Indeed, in all forms of contemplation, only one root (the root *dhyai*) is taught;
for when thought occurs in a pure mind, that is declared to be meditation (*dhyāna*).
Meditation is of two kinds: with parts (*sakala*) and likewise without parts (*niṣkala*).
Through the dissolution of all distinctions of color, it becomes partless and devoid of qualities.
Having established a comfortable posture with the mind turned inward and the eyes directed downward,
and maintaining equilibrium of the body, meditation arises which bestows perfection.

Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single yoga of meditation. (5) The first wheel is the foundation; it has the luster of gold and possesses four petals.
Having meditated upon [the Self] as united with Kuṇḍalinī, one is liberated from sins.
(6) And in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which has six petals and a luster like a fine ruby, the yogi, fixing his gaze on the tip of the nose and meditating upon the Self, shall become happy. (7)
In this Maṇipūraka wheel, which resembles the rising sun,
one should meditate upon the Self with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and thus agitate the universe.
One should [meditate upon] Śambhu, who resides in the space of the heart, fierce and possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Fixing his gaze on the tip of the nose, the yogi becomes identical with Brahman.

(9) And by means of the piercing of the vital breaths within the heart-lotus, which has the brilliance of lightning, one who meditates on the Self while fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose becomes identical with Brahman. (10)
Constantly, within the throat-center (ghaṇṭikā), which is pure like the radiance of a lamp,
one who meditates upon the Self with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose is liberated from suffering.
[11] In the lunar orb of the uvula (lambikā), which is filled with flowing nectar, [one should likewise meditate].
By meditating on the Self with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one is released from death.
(12) The deity situated between the eyebrows resembles a smooth pearl;
by meditating on the Self with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one becomes filled with bliss. (13)
Meditating constantly on the Supreme Lord, who resembles a dark blue sapphire, between the eyebrows,
the yogi who has conquered his vital breaths shall attain Yoga.
He beholds Śiva, who is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa), peaceful, and facing all directions within the sky of consciousness.
Fixing one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditating upon the Self, one becomes composed of Brahman.
(15) Wherever there is sound in space, that is called the Ājñā-cakra;
having meditated upon Śiva as the Self there, the yogi shall attain knowledge. (16)

Having meditated upon the Self as stainless, having the form of the sky, resembling water in a mirage, and all-pervading, the yogi shall attain liberation. [17] The anus, the penis, the nose, the heart-lotus, and the lunar orb—
The uvula, the region of the lambikā, and the space between the eyebrows are the openings of the sky;
these have been described to you as the places of meditation for yogis.
By practicing them while joined with the reality of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), one brings about the arising of the eightfold qualities.

"Having known and meditated upon this unsurpassed, auspicious light, which is the splendor whose essence is Brahman, one shall be liberated; thus was it spoken by Gorakṣa. (20) In the *Yājñavalkyagītā*, meditation on both the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the qualified (*saguṇa*) is described:

Having understood individually the vital points (*marmasthāna*), the arrangement of the channels (*nāḍī*), and the locations and functions of the vital airs (*vāyu*), one should practice self-realization.
[One perceives] that which is one, consisting of light, pure, all-pervading, situated in space, and firm.
It is absolutely immovable, eternal, and devoid of beginning, middle, or end;
it is gross and subtle, formless, colorless, and without eyes;
it has no taste, nor is it rich in smell; it is immeasurable and free from ailment.
Blissful, undecaying, eternal, the cause of both the existent and the non-existent, the support of all, having the form of the universe, yet formless, unborn, and imperishable;
invisible yet visible, situated within and without, facing in every direction. 24.

Seeing all, with feet everywhere; touching all, with a head everywhere—(25) that realization which occurs, "I am Brahman, consisting of Brahman," the knowers of Brahman know this to be meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa). (26)
And he has described the qualified [Brahman] in many ways:
"Alternatively, having realized through the instruction of the Guru the Supreme Self— the Supreme Self, the imperishable Supreme Bliss, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny"— (27).
In this city that has become Brahman, within the center of the space called the "small" (dahara),
the virtuous perceive through practice the remedy for the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
[This occurs] in the heart-lotus, endowed with eight petals, which has arisen from the middle of the bulb (kanda).
In this [lotus] with a twelve-finger-long stalk and a four-finger-wide opening,
which has blossomed through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and possesses a pericarp adorned with filaments,
one should meditate upon Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, the unborn and all-pervading Lord.
Four-armed and of noble form, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
wearing a crown and armlets, with eyes like lotus petals;
the Lord of Śrī, with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and a face resembling the full moon. (31)
Having the luster of lotus and water-lily petals, serene and with a pure smile;
resembling pure crystal, clad in yellow garments, and infallible; with a pair of feet having the complexion of a lotus—the immutable Supreme Self. 32–33.

Having mentally beheld the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Person, who illumines his form on all sides with radiance and dwells within the hearts of all beings, the realization "I am that Self" is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna). 34.
Alternatively:
"In this lotus of the heart, which has the *prakṛti* as its pericarp, is endowed with the eight supernatural powers as its petals, and is joined with knowledge as its filaments... (35)
Upon the stalk of knowledge, with its great bulb awakened by *prāṇāyāma*,
[he perceives] the great fire Vaiśvānara— the source of the universe, blazing with universal radiance and facing in all directions,
the Lord whose crest is the [supreme] reality. (36)

Beholding his own body being heated from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head like a lamp in a windless place, he saw within the flame of that lamp-like sacrificial fire the imperishable name of the Supreme Self.

Resplendent like a streak of lightning in the midst of dark clouds, having the form of the awn of wild rice and yellowish in hue, one knows the divine Vaiśvānara as the cause of all; the realization that "I am He" is [the true knowledge]. (39)
For those who know meditation, this is known as the highest meditation among those with attributes (saguṇa).
Having attained the state of Vaiśvānara, one goes to liberation by that very means.
Alternatively, one may behold the orb of the high-souled Āditya.
[He saw] himself as the Person of the entire world, having the form of gold;
with golden beard and hair, and golden nails—Hari, seated upon his chariot, four-faced, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. (41–42)
Having seen him, the sole witness of the world, seated in the lotus posture, gentle, with a face like a blossomed lotus,
possessing the luster of the interior petals of a lotus, bestowing fearlessness upon all the worlds,
and illuminating the entire universe.
The realization that "I am that Self" is what is described as meditation (dhyāna). By means of this solar meditation, the wise shall go forth liberated.
O lady rich in austerity, this alone is the great path to liberation.
Alternatively:
One should perceive the inner self between the eyebrows as consisting of light, the cause of all things, risen from the middle of the body and reaching up to the crown of the head like a pillar. (46)
"Having perceived with the mind the unmanifest cause of the world, blazing and of immeasurable splendor, [thinking] 'I shall become that'— this is the supreme meditation.
Or else, sitting in the bound posture (paryaṅka) with the body relaxed.
Having become Śiva himself, with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose,
O fair-faced one, he should meditate between the eyebrows upon the supreme Self— the immutable, changeless, supremely peaceful, immortal, and effulgent form.

The cognition that "I am that Self" is what is called meditation (*dhyāna*). Alternatively, [it is performed] within the eight-petaled lotus of the heart, complete with a pericarp and filaments, fully blossomed and situated in the midst of the lunar orb. (50)
One's own self, appearing in the form of a child, imperishable and possessing the nature of an enjoyer, is surrounded by moonbeams emitting the essence of nectar;
it faces downward from the sixteen-petaled lotus of the head. 51–52.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon the Person being bathed on all sides by thousands of streams of nectar flowing forth,
[one should contemplate] that very essence of nectar within the body, including its limbs and minor parts. 53.
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman; I am the immutable Supreme Self.
(54) Such knowledge of That is called meditation with attributes (*saguṇa-dhyāna*).
By practicing this nectar of meditation, one shall become a conqueror of death within six months. (55)
Within a year, he shall indeed be liberated while still alive; of this there is no doubt.
For one who is liberated while living, the attainment of suffering never occurs in any way whatsoever.
How much more so for one who is eternally liberated—for such a person, liberation itself is as good as already attained. (56)

"Therefore, O beautiful lady, you too, having constantly abandoned the fruit [of action], should perform meditation alone according to the rules while performing your duties. (57) Thus it is said in the *Agnipurāṇa*.
The verbal root *dhyai* is traditionally understood in the sense of "thinking"; it is the repeated contemplation of Viṣṇu with an undistracted mind that is designated as *dhyāna*.
It occurs in whatever place the mind of one whose thoughts are fixed on the object of meditation may be situated.
This is declared to be dhyāna: the one-pointedness of the mind upon its object.
(59) Thus, he who, endowed with such dhyāna, should abandon his own body, having uplifted his family, kinsmen, and friends, shall become Hari. (60)
Even he who meditates upon Hari with faith for a mere moment or half a moment attains a destination that cannot be reached even by all the great sacrifices.
Such a person is endowed with knowledge and dispassion, possessed of faith, and filled with forgiveness.
A person who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and always full of enthusiasm is considered fit for meditation.
Indeed, the contemplation of Hari is the meditation upon the Supreme Brahman, both with and without form.
The omniscient and supreme Hari is to be meditated upon as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
The mastery of qualities such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest, as well as liberation, are the purposes of meditation.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, or even opening and closing one's eyes—
whether pure or impure— one should constantly meditate upon the Lord.
The sacrifice of meditation is supremely pure, devoid of all defects;
it is free from the fault of violence, perfectly refined, and established in its own means.
This supreme sacrifice of meditation is superior to all others, bestowing the fruit of liberation.
One should meditate in the heart upon the Lord as the syllable Om, pure and the size of a thumb,
having the form of a *kadamba* bud and appearing like a star.
Or [one may meditate on Him] with four arms and so forth.
Tired from meditation, one should recite the mantra; tired from recitation, one should meditate.
Viṣṇu quickly becomes pleased with one who is devoted to both recitation and meditation.
Indeed, other sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation.
Diseases, mental afflictions, and malevolent spirits do not approach the one who performs *japa*.
Through *japa*, every fruit—beginning with worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*)—is obtained.

(69) That which is to be recited begins with the syllable *Oṃ*. By means of both the power of its individual components and the power of their collective totality, it is the threefold deity consisting of Brahman and others—distinguished as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*—which is the very essence of consciousness and bliss existing throughout all space and time, the body of Brahman that is the soul of the universe. May there be auspiciousness! (70)
Thus ends the tenth instruction, titled "Instruction on Meditation," in the *Yuktabhavadeva*, a treatise on yoga composed by Śrī Bhavadeva, the son of the illustrious Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva.
The Eleventh Instruction: *Yuktabhavadeva* [continues].
Now, regarding *samādhi*:

even there, one [type] is to be grasped by the intellect. The subtle element (*tanmātra*), which has become the object of focus and is qualified by attributes such as a manifested jar and so forth, presents itself to the wisdom (*prajñā*) of *samādhi*.

(1) Furthermore, that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which occurs with respect to all things—whether past, present, or yet to be designated—which are unconditioned by specific attributes, which follow after all attributes, and which consist of the nature of all attributes, is called "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*). (2)
For when that [object] has become of such a nature—that is, when it becomes the support by means of this very nature—it masters the wisdom of meditative concentration (samādhi-prajñā).

(3) And wisdom is of such a nature; when wisdom becomes subtle, having become of that nature, and when it is as if empty of its own nature and appears as the object alone, then it is called "without deliberation" (nirvicārā).

(4) This is the summary of the meaning: regarding earth and the other elements, there are two types of attainment (samāpatti)—with deliberation (savitarkā) and without deliberation (nirvitarkā)—pertaining to the whole (avayavin) as it is well-known in the treatises through its grossness. (5)

[Objection: Since the object to be proven—the whole—is established by the collection of its parts alone, there arises a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the whole due to the contemplation of its non-existence; thus, both reasoning (*vitarka*) and the cessation of reasoning (*avitarka*) are possible. (6) [Reply:

This is not so, because among atoms, *tanmātras*, and so forth—which are established as the causes of wholes and are well-known in the scriptures for their subtlety—one perceives the specific characteristic of being the cause of a whole. Consequently, since a doubt regarding their existence cannot arise, reasoning is impossible. (7)

In the absence of *vitarka* (gross thought), there are two types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*): those accompanied by *vicāra* (subtle thought) and those free from *vicāra*. In that regard, even when *vitarka* is absent, *vicāra* is possible because one can still inquire, "What is the subtle form of what? (8).

Through yoga, whatever effect exists in its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) in a subtle state beforehand, becomes manifest in the interim through a gross state, and finally dissolves back into a subtle state. That which is the material cause of a thing is designated as its "subtle" form (9).

In this context, if one does not accept the existence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and triads (*tryaṇuka*), then the *trasareṇu* (the mote visible in a sunbeam) is the subtle [form] of the gross earth and so forth; however, if those are accepted, then the earthly atom (*paramāṇu*) and so on are the subtle [forms]. Furthermore, for the earthly atom, the subtle [form] consists primarily of the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), while the fourfold set beginning with the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) exists in a subordinate state. 10.

Thus, for a watery atom (*āpya-aṇu*), the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) is predominant while the triad beginning with the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) is subordinate; for a fiery atom (*taijasa-aṇu*), the subtle element of form is predominant while the dyad beginning with the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) is subordinate; for an airy atom (*vāyavīya-aṇu*), the subtle element of touch is predominant while even the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) is subordinate; and for ether (*ākāśa*), there is only the subtle element of sound. The ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the subtle [cause] of the subtle elements. (11) The Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) is also the subtle [cause] of the ego. The Great Principle is also the subtle [cause] of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). But in primordial nature, there is no attainment of further subtlety. This has been stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra]: [2.19] "The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is not preceded by anything else."
And the state of having a subtle object culminates in the signless (aliṅga).

[Sūtra 12] "Signless" means that which is not the sign (effect) of anything; this refers to primordial matter (prakṛti). If it is objected: "But since the Puruṣa is subtler even than primordial matter, how can the culmination of the excellence of subtlety reside in primordial matter alone? [Reply: True. However, the Puruṣa is not the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) of primordial matter. [Sūtra 13] They are non-distinct entities.

The subtle [state] of the entire universe, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahattattva*), is the Person (*puruṣa*) as distinguished from primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Therein also, there are two types of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*): that with deliberation (*savicārā*) and that without deliberation (*nirvicārā*). In this regard, although both [types] beginning with "with deliberation" are possible even in the gross [objects], [the first type] is not possible therein because of the absence of deliberation (*vicāra*). Likewise, both [types] beginning with "with reasoning" (*savitarkā*) are possible even in the subtle [objects], because various kinds of reasoning (*vitarka*) are possible there as well. (Sūtras 14–15)

Nevertheless, because the aforementioned reasoning and technical definition are dependent upon one's own will, and because the yogis have described them in that manner, the first two attainments (*samāpatti*) have gross objects, while the final two have subtle objects. This is the traditional teaching; such is the direction [of the argument].
(16) Now, the application of *samādhi*:

The yogi, disciplined by the observances (niyamas) characterized by various forms of purity, contentment, and devotion to the Lord, sits comfortably upon an easy seat such as a cloth mat and remains undisturbed. Having burned away the fuel of sin through breath control (prāṇāyāma), and having abandoned the excessive desires for pleasure, anger, and so forth by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) which brings mastery over the senses, he—through concentration (dhāraṇā)—steadfastly unifies the vital breath and the mind within the heart and other centers. Then, preceded by meditation upon the chosen deity mentioned previously, he attains [the goal]. 17.

First, having practiced the attainment accompanied by *vitarka* (gross reflection) when its object consists of gross elements and elemental products, one should then practice the attainment free from *vitarka* (*nirvitarkā*) upon the disappearance of *vitarka*. Next, one should practice the attainment accompanied by *vicāra* (subtle deliberation) when its object consists of subtle elements—characterized by the atoms, the five *tanmātras*, *ahaṃkāra*, *mahat-tattva*, and *pradhāna*—and free from *vicāra* when such [deliberation] is absent. Having thus practiced these two types of *samādhi* accompanied by *vitarka* and *vicāra*, one should practice the *samādhi* accompanied by that [subtler state] which has as its object the intellect (*buddhi*) itself, characterized by its own nature. 18.

Now, the intellect (*buddhi*)—which consists of transformations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) assuming the forms of various objects such as jars, which is by nature non-conscious due to its being composed of the three *guṇas*, which is visible and characterized by tendencies following the predominance of specific qualities like *sattva* and so forth—is distinct from that. The [Self] is its unchanging witness, devoid of the three *guṇas*, whose nature is consciousness, who undergoes no transformation, who is the witness of all, the enjoyer of all, the enjoyer of the intellect endowed with the eight attributes such as *dharma*, and who appears as if possessing action and other qualities, just as the intellect does.

Having taken as the object of the mind one's own self—which is determined as "I" and delimited by the reflection of that [external] cognition—and which is essentially bliss delimited by that [reflection], one should practice samādhi accompanied by that delimited bliss. 19.

Then again, having recollected the meaning of the great sayings (mahāvākyas) such as "That thou art," as taught through the lineage of gurus, [one realizes that] although it is one, it appears as mutually distinct within the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Indra, and other world-protectors (dikpālas), as well as within the sun and other celestial bodies—due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the various mental reflections—and just as space appears as many due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts such as jars, pots, villages, cities, and regions. ||20||

The Blessed One is the Self; this is to be meditated upon. Having set aside the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) characterized by the various reflections in the intellect, one should contemplate His nature as existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), all-pervading like space. This is the samādhi that follows uninterrupted bliss.

(21) And that Self abides within all things—earth, water, fire, the moon, stars, sun, wind, ether, the directions, lightning, thunder, all worlds, all Vedas, all sacrifices, all beings, and all vital breaths, speech, eyes, ears, mind, semen, bodies, and so forth—as the inner and outer controller. (22)

All these [elements] are indeed insentient; therefore, they do not know this [Self], that all these are its bodies, and that it is the immortal inner controller of all. And so says the Śruti: "He who dwells in all worlds, yet is internal to all worlds; whom all worlds do not know, whose body all worlds are, who from within controls all worlds—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," and so forth.
Also: "All this is indeed Brahman"; "Brahman alone is all this"; "The Self alone is all this," and so on. (23) And Gorakṣanātha says:
Thus, these two have been illustrated: the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and the reality (*tattva*).
Color is called the limiting adjunct, while the essence of reality is designated as the *ātman*.
The cognition of the limiting adjunct is one way, and the established state of reality is another.
Through constant practice, that which destroys all limiting adjuncts arises.
(25) As long as the subtle elements of sound and the rest remain within the ears and other sense organs, so long does meditation remain; beyond that, it becomes samādhi. (26)
Retention (*dhāraṇā*) occurs through five *nāḍīs*, meditation (*dhyāna*) through six *nāḍīs*,

and through twelve *ghaṭikās* of breath control (*prāṇasaṃyama*), there arises absorption (*samādhi*). That which is the unification of all dualities— the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)— is [this state].
That state in which all volitional thoughts have completely vanished is called samādhi. Just as water and salt become one through their union,
so too the unification of the self and the mind is designated as samādhi.
When the vital breath is completely attenuated and the mind dissolves,
and when there is a state of equal flavor— that is then called samādhi. Therein, one perceives neither smell, nor taste, nor touch, nor form, nor sound.
The yogi who is disciplined through meditative absorption knows neither self nor other.
(31) He is not devoured by time, nor is he afflicted by karma; the yogi who is disciplined through meditative absorption cannot be overcome by anyone. (32)
Impenetrable by all weapons, unslayable by any embodied being,
and ungraspable by mantras or yantras, the yogi remains absorbed in samādhi.
For one whose food and recreation are regulated, and whose exertion in actions is disciplined...
For one who is disciplined in sleep and awakening, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
Those who know reality know that reality to be without beginning or end, without support, free from conceptual proliferation, without dependence, free from affliction, and formless. (34–35)
The knowers of Brahman know it to be stainless, immovable, eternal, devoid of qualities, free from action, vast, like space, pure consciousness, and bliss— thus,
as fearless, supportless, foundationless, and free from ailment. (36)

The yogi, through the practice of yoga, merges into the supreme Brahman. Those who know reality recognize that reality as being free from causes and examples, beyond the reach of mind and intellect, the consciousness of space, and bliss. (37–38)
Just as when ghee is poured into ghee, it indeed becomes ghee;
and as milk into milk, so the yogi indeed becomes the Reality itself.
(39) Like milk into milk, like clarified butter into clarified butter, or like fire cast into fire.
The yogi who is absorbed in the supreme state indeed attains identity with it.
(40) As stated in the Agni Purāṇa: [He perceives] that which is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breaths, and ego.
The fourth state of Brahman is liberated from waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
it is the eternal reality, endowed with pure intellect, perpetual bliss, and immutable.
"I am Brahman, I am Brahman"—this is for the sake of liberation through supreme knowledge.
"I am Brahman, the Self"—this indeed is the supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that bestows liberation. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"Know this entire world to be thus one; there is no duality."
"The nature of the Supreme Self, whose designation is Vāsudeva"—
this was the speech of Ṛbhu to Niṣadha. (44) Likewise—
You and I are one and the same; Viṣṇu is the primordial Lord of all.
Just as the single sky appears divided by distinctions such as yellow or blue, so too is that one Self perceived as distinct and separate by those with deluded vision. (45)
Likewise, the word of the Blessed One is:
"All beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass are my manifestations; all those who are prosperous and powerful are known as my own portions."

"Knowing 'I alone am the one whose form is the universe,' one is liberated. (46) Indeed, through action, mind, and speech, and at all times and in all states, one should perceive with one's intellect the entire world— from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— as Viṣṇu.
A devotee of the Blessed One, a follower of the Lord, certainly attains perfection.
In the Bhagavad Gītā:
"I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains the immortal."
Brahman is without beginning and supreme; it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all. 48–49.
It manifests the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all senses; it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is without qualities and yet the experiencer of qualities;
it is both outside and inside of beings, and is both unmoving and moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; though situated afar, it is also near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings.
It should be known as the sustainer of beings, as well as their devourer and their progenitor.
That is said to be the light of even the lights, beyond darkness;
it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attained through knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
Some perceive the Self by means of the self within the self through meditation.
"Others [attain it] by the yoga of Sāṃkhya, and others by the yoga of action;
yet others, not knowing thus, worship having heard from them.
They too, being devoted to what they have heard, surely cross over death. Thus it is said in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
This body of His is a particular manifestation, the grossest among the gross;
within it is seen this entire universe—whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever currently exists.
Within this egg-like body, which is composed of seven coverings, [resides the Lord].
This Vairāja Puruṣa is the Blessed One who is the support of *dhāraṇā*.
They declare that Pātāla is the root of his feet; Rasātala is his heels and forefeet;
Mahātala is the two ankles of this Creator of the universe; and Talātala is indeed the shanks of the Puruṣa. (57–58)
O Lord of the Earth, they declare that His two knees are Sutala, His two thighs are Vitala and Atala, His hips are Mahītala,
and the expanse of the sky is His navel.
The host of luminaries is His chest, the day is His neck, and the Janaloka is indeed His mouth.
They know austerity to be the forehead of the Primal Person, and truth to be the heads of the thousand-headed one.
Indra and the other gods are said to be his arms; the suns are his hands, the quarters are his ears, and sound is his hearing.
The two Aśvins, Nāsatya and Dasra, are the nostrils of the Supreme; scent is his sense of smell, and the blazing fire is his mouth. (60–61)
The sky became his eye, and the sun became its pupil; both day and night became the eyelashes of Viṣṇu.
The expansion of his eyebrows was the abode of Parameṣṭhin (Brahmā); the waters were his palate, and taste itself was his tongue.
They declare that the Vedas are the head of the Infinite One; Yama is his tusks, and the digits of the moon are his teeth.
His laughter causes madness among people, and his release of water is a creation of endless consequence.
His upper lip is shame, while his lower lip is greed; righteousness is his breast, and the path of unrighteousness is his back.
What could be his penis and testicles? His two friends are the oceans, his belly is the mountains, and his collection of bones is the world. (63–64)
O King, the rivers are the channels of this Universal Being, and the trees are His body hairs;
the wind is His breath of infinite power, and the flow of actions and qualities is His movement and vitality.
O best of the Kurus, they know the clouds to be the hair of the Lord, while the twilight is the garment of Him who is the Infinite.
They say the heart and the mind are the unmanifest; that moon is the sheath of all transformations.
They declare the power of discernment to be the majesty of the inner organ of the Universal Self, O Giritra.
Horses, mules, camels, elephants, and wild beasts—all animals—are located in the region of the hips.
He is the seasons, that diverse grammar, the wisdom of Manu, and the refuge of humanity.
He is the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and Apsarases; he is the musical scales, the sacred traditions, and the foremost among the Asuras.
He is the face of the Brahmins, the arms of the Kṣatriyas, the great soul, and the dark-hued one who dwells within the thighs, the anus, and the private parts.
The ritual application of the sacrificial system consists of various types of worship, endowed with specific qualities and composed of material substances.
(69) Such is this configuration of the Lord’s form that has been described by me to you;
when one directs the mind toward this most massive body through one's own intelligence, there is nothing [else] to be attained. (70)
That Self, which has experienced all mental modifications, is one, just as the single person seen by those born in a dream;
one should worship that true treasure-house of bliss, for attachment elsewhere leads to the downfall of the self. Thus, and so forth. (71) The Blessed Lord said:
For the yogi who has conquered the senses, who is disciplined, who has mastered his breath,
and who fixes his mind upon Me, the supernatural powers (siddhis) manifest.
Seventeen such powers have been proclaimed by those who have reached the further shore of the yoga of concentration (dhāraṇā).
Of these, eight have me as their primary essence, while ten are indeed the causes of the qualities (guṇas). They are:

atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), form (mūrti), lightness (laghimā), attainment through the senses (prāpti), irresistible will (prākāmya), power over what is heard or seen (śrutadṛṣṭeṣu), the capacity for action (śakti), instigation (preraṇa), and lordship (īśitā).
Non-attachment to the qualities (guṇas) and mastery [over them], by which one attains whatever one desires—
these, O gentle one, are my eight innate perfections (siddhis).
[They include] freedom from distress in this body, as well as hearing and seeing from afar.
Speed equal to the mind, the ability to assume any form at will, entry into another's body, knowledge of the three times, freedom from duality, and supernormal knowledge of the minds of others;
the power to arrest fire, sun, water, poison, and the like, and invincibility. (76–77)
These perfections resulting from the practice of yoga have been declared by way of enumeration.
Learn from me, according to their nature, which perfection arises through which specific concentration.
One should fix the mind upon Me, who am the subtle essence of the elements, existing as the mere subtle element itself.
My devotee who worships the subtle elements (tanmātras) attains the power of atomization (aṇimā).
Placing the mind upon Me, the Great Self, according to their respective positions,
he attains the power of magnitude (mahimā) and [the knowledge of] all beings individually.
By concentrating the mind upon the atoms that constitute the elements,

the yogi who delights in them shall attain the power of minuteness (laghimā) through the realization of the subtle nature of time. One should fix the entire mind, along with its egoic and transformative functions, upon Me, the principle of the "I" (Ahaṃ-tattva).
One whose mind is fixed on Me attains the state of being the self of all the senses and achieves [union with] Me.
He who holds his mind upon Me— the Great Self, the Thread—
attains my sovereignty and the supreme status of Brahmā, even though he is born from a manifest womb.
One should fix the mind upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds, whose form is Time. He attains lordship and the impelling of the field and the knower of the field (kṣetra-kṣetrajña).
[This occurs] in Nārāyaṇa, who is called the Fourth (turīya) and designated by the term "Bhagavat."
By fixing [the mind] in the mind-made [body], the yogin attains mastery over my powers (maddharmavaśitā).
One should fix the clear mind upon me, the Brahman devoid of qualities;
there one attains supreme bliss, wherein all desire ceases.
