O Lord of Śvetadvīpa, the person who, free from the six waves [of affliction], maintains his mind fixed upon me—who am pure and composed of Dharma—attains whiteness. Carrying forth the resonance with the mind within the vital breath, which is of the nature of space, in me; 87.0. [Thus he attains liberation.]
There, having perceived it, he hears the speech of living beings as a *haṃsa*.
Having joined his eye with Tvaṣṭṛ and Tvaṣṭṛ with his eye, meditating upon me there with his mind, the one of subtle vision beholds the universe. (88–89)
Having well-yoked the mind to Me, and thereafter the body by means of that [mind],
the Self comes to abide where the mind is, through the power of meditation upon Me (maddhāraṇā).
When, having taken hold of the mind, one desires to become whatever form [one wishes], [that form one attains].
Assuming the form of various beings by relying on the power of my yoga,

Celestial women, whose conduct is virtuous, attend upon him in a celestial chariot.
Just as one might conceive with the intellect, or just as a person devoted to Me might do, so too they worship Me, yoking the mind to the Truth. Indeed,

His command shall not be thwarted by anything, just as mine is;
for that yogin of pure being who knows the method of concentration through devotion to me,
his intellect, encompassing the three periods of time, transcends birth and death.

While remaining indifferent toward the functions of the qualities of nature, one should fix the mind upon Me, the Supreme, who am pure consciousness; thus one is never overcome by the pairs of opposites.
[96] One should meditate on Me, the Self, dwelling in the hearts of all beings, the witness of all.
One should contemplate the mind as being one's own self and perceive it in others.
The yogic body of the sage cannot be harmed by fire or other such elements,
just as water does not wet the feet of one whose mind is weary from my yoga.
One who meditates upon my manifestations, adorned with the Śrīvatsa and weapons,
and [honored] with banners, parasols, and fans, shall become unconquered.
O Sage, for such a practitioner, I am thus attained through the practice of yoga.
All the accomplishments (siddhis) that have been described approach him in their entirety.

For the sage who has conquered his senses, who is self-controlled, who has mastered his breath, and who maintains concentration on me—what accomplishment would be difficult for him to attain? (100–101)
These are the obstacles for one engaged in the highest yoga who is attaining union with Me; they are the causes for the mere wasting away of time.
Whatever supernatural powers exist here through birth, herbs, austerities, or mantras—
One attains all of these through yoga; one cannot reach the state of yoga by other means.
All those perfections attend upon the mind of the yogi.
I alone am the cause, the lord, and the master of all perfections.
I am likewise the Yoga, the Sāṃkhya, and various forms of knowledge; I am within and without all beings, as well as myself. 105.
Herein, therefore, is the instruction in brief:

Whenever, wherever, and whatever specific accomplishment (*siddhi*) is desired, at that time and in that place, one should meditate upon the Lord as characterized by that particular accomplishment, and likewise meditate upon oneself as being of such a nature. Even the pleasure produced by various supernatural powers (*siddhis*) is indeed limited because it is constrained by space and time; therefore, having experienced that [pleasure] like a magical illusion out of curiosity and having abandoned attachment to it, one should fix the mind on Brahman alone, whose nature is pleasure unconditioned by space and time, so that there may be a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that pleasure at all times. (108) Thus, for the yogi who realizes that [Brahman] day and night, both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) remain present in every respect.
(109) For instance, Gorakṣanātha says:
This is the stairway to liberation; this is the deception of time:
that the mind, having turned away from worldly enjoyments, is attached to the Supreme Self.

(110) And this is appropriate, because scriptures such as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" establish that the direct realization of Him alone is the cause of both enjoyment and liberation. (111)

Furthermore, because the mind has been transformed by that [knowledge], there is even the possibility of deceiving time through the experience of suffering and so forth. Moreover, even acts such as giving performed out of ignorance do not produce results in that same way.
As it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:

Pressing the anus with the left ankle and likewise pressing the joint with the other [right ankle], placing the left hand upon the right hand on the right side, and fixing the eyes evenly upon the tip of the nose, the middle of the eyebrows, or [the space between them], one should, by means of the mind, behold the flame situated at the Mūlādhāra. 121.

Thus, for a yogi who practices with equanimity even for a single *muhūrta* during the morning, midday, twilight, and midnight, the fire—fed by the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) as it rises upward due to the closing of the anal passage—becomes a flame directed upwards within ten days alone.

Likewise, if the shadow-person is seen lacking shoulders, armpits, hands, palms, mouth, sides, or heart, the connection is that he lives for a number of years corresponding respectively to seven, ten, one, three, two, and [the remainder]; and if the shadow-person is seen without a head, the meaning is that he lives for six months. (137) By observing the cavity of the heart, he lives for as many months as there are sages (seven); however, by seeing two bodies, death occurs at that very moment.
They say it is true that when the full shadow-man (chāyānara) is seen, there is neither disease nor death within the year.

(138) If a hole is seen in the heart of the shadow-man, then the lifespan is limited to seven months; if two shadow-men are seen, then death occurs at that very moment. The meaning is that seeing the complete shadow-man implies no disease and no death within the year.
(139) He says something else as well:

If, after bathing, the ears and other parts dry first, the result is as previously stated. If the heart dries while the rest of the body remains moist, death occurs within six months. For a man who has merely completed his bath, if the ears and so forth—specifically the ears, shoulders, hands, face, sides, and heart—dry first, the result is as previously stated. He lives for twelve, seven, ten, one, three, or two years respectively. The meaning is that if the heart dries while the entire body remains moist, death occurs within six months. (140) He says something else as well: "If, when the hand is placed upon the head, no broken staff is seen [upon it]..."

Within six months there is no fear of death if [the breath] is placed upon the head in the *sampuṭa* position with both hands; and if that which resembles the bud of a plantain flower is seen within it, and if the penis does not sink into water, there is no death. 141.

If, when one's own hand is placed upon the head, a form resembling a plantain bud (*kadalī-koraka*) is not seen on the severed stalk, then there is no fear of death. Likewise, when the two hands are joined in a hollowed cup over the head, if that which resembles a plantain bud is seen within the space between those two forearms, then too there is no fear of death. Furthermore, if the penis floats in water, then also there is no fear of death. (142)

Thus, when one blocks the ears with the hands, that internal sound of the vital breath which is always heard by everyone—if it is not heard, or if suddenly an inversion of the natural state occurs, then too that danger should be recognized. 143.

In this very way, having anticipated untimely death from these or other causes, one who knows the supreme truth remains fearless, serene in soul, with senses conquered, devoted to his own duties, peaceful, and intent on the welfare of all beings; having duly instructed his sons and others in both worlds, he departs surrounded by those who know yoga. 144.

Being pure, having gone to a sacred field such as the banks of the Gaṅgā, and having spread upon the ground kuśa grass, a black antelope skin, and so forth, one should sit with legs bound in the paryañka posture, facing either east or north. Having duly performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the installation of vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), the nyāsa on the limbs, the nyāsa on the hands, the mātṛkā-nyāsa, the ṣoḍhā-nyāsa, and so on, along with their respective meditations, one should contemplate oneself as the ageless and immortal essence of the deity. Then, having prostrated to and worshipped the Guru, Gaṇeśa, Baṭuka, Bhairava, Kṣetrapāla, and the Yoginīs, one should worship the Lord who is free from all ailment.

Having meditated upon Vāsudeva, who is endowed with Śrī and consists of all things, and having beheld and worshipped Him, one should bestow land, gold, boons, fearlessness, divine medicines, elixirs, and the knowledge of Brahman upon the Brāhmaṇas and others. Then, having restrained the nine gates [of the body] through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and while the lotus of the heart has been awakened, one should contemplate Brahman—the cause of all, whose form is light, consisting of consciousness and bliss, of the nature of space, and possessing all powers—while reciting the single syllable "Om," encapsulated by the seed-syllable of Mṛtyuñjaya. || 145 ||

With the tongue turned upward and placed at the root of the palate, one should drink the nectar of the moon situated in the Viśuddhi-cakra while making a *sītkāra* sound; then, with a stream of nectar flowing from the lunar orb in the head, one should flood one’s own body. One should likewise perform both *savikalpaka* and *nirvikalpaka* samādhi within Brahman, whose nature is supreme bliss, in such a way that the mind does not reach any other object. For the yogin who thus practices samādhi upon the Supreme Lord, death does not bring about anything undesirable. (146) And so says Gorakṣanātha:

Having meditated upon oneself within the moon-maṇḍala of the hanging uvula, which is filled with flowing nectar, and fixing one's gaze on the tip of the nose, one escapes death. And by means of the various types of breath control (prāṇāyāma), [one perceives] the heart-lotus as having the brilliance of lightning.
With the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, having meditated upon the Self, one becomes composed of Brahman.

(148) As long as the sky-mudrā is maintained, as long as the mind is free from affliction, and as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows—for that long, whence can there be fear of death? (149)
As long as the vital air remains in the body, it does not abandon the body.
Death is its departure; therefore, one should restrain the vital air.
Such a person is not devoured by time, nor is he afflicted by karma. (150)
A yogi who is disciplined in samādhi cannot be overcome by anyone.
(151) A yogi who is disciplined in samādhi is impenetrable by all weapons, unslayable by any embodied beings, and ungraspable by mantras or yantras. (152)

This, however, should be noted: if the body is to be protected, then one should unify the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*), and having established them within the body—such as in the heart-lotus, the space between the eyebrows, the *viśuddhi-cakra*, the navel, or other centers—one should perform *samādhi*. (153)

If, however, the attainment of another body is desired, then one should practice *samādhi* within such a body. But if the attainment of another body is not desired, then, having withdrawn the five elements through the process of dissolution (*saṃhāra-krama*), and having led the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) through the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūra*, *anāhata*, *viśuddhi*, *ājñā*, and the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-cakra*), one should fix them in the pure Brahman, which consists of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*). Through that, union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*) occurs.
This is stated in the *Gītā*: [154]...
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga,
having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows, he attains that supreme, divine Person—
whom those who know the Vedas call the Imperishable, and into whom enter the ascetics free from passion. 155.
If they practice the life of celibacy desiring that goal, I shall declare to you that state in brief:
having restrained all the gates of the body, having confined the mind within the heart,
and fixing one's vital breath in the head, one remains established in the concentration of yoga.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering Me,
he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal.
(158) And likewise:

"Whatever state a mortal remembers when he leaves the body at the end, to that very state he goes, O son of Kuntī, being constantly permeated by that state," and so forth. (159) And thus, in the case of maintaining the body, if death is brought about prematurely during the practice of *samādhi*, a disciple or a friend should rub fresh butter (*navanīta*) into the practitioner’s *brahmarandhra* in order to remove the *samādhi*. (160)

By that, his awakening occurs and his tongue becomes turned downward; thus it has been stated by the lords of yogins, which should be heeded. I, however, have spoken only a portion for the sake of understanding the reality—may there be auspiciousness!
(161) In the year marked by five arrows, two yugas, and the moon [1525] of the Śaka king, having perceived this Lord who consists of the three worlds, I have beheld Him through my own intellect.
Bhavadeva, the son of Kṛṣṇadeva, has composed this commentary on the Yogaśāstra in the land of Mithilā by those who have accomplished their virtuous deeds.
Whatever is appropriate herein that has been stated, by this [work] Viṣṇu [is pleased]. 162.
May the Lord, the teacher of the three worlds, be forever pleased with me.
Now, if anything herein is improper, let the learned correct it all; for who is omniscient except for the illustrious Maheśvara? (163)

Thus ends the eleventh instruction, titled "Instruction on Samādhi," in the *Yoganibandha* named *Yuktabhavadeva*, composed by Mahāmahopādhyāya Bhavadeva—the elder brother of Śrī Baladeva, son of Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva, and grandson of the Maithila Sanmiśra.
May there be auspiciousness! May there be prosperity! May this be an offering to Śrī Rāmacandra! May this be an offering to Śrī Nṛsiṃha!
